passages.title: FL01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 1
text: Kinase KinA transfers a phosphoryl group from ATP to a negatively charged phosphorylated sugar, substrate S. Researchers measured initial velocity (v) at several concentrations of S in the absence and presence of 20 µM compound I, a small molecule whose structure resembles S. ATP was kept at a saturating concentration, and the enzyme concentration was identical in all assays. Results are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1.

In a separate experiment, a variant of KinA in which one active-site lysine was changed to alanine (K to A) bound S with markedly lower affinity than wild-type KinA. ATP binding and the maximum velocity measured at very high S were not noticeably altered by the substitution. Structural modeling indicated that the lysine side chain lies close to the carbon-6 phosphate group of S when S is bound.
The researchers concluded that compound I binds reversibly to the same site as S. They plan to use the inhibition constant (Ki) to compare compound I with related inhibitors.

qs.q: The data in Table 1 are most consistent with compound I acting as which type of inhibitor?
o: Noncompetitive, because the velocity is lower at every [S]
Not quite. Every inhibitor lowers velocity at each [S]. Noncompetitive inhibition also lowers Vₘₐₓ, and here the curves head to the same ceiling.
Uncompetitive, because both the apparent Kₘ and Vₘₐₓ decrease
Not quite. Uncompetitive inhibition lowers both Kₘ and Vₘₐₓ. In Table 1 apparent Kₘ goes up and Vₘₐₓ stays about the same.
Competitive, because Vₘₐₓ is unchanged while the apparent Kₘ increases
Correct: Vₘₐₓ stays near 100 µmol/min while the [S] for half-maximal velocity rises from 2 mM to about 6 mM.
Mixed, because the inhibitor binds both free enzyme and enzyme-substrate complex
Not quite. Mixed inhibition lowers Vₘₐₓ. The data show Vₘₐₓ unchanged, so this doesn't fit.
qs.x: Correct: Look at what happens to the two curves as [S] gets big. Without inhibitor, the velocity climbs toward a ceiling of about 100 µmol/min (the maximum velocity, Vₘₐₓ). With compound I, Table 1 shows 72.7 at 16 mM and the numbers are still climbing toward that same ceiling. Meanwhile the [S] needed to reach half of the ceiling (that's Kₘ) moves from 2 mM to about 6 mM. Same Vₘₐₓ, bigger apparent Kₘ: that's the signature of a competitive inhibitor, which fits the passage's claim that compound I sits in the same site as S. More substrate can crowd the inhibitor out, so the ceiling is still reachable. Why the others are wrong: noncompetitive and mixed inhibition both lower Vₘₐₓ, and Vₘₐₓ here doesn't drop; uncompetitive inhibition lowers both Kₘ and Vₘₐₓ, but Kₘ went up here. Trap: Seeing lower velocity at every [S] and deciding Vₘₐₓ fell. Every inhibitor lowers velocity at a given [S], so that alone tells you nothing.

qs.q: Using the data in Table 1, what is the approximate Ki of compound I?
o: 5 µM
Not quite. Ki = 5 µM would give 1 + 20/5 = 5 times the Kₘ. The table shows 6 mM ÷ 2 mM = 3.
20 µM
Not quite. Ki = 20 µM gives 1 + 20/20 = 2, so Kₘ would only double. The table shows it triples.
40 µM
Not quite. Ki = 40 µM gives 1 + 20/40 = 1.5 times the Kₘ. That is far less than the 3 seen.
10 µM
Correct: 6 mM = 2 mM × (1 + 20 µM/Ki), so 3 = 1 + 20/Ki, 20/Ki = 2, and Ki = 10 µM.
qs.x: Correct: For a competitive inhibitor, Kₘ,app = Kₘ(1 + [I]/Ki), where Kₘ,app is the apparent Kₘ with inhibitor, Kₘ is the normal one, [I] is the inhibitor concentration and Ki is the inhibition constant. Find Kₘ first. Vₘₐₓ is about 100 µmol/min (Table 1 climbs toward it), so half is 50 µmol/min. Without inhibitor, v = 50.0 at [S] = 2 mM, so Kₘ = 2 mM. With inhibitor, half of 100 is still 50, and the Michaelis-Menten equation v = Vₘₐₓ[S]/(Kₘ,app + [S]) fits the table when Kₘ,app = 6 mM (check [S] = 6 would give 100 × 6 ÷ 12 = 50; at 1 mM, 100 × 1 ÷ 7 = 14.3, matching the table). Values: Kₘ = 2 mM, Kₘ,app = 6 mM, [I] = 20 µM. Plug in: 6 = 2(1 + 20/Ki). Divide both sides by 2: 3 = 1 + 20/Ki. Subtract 1: 2 = 20/Ki. So Ki = 20 ÷ 2 = 10 µM. Why the others are wrong: 5 µM would make the ratio 1 + 4 = 5, not 3; 20 µM would make the ratio 1 + 1 = 2, doubling Kₘ instead of tripling it; 40 µM would give 1 + 0.5 = 1.5. Trap: Setting the Kₘ ratio equal to [I]/Ki and forgetting the 1 in (1 + [I]/Ki).

qs.q: Assuming the same Kₘ,app and Vₘₐₓ, what is the approximate velocity with compound I present at [S] = 60 mM?
o: 91 µmol/min
Correct: v = 100 × 60 ÷ (6 + 60) = 6000 ÷ 66, about 91 µmol/min. High [S] gets close to Vₘₐₓ but not all the way.
60 µmol/min
Not quite. 60 µmol/min is the velocity at about 9 mM [S] with the inhibitor. At 60 mM it is much higher.
75 µmol/min
Not quite. 75 µmol/min is what you'd see near 18 mM [S]. At 60 mM the velocity is higher.
100 µmol/min
Not quite. Velocity only approaches Vₘₐₓ and never reaches it at any finite [S].
qs.x: Correct: Use the Michaelis-Menten equation, v = Vₘₐₓ[S] ÷ (Kₘ,app + [S]). The values are Vₘₐₓ = 100 µmol/min (the ceiling the table heads toward), Kₘ,app = 6 mM (the apparent Kₘ with compound I), and [S] = 60 mM. Plug in: v = 100 × 60 ÷ (6 + 60). Top: 100 × 60 = 6000. Bottom: 6 + 60 = 66. So v = 6000 ÷ 66 = about 90.9, which rounds to 91 µmol/min. Lots of substrate crowds out a competitive inhibitor, so the velocity gets very close to Vₘₐₓ, just not all the way. Why the others are wrong: 60 µmol/min is the velocity when [S] is only about 9 mM (100 × 9 ÷ 15 = 60); 75 µmol/min fits [S] of about 18 mM (100 × 18 ÷ 24 = 75); 100 µmol/min would need infinite [S], since the velocity only approaches Vₘₐₓ. Trap: Thinking that a competitive inhibitor is completely overcome at high [S], so v equals Vₘₐₓ.

qs.q: How would a Lineweaver-Burk (double-reciprocal) plot of the inhibited data compare with the uninhibited data?
o: Same x-intercept, steeper slope, and a larger y-intercept on the double-reciprocal plot
Not quite. Same x-intercept with a different y-intercept describes noncompetitive inhibition, where Vₘₐₓ changes. Here Vₘₐₓ is unchanged.
Parallel lines, with a larger y-intercept and an x-intercept closer to the origin
Not quite. Parallel lines describe uncompetitive inhibition. This inhibitor changes the slope and keeps the y-intercept.
Same y-intercept, steeper slope, and an x-intercept closer to zero
Correct: 1/Vₘₐₓ is unchanged, the x-intercept moves from −0.5 to about −0.17 mM⁻¹, and the slope Kₘ/Vₘₐₓ rises.
Same slope as the uninhibited line and a smaller y-intercept, indicating a higher Vₘₐₓ
Not quite. A smaller y-intercept means a higher Vₘₐₓ, and the inhibitor doesn't raise Vₘₐₓ. The slope also changes.
qs.x: Correct: A Lineweaver-Burk plot graphs 1/v on the y-axis against 1/[S] on the x-axis, which turns the curve into a straight line. The y-intercept is 1/Vₘₐₓ, the x-intercept is −1/Kₘ, and the slope is Kₘ/Vₘₐₓ. For a competitive inhibitor, Vₘₐₓ doesn't change, so the y-intercept stays put. The apparent Kₘ goes up (2 mM to 6 mM), so the x-intercept moves from −1/2 = −0.5 mM⁻¹ to −1/6 = about −0.17 mM⁻¹. That is closer to zero. The slope Kₘ/Vₘₐₓ also grows, so the line is steeper. The two lines cross on the y-axis. Why the others are wrong: same x-intercept with a different y-intercept is how noncompetitive inhibition looks; parallel lines are uncompetitive inhibition; a smaller y-intercept would mean a bigger Vₘₐₓ, and the data show no such change. Trap: Mixing up which intercept moves for which inhibitor type. Competitive changes the x-intercept, noncompetitive changes the y-intercept.

qs.q: Which statement best explains why the K to A variant bound S poorly?
o: The lysine side chain normally forms a disulfide bond with S
Not quite. Disulfide bonds form between cysteines. Lysine has no sulfur, so it can't make one.
Lysine contributes a hydrophobic surface that buries the sugar ring of S
Not quite. Lysine is long and charged, not hydrophobic. The key point is its charge pairing with the phosphate on S.
The protonated lysine side chain normally forms an ionic interaction with the negatively charged phosphate of S
Correct: At physiological pH, lysine's amine is positively charged and forms a salt bridge with S's phosphate. Alanine is nonpolar and can't.
Lysine normally forms a covalent bond with the phosphate of ATP
Not quite. ATP binding was unaffected by the change, so lysine isn't forming a bond with ATP's phosphate.
qs.x: Correct: Passage paragraph 1 says S is a negatively charged phosphorylated sugar, and paragraph 2 says the lysine sits close to the phosphate group of S. At body pH (about 7.4), the amine on a lysine side chain picks up an extra hydrogen and carries a positive charge. A positive charge next to a negative phosphate makes an ionic bond, also called a salt bridge. Alanine has only a small nonpolar methyl side chain, so it can't do this, and S binds more weakly. ATP binding was not changed, so the lysine isn't doing a job for ATP. Why the others are wrong: a disulfide bond forms between two cysteine side chains, and lysine has no sulfur; lysine's long side chain is charged, not hydrophobic, so it can't be there to bury a sugar ring; a covalent bond to ATP's phosphate would affect ATP binding, which paragraph 2 says stayed normal. Trap: Picking a hydrophobic or covalent explanation and ignoring the charge on lysine at physiological pH.

passages.title: FL01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 2
text: MicroRNAs are approximately 22-nucleotide RNAs that regulate gene expression after transcription. Researchers studied miR-X, which has partial complementarity to a seven-nucleotide site in the 3' untranslated region (3' UTR) of the mRNA for gene G.

Cultured cells were treated in one of three ways: (1) a synthetic miR-X mimic was introduced; (2) an anti-miR-X oligonucleotide, which is perfectly complementary to miR-X and sequesters it, was introduced; or (3) cells expressing a version of gene G with the miR-X binding site in the 3' UTR mutated were given the miR-X mimic. After 48 hours, mRNA for G was measured by reverse transcription followed by quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR), and protein G was measured by Western blot. Both measurements were normalized to control genes and then expressed relative to untreated cells, which were set to 1.00. Results are shown in Table 1.
The researchers noted that the miR-X mimic had no effect on the abundance of the mRNA for an unrelated gene lacking the binding site.

qs.q: Which mechanism best explains the effect of the miR-X mimic on gene G?
o: miR-X binds the promoter of gene G in the nucleus and prevents RNA polymerase II from initiating transcription
Not quite. MicroRNAs work after transcription by pairing with mRNA. A promoter effect also wouldn't depend on a 3' UTR site.
miR-X enters the nucleus and base-pairs with the pre-mRNA of gene G, blocking splicing of its exons before export
Not quite. The tested site is in the 3' UTR, which isn't involved in splicing. Mutating that site removed the effect.
miR-X binds protein G after translation and tags it with ubiquitin, targeting it for degradation by the proteasome in the cytosol
Not quite. miR-X is an RNA and base-pairs with RNA. It doesn't bind or ubiquitinate protein.
miR-X, within a silencing complex, base-pairs imperfectly with the 3' UTR to reduce translation and promote mRNA decay
Correct: Both mRNA and protein fell (protein more), as expected when a microRNA pairs partly with the 3' UTR and represses translation and speeds decay.
qs.x: Correct: Table 1 shows the miR-X mimic dropped mRNA of G to 0.45 and protein to 0.20. Protein fell more than mRNA, which tells you both things happened: some mRNA was destroyed and the remaining mRNA was translated less. That's how microRNAs work. Inside a silencing complex, the microRNA pairs imperfectly with a site in the 3' UTR (the stretch of mRNA after the coding part), which blocks translation and speeds up mRNA breakdown. Passage paragraph 2 also shows that mutating the site wipes out the effect. Why the others are wrong: microRNAs act on RNA after transcription, not on promoter DNA, and a promoter effect wouldn't depend on a 3' UTR site; splicing doesn't involve the 3' UTR site, and the effect vanished when the site was mutated; miR-X is an RNA and pairs with RNA, so it doesn't tag a protein with ubiquitin. Trap: Choosing a transcription mechanism because mRNA went down, while ignoring that the effect needed a particular 3' UTR sequence.

qs.q: What is the most valid conclusion from the mutated-site condition?
o: The mimic cannot enter cells expressing the mutated gene, so no repression is seen
Not quite. The same mimic was given and nothing in Table 1 tests cell entry. The simplest reading is that the binding site is needed.
miR-X reduces expression of all genes equally, regardless of sequence match
Not quite. Paragraph 3 says an unrelated gene without the site was unaffected, so repression depends on the sequence match.
Repression of G by the mimic depends on the miR-X site in the 3' UTR
Correct: Mutating only the site erased the mimic's effect (0.98 and 0.95 versus 0.45 and 0.20), so repression depends on that site.
Translation of G does not require the 3' UTR, so the mutation is irrelevant
Not quite. The experiment tests one binding site, not whether the 3' UTR is needed for translation in general.
qs.x: Correct: Compare the last row of Table 1 to the mimic row. With the miR-X site mutated, the mimic leaves mRNA at 0.98 and protein at 0.95, basically no change from 1.00. With the normal site, the same mimic gave 0.45 and 0.20. The only thing changed was the binding site, so the effect depends on that site in the 3' UTR. Why the others are wrong: the same mimic was given in both conditions and nothing in the table tests uptake, so a cell-entry claim is unsupported; paragraph 3 says an unrelated gene lacking the site was unaffected, so miR-X doesn't hit all genes equally; the experiment tests one binding site, not whether the 3' UTR as a whole is needed for translation. Trap: Stretching one result into a broad claim the data never tested.

qs.q: The anti-miR-X condition increased protein G to 1.50. This result suggests that:
o: endogenous miR-X normally represses gene G in these cells
Correct: Sequestering miR-X relieved repression, so protein G rose above the untreated level. Cells already make miR-X.
gene G is not a target of miR-X, so anti-miR-X should have no effect
Not quite. If G weren't a target, removing miR-X would change nothing. Protein G rose to 1.50.
miR-X increases transcription of gene G through its promoter in these cells
Not quite. The mimic lowered G, so miR-X represses rather than activates. Adding anti-miR-X wouldn't raise it by that route.
anti-miR-X is translated into additional protein G in these cells
Not quite. Anti-miR-X is an oligonucleotide complementary to miR-X. It has no sequence from G and isn't translated into protein G.
qs.x: Correct: The anti-miR-X oligonucleotide grabs miR-X and ties it up. If protein G goes up to 1.50 (compared with 1.00 in untreated cells), then something was holding protein G down before, and removing it let protein G rise. That something is the cell's own miR-X, so the cells already make miR-X and it normally represses gene G. Why the others are wrong: if G weren't a target of miR-X, taking miR-X away would change nothing, but protein rose by half; the mimic lowered G, so miR-X isn't a transcriptional activator; anti-miR-X is just a short piece of nucleic acid complementary to miR-X and has no sequence from G, so it can't be turned into protein G. Trap: Assuming untreated cells have no miR-X, so an inhibitor of it can't have any effect.

qs.q: Using Table 1, by approximately what percent did the miR-X mimic reduce protein produced per mRNA molecule?
o: Not quite. 0.20 is the relative protein level, not a per-mRNA value. It also leaves out the fall in mRNA.
Correct: 0.20 ÷ 0.45 = about 0.44 of baseline per mRNA, so the drop is 1.00 − 0.44 = 0.56, or 56%.
Not quite. 44% is how much remains per mRNA. The question asks how much it fell.
Not quite. 80% is the total protein drop (1.00 − 0.20). It ignores that mRNA fell too.
qs.x: Correct: Protein per mRNA molecule = relative protein ÷ relative mRNA. Values from Table 1 for the mimic row: relative protein = 0.20 and relative mRNA = 0.45. The untreated ratio is 1.00 ÷ 1.00 = 1.00. Plug in: 0.20 ÷ 0.45 = 0.444, or about 0.44 of baseline. A drop from 1.00 to 0.44 is 1.00 − 0.44 = 0.56, which is 56%. So each mRNA molecule made about 56% less protein. This makes sense: protein fell more than mRNA did, because translation was also repressed. Why the others are wrong: 20% is just the leftover protein level and ignores the mRNA; 44% is the fraction that remains, not the amount of reduction; 80% is the total protein drop (1.00 − 0.20) and doesn't adjust for mRNA that was lost. Trap: Using the protein number alone, or giving the fraction that remains when the question asks for the drop.

qs.q: Why must RNA be converted to complementary DNA before the qPCR step used to measure mRNA of gene G?
o: The DNA polymerase used in PCR requires a DNA template
Correct: The DNA polymerase in PCR needs a DNA template, so reverse transcriptase first makes cDNA from the mRNA.
Introns must be removed from mRNA before amplification
Not quite. Mature mRNA is already spliced in the cell. Removing introns isn't the reason for making cDNA.
The 5' cap must be added to mRNA for primers to bind
Not quite. A 5' cap isn't needed for primers to bind cDNA, and reverse transcription doesn't add one.
The mRNA must be degraded to remove genomic DNA contamination
Not quite. Reverse transcription copies RNA into DNA. It doesn't degrade the mRNA or remove genomic DNA.
qs.x: Correct: PCR copies DNA. The DNA polymerase used in PCR needs a DNA template and can't copy RNA. So the first step, reverse transcription, uses the enzyme reverse transcriptase to build a complementary DNA (cDNA) copy from the mRNA. Then the heat-stable DNA polymerase amplifies that cDNA, and the amount of product tells you how much mRNA of gene G started out. Why the others are wrong: mature mRNA has already been spliced in the nucleus, so introns are already gone; the 5' cap has nothing to do with primers annealing to cDNA; reverse transcription makes cDNA and doesn't break down the mRNA or remove genomic DNA. Trap: Thinking reverse transcription does RNA processing like splicing, when all it does is copy RNA into DNA.

passages.title: FL01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 3
text: A rare autosomal recessive metabolic disorder results from homozygosity for a loss-of-function allele (a) of a single gene. Heterozygous carriers (Aa) are healthy. Public health researchers genotyped random samples from two geographic regions and counted affected individuals (genotype aa). Results are shown in Table 1.

For analysis, the researchers assumed that each region was in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for this gene, with p representing the frequency of the dominant allele (A) and q representing the frequency of allele a. They also assumed that affected individuals were identified without error and that the allele has no effect on survival before reproduction in either region.

In follow-up interviews, the researchers learned that marriage between relatives is more common in Region B than in Region A. They plan to compare observed genotype frequencies with Hardy-Weinberg expectations in a larger study. Both regions have similar age distributions, and migration between the regions is negligible, so differences in allele frequency are attributed to local population history.

qs.q: What is the frequency of allele a in Region A?
o: Not quite. 0.0004 is q², the fraction of people who are aa. You still need the square root.
Correct: q² = 4 ÷ 10,000 = 0.0004, and the square root is q = 0.02.
Not quite. 0.04 is q for Region B (16 affected), not Region A (4 affected).
Not quite. q = 0.20 would give q² = 0.04, which is 400 affected per 10,000, far above the 4 seen.
qs.x: Correct: Hardy-Weinberg says genotype frequencies are p² (AA), 2pq (Aa) and q² (aa), where q is the frequency of allele a. Affected people are aa, so q² = affected individuals ÷ people genotyped. Values for Region A from Table 1: 4 affected, 10,000 genotyped. Plug in: q² = 4 ÷ 10,000 = 0.0004. To get q, take the square root: the square root of 4 is 2, and the square root of 10,000 is 100, so q = 2 ÷ 100 = 0.02. Why the others are wrong: 0.0004 is q², the share of people who are affected, not the allele frequency; 0.04 is the Region B answer (16 ÷ 10,000 = 0.0016, square root 0.04); 0.20 would give q² = 0.04, which is 100 times too big. Trap: Stopping at q² and calling it the allele frequency without taking the square root.

qs.q: Under the Hardy-Weinberg assumption stated in the passage, what is the expected carrier frequency in Region B?
o: Not quite. 0.16% is q² = 0.0016, the affected fraction (aa), not the carriers.
Not quite. 4% is just q, the allele frequency. Carriers are 2pq, so multiply by 2 and by p.
Not quite. 16% isn't produced by any correct step. Carriers are 2pq, about 7.7%.
qs.x: Correct: Carriers are Aa, and under Hardy-Weinberg their frequency is 2pq. Here p is the frequency of allele A and q is the frequency of allele a, and p + q = 1. Values for Region B (Table 1): 16 affected out of 10,000. So q² = 16 ÷ 10,000 = 0.0016. The square root of 16 is 4 and of 10,000 is 100, so q = 0.04. Then p = 1 − 0.04 = 0.96. Plug in: 2pq = 2 × 0.96 × 0.04. First 2 × 0.96 = 1.92, then 1.92 × 0.04 = 0.0768. As a percent, 0.0768 × 100 = 7.68%, about 7.7%. Why the others are wrong: 0.16% is q², the affected fraction; 4% is q alone, which forgets there are two ways to be a carrier (Aa or aA) and that p matters; 16% doesn't come from any step of the calculation. Trap: Using q or 2q as the carrier frequency instead of 2pq.

qs.q: A healthy person in either region has an affected sibling, and both parents are unaffected. What is the probability that the healthy person is a carrier?
o: Correct: Both parents are Aa. Among unaffected children (AA 1/4, Aa 1/2), carriers are (1/2) ÷ (3/4) = 2/3.
Not quite. 1/4 is the chance of an affected (aa) child, not the chance a healthy person is a carrier.
Not quite. 1/2 is the chance of Aa for any child. We know this person is healthy, so aa is excluded.
Not quite. 3/4 is the chance of being unaffected. It says nothing about being a carrier.
qs.x: Correct: Both parents are healthy but they had an affected child (aa), so each parent must carry one a. That makes both parents Aa. A cross of Aa × Aa gives AA 1/4, Aa 1/2, aa 1/4. The healthy person is not aa, so throw out that 1/4. Only AA (1/4) and Aa (1/2) are left, a total of 1/4 + 1/2 = 3/4. The chance of being a carrier among those left is (1/2) ÷ (3/4) = 1/2 × 4/3 = 4/6 = 2/3. The population frequencies from the table don't matter here because the parents' genotypes are already known. Why the others are wrong: 1/4 is the chance of an affected child; 1/2 is the chance of Aa before you use the fact that the person is healthy; 3/4 is the chance of being unaffected, not the chance of being a carrier. Trap: Forgetting to shrink the pool to unaffected people before computing the probability.

qs.q: Which factor would most likely cause the observed frequency of affected individuals in Region B to exceed the Hardy-Weinberg expectation based on its allele frequency?
o: Random mating among all individuals, so genotype frequencies match p², 2pq, and q² expectations
Not quite. Random mating is a Hardy-Weinberg assumption, so it would give the expected frequencies, not an excess of aa.
Mating among relatives, raising homozygosity without changing allele frequency
Correct: Inbreeding raises homozygotes (aa) above q² while q stays the same.
A very large population size, which minimizes random changes in allele frequency by drift
Not quite. A large population limits drift and is a Hardy-Weinberg assumption. It wouldn't raise aa above expectation.
Absence of mutation and migration, so no new alleles enter or leave the gene pool
Not quite. No mutation or migration is a Hardy-Weinberg assumption, so it keeps genotype frequencies on target.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 3 says marriage between relatives is more common in Region B. Relatives are more likely to share the same rare allele, so their children are more likely to get two copies of it. That raises the share of homozygotes (aa) above the q² Hardy-Weinberg predicts, and it does so without changing the allele frequency q. More aa means more affected people than expected from q alone. Why the others are wrong: random mating is one of the Hardy-Weinberg assumptions, so it would make observed numbers match the expected ones; a very large population is also an assumption of the model (it limits drift) and wouldn't create extra aa; no mutation or migration is another assumption, so it too would keep the numbers on target. Trap: Picking a condition that sounds like a population-genetics term but actually matches the model's assumptions rather than breaking them.

qs.q: About how many carriers are expected among the 10,000 people genotyped in Region A?
o: Not quite. 39 is 10 times too small. 0.0392 × 10,000 is 392, not 39.
Not quite. 196 is half the right count, which comes from leaving out the 2 in 2pq.
Not quite. 980 would mean a carrier frequency of 9.8%, much larger than 2pq = 3.9%.
qs.x: Correct: Carrier frequency is 2pq, and the number of carriers is that frequency times the number of people. Values for Region A (Table 1): q² = 4 ÷ 10,000 = 0.0004, so q = 0.02 (the square root, as in the earlier question). Then p = 1 − q = 1 − 0.02 = 0.98. Individuals genotyped = 10,000. Plug in: 2pq = 2 × 0.98 × 0.02. First 2 × 0.98 = 1.96, then 1.96 × 0.02 = 0.0392. Number of carriers = 0.0392 × 10,000 = 392. Why the others are wrong: 39 is a decimal slip, 10 times too small; 196 is half of 392, which happens if you drop the 2 in 2pq; 980 would be a carrier frequency of 9.8% and doesn't come from any correct step. Trap: Dropping the 2 in 2pq, because there are two ways to be a heterozygote (A from mom and a from dad, or the reverse).

passages.title: FL01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 4
text: Researchers measured the oxygen consumption rate (OCR) of cultured cells in a sealed microplate with an oxygen sensor. After baseline measurements, compounds were injected sequentially at the times indicated and OCR was measured every 10 minutes. Oligomycin inhibits ATP synthase. FCCP is a lipid-soluble weak acid that carries protons across membranes. A mixture of rotenone, which inhibits Complex I, and antimycin A, which inhibits Complex III, was used at the end of the experiment. Cells were supplied with glucose and other nutrients throughout.

Mean OCR values are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1. Oligomycin was added after the 20-minute measurement, FCCP after the 40-minute measurement, and rotenone with antimycin A after the 60-minute measurement. The researchers attributed the OCR remaining after the final injection to oxygen-consuming reactions outside the mitochondrial electron transport chain.

The researchers used the values to estimate ATP-linked respiration, proton leak, and spare respiratory capacity. Spare respiratory capacity is the difference between the maximal OCR and the basal OCR.

qs.q: Why does OCR fall after oligomycin is added?
o: Oligomycin directly inhibits Complex IV, preventing the transfer of electrons to oxygen
Not quite. Oligomycin targets ATP synthase, not Complex IV.
Oligomycin depletes NADH by blocking glycolysis upstream of the citric acid cycle
Not quite. Oligomycin doesn't act on glycolysis, and NADH supply isn't what limits oxygen use here.
Blocking ATP synthase stops proton re-entry, so the gradient rises and slows electron transport
Correct: Blocking ATP synthase stops proton re-entry, so the gradient builds and slows electron transport and oxygen use.
Oligomycin makes the inner membrane freely permeable to protons, dissipating the gradient across the membrane
Not quite. Making the membrane leaky to protons is what FCCP does, and that raises OCR.
qs.x: Correct: Normally the electron transport chain pumps protons out of the matrix, and protons flow back in through ATP synthase, which makes ATP. That flow keeps the gradient from getting too strong. Oligomycin blocks ATP synthase, so protons can't flow back through it. The gradient builds up and pushes back against more pumping. With that back-pressure, electrons move more slowly and less oxygen gets used. The leftover oxygen use (40 in Table 1) is mostly the small amount driven by protons leaking back across the membrane, plus a little non-mitochondrial use. Why the others are wrong: oligomycin targets ATP synthase, not Complex IV; it doesn't block glycolysis or limit NADH, and the cells still had glucose; making the membrane leaky to protons is what FCCP does, and that would raise OCR, not lower it. Trap: Assuming any drug that stops ATP production must block the electron transport chain directly.

qs.q: Based on Table 1, what is the ATP-linked respiration in pmol O₂/min?
o: Not quite. 30 is 40 − 10, the proton leak, not the ATP-linked part.
Not quite. 120 is the entire basal OCR, which includes proton leak and non-mitochondrial use.
Not quite. 140 is the spare respiratory capacity, 260 − 120.
Correct: ATP-linked OCR = basal − after oligomycin = 120 − 40 = 80 pmol O₂/min.
qs.x: Correct: ATP-linked respiration is the oxygen use that goes to making ATP. Oligomycin shuts off ATP synthase, so the part of OCR that disappears after oligomycin is the ATP-linked part. Formula: ATP-linked OCR = basal OCR − OCR after oligomycin. Values from Table 1: basal = 120 pmol O₂/min, after oligomycin = 40 pmol O₂/min. Plug in: 120 − 40 = 80 pmol O₂/min. Why the others are wrong: 30 is 40 − 10, which is the proton leak (oxygen use that remains after oligomycin but isn't from the chain); 120 is the whole basal OCR, which includes leak and non-mitochondrial use; 140 is the spare capacity (260 − 120). Trap: Subtracting the final residual value of 10 instead of the value after oligomycin, 40.

qs.q: Which statement best explains the increase in OCR after FCCP?
o: FCCP carries protons into the matrix, dissipating the gradient so electron transport runs unrestrained
Correct: FCCP carries protons into the matrix and collapses the gradient, so electron transport runs flat out without making ATP.
FCCP activates ATP synthase to its maximal rate, which consumes the gradient faster than it forms
Not quite. Oligomycin had already blocked ATP synthase, and FCCP doesn't reactivate it.
FCCP donates electrons directly to oxygen, bypassing Complexes III and IV and raising consumption in the matrix
Not quite. FCCP carries protons. It doesn't donate electrons to oxygen.
FCCP inhibits Complex I, relieving feedback inhibition on glycolysis and increasing NADH supply
Not quite. Inhibiting Complex I would lower OCR. OCR went up with FCCP.
qs.x: Correct: FCCP is a weak acid that can carry protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane. It picks up protons outside the matrix and drops them off inside, so the proton gradient collapses. Normally that gradient pushes back on the chain. With the push-back gone, the electron transport chain runs as fast as it can and uses oxygen at its maximum, which is the 260 in Table 1. The energy is lost as heat instead of being used to make ATP. Why the others are wrong: ATP synthase was already blocked by oligomycin, and FCCP doesn't activate it; FCCP carries protons and doesn't give electrons to oxygen; inhibiting Complex I would lower OCR, and FCCP raised it. Trap: Assuming more oxygen use must mean more ATP is being made.

qs.q: What is the spare respiratory capacity of the cells, in pmol O₂/min?
o: Not quite. 80 is the ATP-linked OCR (120 − 40), not spare capacity.
Correct: Spare capacity = maximal − basal = 260 − 120 = 140 pmol O₂/min.
Not quite. 130 is half of 260 and isn't part of the definition.
Not quite. 260 is the maximal OCR. Spare capacity subtracts the basal value.
qs.x: Correct: Passage paragraph 3 defines spare respiratory capacity as the maximal OCR minus the basal OCR. The maximal OCR is what the cells reach after FCCP, when the chain runs unrestrained. Formula: spare capacity = maximal OCR − basal OCR. Values from Table 1: maximal (after FCCP) = 260 pmol O₂/min, basal = 120 pmol O₂/min. Plug in: 260 − 120 = 140 pmol O₂/min. It tells you how much extra the cells could do beyond what they use at rest. Why the others are wrong: 80 is the ATP-linked OCR (120 − 40); 130 is half of 260 and doesn't come from the definition; 260 is the maximal OCR itself, with basal not subtracted. Trap: Reporting the maximal OCR instead of the difference from basal.

qs.q: If only rotenone were added to the cells, which substrate would most likely still support substantial oxygen consumption?
o: Pyruvate
Not quite. Pyruvate leads to NADH, which enters at Complex I, the step rotenone blocks.
Succinate
Correct: Succinate is oxidized by Complex II, which passes electrons to ubiquinone below the rotenone block.
Malate
Not quite. Malate is oxidized to make NADH, which needs Complex I.
Glutamate
Not quite. Glutamate breakdown yields NADH, which needs Complex I.
qs.x: Correct: Rotenone blocks Complex I, which is where electrons from NADH enter the chain. Substrates that make NADH therefore can't feed the chain anymore. Succinate is different. It is oxidized by Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase), which passes electrons to ubiquinone. That's after the Complex I block, so electrons still reach Complexes III and IV and oxygen use continues. Why the others are wrong: pyruvate is turned into acetyl-CoA, and the citric acid cycle that follows makes NADH, which needs Complex I; malate is oxidized to make NADH, so it also depends on Complex I; glutamate is broken down by dehydrogenases that make NADH, again feeding Complex I. Trap: Forgetting that Complex II feeds the chain from a different entry point, below the rotenone block.

passages.title: FL01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 5
text: Cytoskeletal elements were probed in cultured epithelial cells using drugs that target specific polymers. Colchicine binds tubulin dimers and prevents their polymerization. Cytochalasin D caps the plus ends of actin filaments and prevents their elongation. Paclitaxel binds microtubules and stabilizes them against depolymerization.

Cells were treated for 24 hours with each drug, fixed, and stained for DNA, keratin, and mitochondria. The percentage of cells in mitosis (condensed chromosomes with no nuclear envelope) and the percentage of cells with two nuclei were determined from at least 500 cells per condition. Mitochondrial distribution was assessed qualitatively. Keratin filament networks appeared intact under all conditions, and cells remained attached to the dish.

In colchicine-treated and paclitaxel-treated cells, most mitotic cells had chromosomes clustered near the cell center without a bipolar spindle (colchicine) or with abnormal multipolar spindles (paclitaxel). Results are summarized in Table 1. The investigators emphasized that all three drugs were used at concentrations that did not reduce cell viability over the treatment period, and that untreated cells were handled identically in every other respect.

qs.q: The increase in mitotic cells after colchicine is best explained by:
o: failure to replicate DNA in S phase, so cells cannot enter mitosis at all
Not quite. Cells that can't replicate DNA stall in G1 or S, not in mitosis. These cells have condensed chromosomes.
loss of the contractile ring during telophase, which prevents separation of daughter cells
Not quite. A failed contractile ring gives binucleate cells. Colchicine cells are only 1% binucleate.
failure to assemble a spindle, which activates the spindle assembly checkpoint and blocks anaphase
Correct: With no spindle, chromosomes can't attach, so the spindle assembly checkpoint holds cells before anaphase.
premature degradation of cyclin B, which would force cells out of mitosis too early
Not quite. Losing cyclin B early pushes cells out of mitosis. Colchicine causes buildup in mitosis.
qs.x: Correct: Table 1 shows 38% of colchicine cells are in mitosis versus 4% untreated. Colchicine stops tubulin from forming microtubules, and microtubules are what build the mitotic spindle (the structure that grabs chromosomes and pulls them apart). Passage paragraph 3 says the colchicine cells have chromosomes clustered with no bipolar spindle. Chromosomes that aren't attached properly trigger the spindle assembly checkpoint, a built-in alarm that holds the cell before anaphase. So cells pile up in mitosis. Why the others are wrong: cells that couldn't replicate DNA would stall earlier, in G1 or S phase, and wouldn't show condensed chromosomes; a failed contractile ring shows up as binucleate cells, and colchicine cells have 1% binucleate; losing cyclin B too soon would push cells out of mitosis early and lower the mitotic percentage. Trap: Placing the block at the wrong stage of the cell cycle just because the drug is called antimitotic.

qs.q: The binucleate cells seen after cytochalasin D most likely arise because:
o: the actin-myosin contractile ring cannot form, so cytokinesis fails after nuclear division
Correct: The actin-myosin ring can't form, so cytokinesis fails after the nucleus has divided, leaving two nuclei in one cell.
chromosomes cannot attach to spindle microtubules, so mitosis stalls before anaphase
Not quite. Spindle attachment depends on microtubules, which this drug doesn't target. Mitotic percentage stayed normal.
DNA replication occurs twice per cycle, producing nuclei with doubled DNA content
Not quite. Re-replicating DNA wouldn't give two normal nuclei in one cell. The defect here is in splitting the cytoplasm.
the nuclear envelope fails to reassemble, leaving chromosomes exposed to the cytoplasm after each division
Not quite. The binucleate cells have two intact nuclei, so the envelope reformed. The problem is the cytoplasm failing to divide.
qs.x: Correct: Table 1 shows cytochalasin D cells have a normal share in mitosis (5% versus 4%), so the nucleus is dividing fine. But 22% have two nuclei. Cytochalasin D caps actin filaments, and the contractile ring that pinches a dividing cell in two is made of actin and myosin. Without the ring, the cell finishes dividing its nucleus (karyokinesis) but can't divide its cytoplasm (cytokinesis). The result is one cell with two nuclei. Why the others are wrong: attaching chromosomes to the spindle depends on microtubules, which this drug doesn't target, and there's no mitotic pile-up; re-replicating DNA wouldn't give two normal nuclei in one cell; the nuclear envelope reformed normally, since the cells have two intact nuclei. Trap: Mixing up karyokinesis (nuclear division) and cytokinesis (cytoplasm division).

qs.q: Which explanation best accounts for perinuclear clustering of mitochondria after colchicine?
o: Colchicine disrupts keratin filaments that anchor mitochondria near the cell center
Not quite. Paragraph 2 says keratin networks were intact in every condition, and colchicine doesn't target keratin.
Loss of microtubule tracks prevents kinesin-driven transport toward the cell periphery
Correct: Without microtubule tracks, kinesin can't carry mitochondria outward, so they stay near the nucleus.
Dynein can only move cargo toward the plus end of microtubules, away from the nucleus, so mitochondria cannot reach the periphery
Not quite. Dynein moves toward the minus end, near the centrosome, not toward the plus end at the periphery.
Colchicine causes mitochondria to fuse with the nuclear envelope near the centrosome
Not quite. Nothing in the passage suggests mitochondria fuse with the nuclear envelope. They just aren't transported outward.
qs.x: Correct: Table 1 shows that after colchicine the mitochondria are clustered near the nucleus, instead of spread through the cytoplasm. Colchicine blocks microtubule formation. Microtubules are the tracks for motor proteins, and kinesin carries cargo such as mitochondria toward the plus end, which points out toward the cell edge. With no tracks, kinesin can't haul mitochondria outward, and they stay near the center. Why the others are wrong: paragraph 2 says keratin filaments looked intact under all conditions, and colchicine doesn't target keratin anyway; dynein moves toward the minus end, which sits near the centrosome (next to the nucleus), not the plus end; nothing in the passage suggests that mitochondria fuse with the nuclear envelope. Trap: Reversing the direction of the motors: kinesin goes to the plus end (out), dynein goes to the minus end (in).

qs.q: Why would paclitaxel, which stabilizes microtubules, also increase the fraction of cells in mitosis?
o: Stable microtubules prevent chromosomes from condensing during prophase and prometaphase
Not quite. Mitotic cells were identified by condensed chromosomes, so condensation clearly happened.
Dynamic microtubule shortening is required for proper chromosome movement and spindle function
Correct: Spindles must grow and shrink to work. Overly stable microtubules give abnormal spindles and checkpoint arrest.
Stabilized microtubules inhibit actin polymerization directly, blocking the cleavage furrow and halting mitosis
Not quite. Binucleate cells stayed at 1%, and no data suggest paclitaxel acts directly on actin.
Paclitaxel prevents cells from entering S phase, so they never reach the spindle stage
Not quite. If cells couldn't enter S phase, none would reach mitosis. Here 36% are in mitosis.
qs.x: Correct: Table 1 shows 36% of paclitaxel cells are in mitosis versus 4% untreated, nearly the same as colchicine's 38%. Paclitaxel locks microtubules in place so they can't depolymerize (shrink). But a spindle has to keep growing and shrinking to find chromosomes and then pull them apart. Paragraph 3 says paclitaxel cells have abnormal multipolar spindles. Faulty spindles trigger the spindle assembly checkpoint, which holds the cells in mitosis. Why the others are wrong: chromosomes did condense in these mitotic cells (that is how mitotic cells were identified in paragraph 2); the passage gives no sign that paclitaxel acts on actin, and binucleate cells stayed at 1%; if cells couldn't enter S phase, they couldn't reach mitosis at all, yet 36% were there. Trap: Thinking that stabilizing a polymer is the opposite of breaking it down and therefore harmless to mitosis.

passages.title: FL01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 6
text: A clinical laboratory found that a drug-resistant bacterial strain could pass resistance to a susceptible strain. Researchers hypothesized that resistance was encoded on a plasmid that is transferred between cells. A donor strain carrying the resistance plasmid was mixed with a susceptible recipient strain and incubated for 1 hour. Mixtures were then plated on medium containing the antibiotic and a nutrient supplement that allowed only recipients to grow, and the number of resistant recipient colonies (transconjugants) per donor cell was calculated.

Four conditions were tested. In condition 1, donor and recipient cells were mixed. In condition 2, the mixture was incubated with DNase I, which degrades DNA outside cells. In condition 3, donor and recipient were separated by a filter with 0.2 µm pores in a U-shaped tube, allowing the medium, but not cells, to pass; bacteriophage particles (about 0.05 µm) can pass through the filter. In condition 4, the donor carried a mutation that prevents production of a pilus. Results are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1.

qs.q: Which conclusion about the transfer mechanism is best supported by condition 2?
o: Transfer requires DNase I to cleave the plasmid before it enters the recipient
Not quite. Transfer was the same with or without DNase I, so cleaving the plasmid isn't needed.
Transfer is carried out by bacteriophage particles that package the plasmid
Not quite. Phage involvement is tested by the filter in condition 3, not by DNase.
DNase I inhibits the recipient's growth, which lowers the number of colonies counted in the DNase-treated sample
Not quite. A growth problem would lower colony counts, and they stayed about the same.
Transfer does not require free DNA in the medium, which argues against transformation
Correct: DNase would destroy free DNA, yet transfer stayed at 1.1 × 10⁻³, so uptake of naked DNA is not the mechanism.
qs.x: Correct: DNase I chews up DNA that's floating free outside cells. In condition 2 it was added to the mix, and transfer stayed at 1.1 × 10⁻³, almost the same as the untreated mix at 1.2 × 10⁻³. If the recipients were picking up naked DNA from the medium (that's called transformation), DNase would have wiped it out and transfer would have dropped. It didn't, so free DNA in the medium isn't how the plasmid moves. An unchanged result is still useful: it rules something out. Why the others are wrong: transfer didn't need DNase, and it was the same with or without it; whether phage is involved is tested in condition 3, not condition 2; if DNase hurt the recipients' growth, colony counts would fall, and they didn't. Trap: Treating an unchanged result as meaningless instead of evidence that rules out a mechanism.

qs.q: The results of condition 3 are best interpreted as indicating that:
o: transfer requires a soluble signal molecule secreted by the donor cells into the medium and acts across the filter
Not quite. A soluble signal would pass through the filter along with the medium, and transfer would still occur.
the filter blocks plasmid DNA but not whole cells, so contact is not needed
Not quite. The filter blocks cells, not DNA. A filter that lets everything but cells through, with no transfer, points to contact.
direct cell-to-cell contact is required, which also excludes phage-mediated transduction
Correct: Medium and phage cross the filter but transfer vanished, so cell contact is needed and transduction is excluded.
phage particles carry the plasmid across the filter and infect the recipient cells
Not quite. Phage particles can cross the filter, and no transfer happened, so phages aren't carrying the plasmid.
qs.x: Correct: In condition 3 a filter with 0.2 µm pores separates donor from recipient. Paragraph 2 says the medium and phage particles (about 0.05 µm) can pass through, but the bacterial cells can't. Transfer dropped to below 10⁻⁹ per donor, compared with 1.2 × 10⁻³ when mixed. So anything small enough to cross the filter, such as a dissolved signal, free DNA or a phage, isn't enough to move the plasmid. What's missing is cell-to-cell contact. Phage-mediated transfer (transduction) is ruled out because phages could cross the filter and nothing happened. Why the others are wrong: a soluble signal would have gone across the filter; the filter blocks cells, not DNA, and free DNA was already ruled out by DNase; phages pass through the filter, yet no transfer occurred. Trap: Forgetting that phage particles are small enough to cross the filter.

qs.q: Which description of the transfer in condition 1 is most accurate?
o: One plasmid strand is nicked and transferred through the pilus junction, then each cell makes a complementary strand
Correct: One plasmid strand passes through the pilus and each cell builds the matching strand, so the donor keeps its plasmid.
Both strands of the plasmid are transferred through the pilus and the donor loses the plasmid permanently, ending the transfer
Not quite. In conjugation the donor keeps its plasmid. Only one strand is passed on.
The plasmid is transferred as a double-stranded linear molecule packaged within a phage protein coat
Not quite. A phage coat isn't involved. Phage particles crossed the filter and no transfer occurred.
The plasmid is integrated into the recipient chromosome by a viral integrase after uptake of free DNA
Not quite. Viral integrase belongs to retroviruses. The plasmid is copied in the recipient without it, and free DNA uptake was ruled out.
qs.x: Correct: Table 1 and the filter and pilus conditions point to conjugation, where a donor connects to a recipient through a pilus (a hollow bridge-like protein tube). One strand of the plasmid is nicked and fed through to the recipient. Then each cell builds a new complementary strand using the strand it has, so both end up with a full double-stranded plasmid. The donor keeps its plasmid, which is why it works as a copy, not a move. Why the others are wrong: if both strands left and the donor lost the plasmid, the donor couldn't keep spreading resistance, and conjugation doesn't work that way; a phage coat isn't involved, as phage particles crossing the filter didn't support transfer; viral integrase is a retrovirus enzyme, and this is a plasmid, which doesn't need to integrate. Trap: Assuming the donor hands over its plasmid, as if the DNA were moved instead of copied.

qs.q: If 5 × 10⁷ donor cells were used in condition 1, about how many transconjugants would be expected?
o: Not quite. 6 × 10³ is a factor of 10 too small. Adding exponents −3 + 7 gives 4, not 3.
Not quite. 4 × 10¹⁰ comes from dividing donors by frequency. A per-donor frequency is multiplied by donors.
Not quite. About 2 × 10⁻¹¹ comes from dividing the frequency by the donors. You should multiply.
qs.x: Correct: The transfer frequency is transconjugants per donor cell, so total transconjugants = frequency × number of donors. Values: frequency = 1.2 × 10⁻³ transconjugants per donor (condition 1, Table 1) and donors = 5 × 10⁷ cells. Plug in: 1.2 × 10⁻³ × 5 × 10⁷. Multiply the front numbers: 1.2 × 5 = 6. Multiplying powers of 10, so add the exponents: −3 + 7 = 4. That gives 6 × 10⁴ transconjugants. Why the others are wrong: 6 × 10³ is off by a factor of 10, which is what you get if you add the exponents wrong (−3 + 6); 4 × 10¹⁰ comes from dividing 5 × 10⁷ by 1.2 × 10⁻³, which flips the operation; about 2 × 10⁻¹¹ comes from dividing 1.2 × 10⁻³ by 5 × 10⁷, which is also the wrong operation. Trap: Dividing instead of multiplying when turning a per-donor frequency into a total count.

graph.title: Figure 1. Transfer frequency by condition
graph.x_label: Condition (1 = mixed, 2 = mixed + DNase I, 3 = filter-separated, 4 = pilus-deficient donor)

passages.title: FL01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 7
text: Researchers studied two investigational compounds, Drug X and Drug Y, in a proliferating human cell line with a doubling time of 24 hours. Cells were treated for 24 hours, fixed, stained with a fluorescent dye that binds DNA stoichiometrically, and analyzed by flow cytometry. Cells with a diploid (2N) DNA content were classified as G1, cells with intermediate DNA content as S, and cells with 4N DNA content as G2/M. Results are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1.

Untreated cells were asynchronous, and the researchers assumed that the fraction of cells in each phase is proportional to the time spent in that phase. Western blots of treated cells indicated that Drug Y-treated cells contained hypophosphorylated retinoblastoma protein (Rb), while Drug X-treated cells showed many cells with condensed chromosomes and a few visible spindle fibers. Drug X had no detectable effect on DNA replication measured by incorporation of a labeled nucleotide.

qs.q: The Drug Y results are most consistent with inhibition of:
o: the spindle assembly checkpoint
Not quite. The spindle checkpoint acts in mitosis. Blocking it wouldn't make cells pile up in G1.
G1 cyclin-dependent kinase activity that normally phosphorylates Rb
Correct: Without Rb phosphorylation, Rb keeps E2F inactive, so cells can't enter S phase and pile up in G1.
DNA polymerase during S phase
Not quite. Blocking DNA polymerase would raise the S fraction. Drug Y cells have only 10% in S.
cyclin B-CDK1 activity at the G2/M transition
Not quite. Blocking cyclin B-CDK1 would raise the G2/M fraction. Drug Y lowers it to 5%.
qs.x: Correct: Table 1 shows Drug Y cells piling up in G1 (85% versus 55% untreated), with fewer in S and G2/M. Paragraph 2 says they contain hypophosphorylated Rb, meaning Rb is missing its phosphate groups. In its unphosphorylated form, Rb holds on to the transcription factor E2F, and E2F is needed to turn on genes for S phase. Normally G1 cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) add phosphates to Rb to release E2F. So blocking that kinase activity keeps Rb active, E2F stays locked up, and cells can't pass out of G1. Why the others are wrong: the spindle assembly checkpoint acts in mitosis, and blocking it wouldn't pile cells up in G1; stopping DNA polymerase would pile cells up in S; blocking cyclin B-CDK1 would pile cells up at the G2/M transition. Trap: Matching the drug to the phase where cells collect, without asking which step the drug stops cells from leaving.

qs.q: Which process is Drug X most likely to interfere with?
o: Initiation of DNA replication at origins
Not quite. Replication was unaffected, and blocking origins would reduce G2/M cells rather than raise them.
Assembly or function of the mitotic spindle
Correct: 4N cells with condensed chromosomes and few spindle fibers fit a mitotic block, with replication unaffected.
Phosphorylation of Rb by G1 cyclin-CDK complexes
Not quite. Rb phosphorylation is a G1 step, and blocking it piles cells up in G1, as with Drug Y.
Synthesis of histones during G1
Not quite. Histone problems would show up in S phase, not as a pile-up of mitotic cells.
qs.x: Correct: Table 1 shows Drug X cells with 65% at G2/M, which means 4N DNA content, compared with 15% untreated. 4N means the DNA has been copied, and paragraph 2 says DNA replication was normal. The cells also show condensed chromosomes and few spindle fibers. So cells copied their DNA and started mitosis, but couldn't finish because the spindle (the microtubule machine that pulls chromosomes apart) wasn't working. They are stuck in mitosis. Why the others are wrong: blocking replication origins would cut S-phase entry and G2/M would go down, and paragraph 2 says replication was unaffected; Rb phosphorylation is the G1 step that Drug Y affects, and it would pile cells up in G1; histone synthesis problems would show up in S phase, not as a mitotic block. Trap: Assuming 4N DNA content means a DNA synthesis problem, when it only tells you replication already finished.

qs.q: Under the assumptions stated, how long does S phase last in untreated cells?
o: 3.6 hours
Not quite. 3.6 hours is 0.15 × 24, the time in G2/M, not S.
7.2 hours
Correct: Time in S = 0.30 × 24 hours = 7.2 hours.
13.2 hours
Not quite. 13.2 hours is 0.55 × 24, the time in G1.
30 hours
Not quite. 30 is the percent, not hours. It is also longer than the 24-hour cycle.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says to assume the fraction of cells in each phase matches the fraction of time spent in it. So time in S = fraction in S × length of the whole cycle. The whole cycle is the doubling time, 24 hours (paragraph 1). The untreated S fraction from Table 1 is 30%, which is 30 ÷ 100 = 0.30. Plug in: 0.30 × 24 hours. 0.30 × 24 = 3 × 24 ÷ 10 = 72 ÷ 10 = 7.2 hours. Why the others are wrong: 3.6 hours is 0.15 × 24, which is the G2/M share; 13.2 hours is 0.55 × 24, the G1 share; 30 hours just uses the percent as if it were hours, and that is longer than the entire 24-hour cycle. Trap: Using the percentage as hours, or picking the percentage for the wrong phase.

qs.q: How many chromatids are present in a human cell in G2?
o: Not quite. 23 is the haploid chromosome number, not the chromatid count in a G2 cell.
Not quite. 46 is the number of chromosomes, and also the chromatid count in G1. In G2 each chromosome has two chromatids.
Not quite. 184 would need DNA to be copied twice. Only one round of replication has happened.
Correct: 46 chromosomes × 2 sister chromatids each = 92 chromatids after S phase.
qs.x: Correct: A human cell has 46 chromosomes. A chromatid is one copy of a chromosome. Before S phase, each chromosome is a single chromatid. During S phase, each chromosome is copied, and the two identical copies (sister chromatids) stay joined. Cells in G2 have already been through S phase, so each of the 46 chromosomes has two chromatids. Plug in: 46 chromosomes × 2 chromatids each = 92 chromatids. This matches the 4N DNA content that Table 1 uses for G2/M. Why the others are wrong: 23 is the number of chromosomes in a haploid gamete; 46 is the number of chromosomes, and it's also the chromatid count in G1, before copying; 184 doubles 92 a second time, which would need two rounds of replication. Trap: Mixing up chromosome number (46, which stays the same) with chromatid number (which doubles after replication).

passages.title: FL01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 8
text: Researchers compared glucose handling in control mice and in mice carrying a liver-specific mutation in a gene required for insulin receptor signaling. After a 6-hour fast, each mouse received an intraperitoneal injection of glucose, and blood samples were collected at the times shown. Blood glucose was measured with a meter and plasma insulin with an immunoassay. Each value is the mean of 8 mice. Results are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1.

Fasting body weights were similar in the two groups. Pancreatic islets isolated from mutant mice and control mice secreted similar amounts of insulin when exposed to the same glucose concentrations in vitro. The researchers also measured liver glycogen content after the fast, finding lower glycogen in the mutant livers.
The investigators interpreted the data as evidence that the mutation produces a state resembling the early stage of type 2 diabetes. They then planned a second study of glucagon during a longer fast.

qs.q: The data in Table 1 are best interpreted as showing that mutant mice have:
o: insulin deficiency caused by impaired islet function
Not quite. Mutant insulin is higher than control, and islets secrete normally in vitro, so there's no deficiency.
enhanced insulin sensitivity in peripheral tissue
Not quite. Greater sensitivity would clear glucose faster. Mutant glucose stays high longer.
reduced insulin sensitivity, with compensatory elevated insulin secretion
Correct: Mutants have higher glucose and higher insulin, and normal islets, so tissues respond poorly to insulin.
excess glucagon secretion that lowers blood glucose
Not quite. Glucagon raises blood glucose. It can't explain the mutant's glucose staying high with high insulin.
qs.x: Correct: Table 1 shows mutant mice with higher glucose than controls at every time after injection (280 versus 220 at 15 minutes, 180 versus 95 at 120 minutes). They also have much higher insulin (6.5 versus 3.0 at 15 minutes). Paragraph 2 says their islets secrete insulin normally in vitro. So the pancreas is working and in fact pouring out extra insulin, but glucose still stays high. That means the body's tissues aren't responding well to insulin: reduced insulin sensitivity (insulin resistance), with the pancreas making extra insulin to compensate. Why the others are wrong: insulin deficiency would mean low insulin, and mutant insulin is higher with islets that work normally; enhanced sensitivity would clear glucose faster, but it clears slower; glucagon raises blood glucose, so it can't be what lowers it. Trap: Equating high blood glucose with low insulin, when here insulin is high and the cells aren't listening.

qs.q: Which sequence best describes how glucose entry stimulates insulin release from pancreatic β cells?
o: Increased ATP/ADP closes K⁺ channels, causing depolarization, Ca²⁺ entry, and exocytosis of insulin
Correct: Higher ATP/ADP closes K⁺ channels, causing depolarization, Ca²⁺ entry and insulin exocytosis.
Increased cAMP opens Na⁺ channels, causing hyperpolarization and insulin degradation
Not quite. This isn't the glucose-sensing pathway, and the cell depolarizes rather than hyperpolarizes.
Decreased ATP opens K⁺ channels, causing depolarization and Ca²⁺ release
Not quite. Lower ATP would leave K⁺ channels open and block depolarization. High ATP is the signal.
Glucose binds a receptor tyrosine kinase that directly triggers vesicle fusion
Not quite. Receptor tyrosine kinases respond to insulin on target cells. Glucose acts on β cells through metabolism.
qs.x: Correct: Glucose enters the β cell and is broken down, which raises the ATP/ADP ratio in the cell. ATP closes ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels, so K⁺ can no longer leak out and the membrane depolarizes (becomes less negative). That opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels, Ca²⁺ flows in, and the Ca²⁺ makes insulin-filled vesicles fuse with the membrane and release insulin (exocytosis). This is why the glucose injection in Table 1 is followed by a rise in insulin. Why the others are wrong: cAMP and opening Na⁺ channels isn't the glucose-sensing pathway, and depolarization is needed, not hyperpolarization; lower ATP would leave K⁺ channels open and prevent depolarization; the insulin receptor is a receptor tyrosine kinase that responds to insulin on target cells, not glucose on β cells. Trap: Reversing the effect of ATP on the K⁺ channel: more ATP closes it.

qs.q: By approximately what percent did mutant blood glucose at 120 minutes exceed its fasting value?
o: Not quite. 47% comes from dividing the change by 180. Divide by the starting value, 95.
Not quite. 53% is 95 ÷ 180, starting over final. Percent increase divides the change by the start.
Not quite. 189% is the final as a share of baseline (180 ÷ 95). The increase subtracts the original 100%.
qs.x: Correct: Percent increase = (final − starting) ÷ starting × 100. Values for mutant mice from Table 1: fasting (0 min) = 95 mg/dL, at 120 minutes = 180 mg/dL. Plug in: (180 − 95) ÷ 95 × 100. First 180 − 95 = 85. Then 85 ÷ 95 = 0.895 (95 × 0.9 = 85.5, so a bit under 0.9). Times 100 gives 89.5%, about 89% as the nearest answer. Why the others are wrong: 47% divides the change by 180, the wrong number (85 ÷ 180 = 0.47); 53% is the starting value divided by the final one (95 ÷ 180 = 0.53); 189% is the ratio 180 ÷ 95 = 1.89, which is the new value as a fraction of the old and doesn't subtract the starting 100%. Trap: Reporting the ratio to baseline as if it were the percent increase.

qs.q: During a prolonged fast, glucagon from pancreatic α cells would be expected to:
o: lower blood glucose by stimulating glycogen synthesis in liver and glucose uptake in muscle
Not quite. Glycogen synthesis and muscle glucose uptake are insulin actions. Glucagon raises glucose.
raise blood glucose by stimulating glucose uptake and triglyceride storage in adipose tissue
Not quite. Adipose glucose uptake and fat storage follow insulin and would lower glucose.
raise blood glucose by stimulating hepatic glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis via cAMP
Correct: Glucagon acts on liver cells via cAMP and PKA to boost glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis, raising blood glucose.
lower blood glucose by inhibiting gluconeogenesis through insulin receptors on hepatocytes
Not quite. Glucagon doesn't act through insulin receptors, and it promotes gluconeogenesis rather than inhibiting it.
qs.x: Correct: During a long fast, blood glucose drops, and α cells in the pancreas release glucagon to push it back up. Glucagon binds a G protein-coupled receptor on liver cells, which raises cAMP and turns on protein kinase A (PKA). PKA drives glycogenolysis (breaking down glycogen into glucose) and gluconeogenesis (making new glucose from other molecules). The liver then releases glucose into the blood. Glucagon is the opposite of insulin. Why the others are wrong: making glycogen and moving glucose into muscle are insulin actions, and glucagon wouldn't lower blood glucose; glucose uptake and fat storage in adipose tissue is also insulin's job and would lower glucose; glucagon doesn't work through insulin receptors, and it wouldn't inhibit gluconeogenesis. Trap: Giving glucagon the role of insulin.

passages.title: FL01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 9
text: To characterize renal handling of several solutes, researchers infused inulin, a polysaccharide that is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, into a healthy volunteer. Timed urine was collected for one hour and a mid-collection blood sample was obtained. Plasma and urine concentrations of inulin, glucose, urea, and a drug (substance X) were measured. Urine flow was constant at 1.0 mL/min.
Substance X is not bound to plasma proteins and is known to be a substrate for an organic anion transporter in the proximal tubule. Results are shown in Table 1.

Clearance of a substance equals its urine concentration times urine flow, divided by its plasma concentration. The researchers compared the clearance of each substance with the glomerular filtration rate (GFR), which is equal to the clearance of inulin. They also compared the filtered load of each solute (GFR times plasma concentration) with the amount excreted (urine concentration times urine flow). Finally, they asked how changes in antidiuretic hormone (ADH) would alter the urinary concentrations.

qs.q: What is the GFR of the volunteer?
o: 31 mL/min
Not quite. 31 isn't produced by the clearance formula. Dividing 62.5 by 0.50 doubles it, rather than halving.
62.5 mL/min
Not quite. 62.5 is only urine concentration × flow. You still have to divide by the plasma concentration, 0.50.
125 mL/min
Correct: (62.5 mg/mL × 1.0 mL/min) ÷ 0.50 mg/mL = 125 mL/min.
180 mL/min
Not quite. 180 is liters of filtrate per day, not mL/min. The calculation gives 125 mL/min.
qs.x: Correct: Inulin is filtered but never reabsorbed or secreted, so everything that gets filtered ends up in the urine. That makes its clearance equal to the GFR, as paragraph 3 says. Formula: clearance = (urine concentration × urine flow) ÷ plasma concentration. Values for inulin from Table 1 and paragraph 1: urine concentration = 62.5 mg/mL, urine flow = 1.0 mL/min, plasma concentration = 0.50 mg/mL. Plug in: (62.5 mg/mL × 1.0 mL/min) ÷ 0.50 mg/mL. Top: 62.5 × 1.0 = 62.5 mg/min. Then 62.5 ÷ 0.50 = 62.5 × 2 = 125. The mg/mL units cancel and leave mL/min. So GFR = 125 mL/min. Why the others are wrong: 31 is 125 divided by 2 twice (62.5 ÷ 2 = 31.25), which doesn't match any step; 62.5 is the top of the fraction, with no division by plasma concentration; 180 is the daily filtrate in liters (125 mL/min × 1440 min/day ÷ 1000 = 180 L/day), which is a different unit and time. Trap: Forgetting to divide by the plasma concentration.

qs.q: Which conclusion about substance X is best supported by the data?
o: It is reabsorbed, because its clearance is below the GFR
Not quite. Reabsorption gives clearance below GFR. X clearance is 150 mL/min, above the 125 mL/min GFR.
It is neither filtered nor secreted
Not quite. X isn't protein bound, so it is filtered, and excretion above the filtered amount needs secretion.
It undergoes net tubular secretion, because its clearance exceeds the GFR
Correct: Clearance of X is (30 × 1.0) ÷ 0.20 = 150 mL/min, above GFR of 125 mL/min, so X is secreted.
It is freely filtered and not reabsorbed or secreted
Not quite. A solute only filtered would have clearance equal to GFR, 125 mL/min. X is 150.
qs.x: Correct: Compare clearance of X with GFR. Formula: clearance = (urine concentration × urine flow) ÷ plasma concentration. Values for substance X (Table 1): urine = 30 mg/mL, plasma = 0.20 mg/mL, flow = 1.0 mL/min. Plug in: (30 × 1.0) ÷ 0.20 = 30 ÷ 0.20 = 150 mL/min. GFR is 125 mL/min, so X clearance is higher. That means more of X leaves in the urine than was filtered. The extra must have been added to the tubule after filtering, which is net tubular secretion. Paragraph 2 supports this: X is a substrate for an organic anion transporter in the proximal tubule. Why the others are wrong: reabsorption would give a clearance below GFR, and this one is above; X is freely filtered (it isn't protein bound), and excretion above the filtered amount can't happen without secretion; a solute that's only filtered, with no reabsorption or secretion, would have clearance equal to GFR (125), and it's 150. Trap: Comparing concentrations instead of clearances.

qs.q: How much urea is reabsorbed per minute?
o: 15 mg/min
Not quite. 15 mg/min is what was excreted. Reabsorbed is filtered minus excreted.
22.5 mg/min
Correct: Filtered is 125 × 0.30 = 37.5 mg/min, excreted is 15 mg/min, so reabsorbed is 37.5 − 15 = 22.5 mg/min.
37.5 mg/min
Not quite. 37.5 mg/min is the filtered load. Subtract what was excreted.
52.5 mg/min
Not quite. 52.5 adds excreted to filtered. Reabsorbed is the difference between them.
qs.x: Correct: Reabsorbed = filtered load − excreted. Paragraph 3 gives filtered load = GFR × plasma concentration and excreted = urine concentration × urine flow. Values: GFR = 125 mL/min (inulin clearance), urea plasma = 0.30 mg/mL, urea urine = 15 mg/mL, urine flow = 1.0 mL/min. Filtered: 125 mL/min × 0.30 mg/mL = 37.5 mg/min (125 × 0.3 = 125 × 3 ÷ 10 = 375 ÷ 10 = 37.5). Excreted: 15 mg/mL × 1.0 mL/min = 15 mg/min. Reabsorbed = 37.5 − 15 = 22.5 mg/min. Why the others are wrong: 15 mg/min is the amount excreted; 37.5 mg/min is the amount filtered; 52.5 mg/min comes from adding excreted to filtered (37.5 + 15), but reabsorption is the amount that was filtered and didn't leave. Trap: Giving the excreted or filtered amount instead of the difference.

qs.q: After water deprivation, urine flow falls to 0.5 mL/min with GFR unchanged and plasma inulin unchanged. What is the urine inulin concentration?
o: 125 mg/mL
Correct: Inulin excretion stays 62.5 mg/min, so 62.5 ÷ 0.5 mL/min = 125 mg/mL as ADH pulls back water.
31 mg/mL
Not quite. 31 mg/mL would apply if urine flow had doubled. Flow fell by half, so concentration rises.
62.5 mg/mL
Not quite. 62.5 mg/mL is the original value. Less urine volume makes it more concentrated.
250 mg/mL
Not quite. 250 mg/mL is double the correct value. Excretion of 62.5 mg/min ÷ 0.5 mL/min gives 125.
qs.x: Correct: Inulin is neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so the amount excreted per minute equals the amount filtered per minute, and that doesn't change when water is reabsorbed. Formula: excretion = urine concentration × urine flow = GFR × plasma concentration. Values: GFR = 125 mL/min (unchanged), plasma inulin = 0.50 mg/mL (unchanged), new urine flow = 0.5 mL/min. Excretion = 125 × 0.50 = 62.5 mg/min. Plug in: urine concentration = 62.5 mg/min ÷ 0.5 mL/min = 125 mg/mL (dividing by 0.5 is the same as multiplying by 2). With water deprivation, ADH rises and makes the collecting duct reabsorb more water, so the same inulin sits in half the volume and gets twice as concentrated. Why the others are wrong: 31 mg/mL is what you'd get if flow doubled to 2.0 mL/min (62.5 ÷ 2); 62.5 mg/mL is the old value, with no concentrating; 250 mg/mL would double the right answer. Trap: Assuming urine concentration stays the same when only urine flow changes.

passages.title: FL01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 10
text: Voltage-clamp recordings were made from isolated squid giant axons to separate the ionic currents underlying the action potential. The membrane potential was stepped from −70 mV to 0 mV, and the peak early inward current and peak late outward current were measured. Inward current is negative and outward current is positive.

In control conditions the axon was bathed in normal artificial seawater. Tetrodotoxin (TTX), a toxin that blocks the pore of one class of voltage-gated channel, was added in the second condition. In the third condition, tetraethylammonium (TEA) was injected into the axon. In the fourth condition, the extracellular Na⁺ concentration was lowered to 30% of normal with choline replacing Na⁺. Each condition was tested on a different axon, and each value is the mean of five axons. Results are shown in Table 1.

In current-clamp experiments on separate axons, application of TEA made the action potentials longer in duration without changing their threshold. The researchers also compared conduction in myelinated and unmyelinated axons from a vertebrate nerve.

qs.q: The effect of TTX on the currents indicates that TTX blocks:
o: voltage-gated K⁺ channels
Not quite. Blocking K⁺ channels would shrink the outward current, as TEA does. TTX left it at +2.0 nA.
Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase
Not quite. The ATPase isn't voltage-gated and doesn't produce this fast current.
voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels
Not quite. Nothing here tests Ca²⁺ channels, and the Na⁺ current explains the lost inward current.
voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
Correct: TTX abolished the early inward current and left the outward current alone, so it blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels.
qs.x: Correct: Table 1 shows TTX takes the peak inward current from −1.2 nA to 0.0 nA, but the outward current stays at +2.0 nA. So TTX removes the early inward current and leaves the outward one alone. In a squid axon, the early inward current is Na⁺ rushing in through voltage-gated Na⁺ channels (Na⁺ is more concentrated outside, so it flows in). The fact that TTX deletes just that current tells you it blocks those channels. Why the others are wrong: blocking K⁺ channels would shrink the outward current, which is what TEA does, and TTX didn't; the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase isn't voltage-gated and doesn't make a fast current like this; Ca²⁺ channels were not part of this experiment, and the whole inward current vanished, which matches Na⁺ channels. Trap: Linking TTX to K⁺ channels because the outward current is the one that is easier to see.

qs.q: Why is the peak inward current smaller in low extracellular Na⁺?
o: Na⁺ channels are inactivated by choline, which reduces the peak inward current and blocks inward current
Not quite. Nothing suggests choline inactivates channels, and the outward current was unchanged.
The Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase reverses its direction and pumps Na⁺ into the axon
Not quite. The pump doesn't reverse direction here, and the pump doesn't produce this fast current.
K⁺ efflux increases enough to cancel the Na⁺ current at the 0 mV step
Not quite. The outward current stayed at +2.0 nA, so K⁺ outflow didn't change.
The Na⁺ equilibrium potential becomes less positive, reducing the driving force for Na⁺ entry
Correct: Lower outside Na⁺ lowers E<sub>Na</sub>, which shrinks the driving force for Na⁺ entry at 0 mV.
qs.x: Correct: Na⁺ moves in because of its driving force, which is the membrane voltage minus the Na⁺ equilibrium potential (E<sub>Na</sub>). E<sub>Na</sub> depends on the Na⁺ concentration ratio across the membrane, via the Nernst equation. When the outside Na⁺ is lowered to 30% of normal (paragraph 2), the ratio of outside to inside falls, so E<sub>Na</sub> becomes less positive. At the 0 mV step, the gap between 0 mV and E<sub>Na</sub> is smaller, so there's less push for Na⁺ to enter. Peak inward current falls from −1.2 to −0.6 nA, and the same channels are open. Why the others are wrong: the passage gives no sign that choline inactivates channels, and the outward current stayed at +2.0 nA; the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase doesn't reverse direction here; K⁺ outflow didn't change (+2.0 nA stayed the same), so it can't be canceling the Na⁺ current. Trap: Assuming that fewer channels must be open when current falls, instead of a smaller driving force.

qs.q: How does TEA most likely lengthen the action potential?
o: By blocking Na⁺ channels, it raises the threshold
Not quite. Blocking Na⁺ channels would abolish action potentials, and the inward current was unchanged with TEA.
By opening Na⁺ channels, it slows inactivation
Not quite. The inward current wasn't enhanced with TEA (it stayed at −1.2 nA).
By increasing the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase rate, it hyperpolarizes the membrane
Not quite. The pump contributes little to repolarization within a single action potential, and TEA isn't shown to affect it.
By blocking K⁺ channels, it slows repolarization
Correct: TEA cut the late outward K⁺ current from +2.0 to +0.3 nA, so repolarization is slower and the action potential lasts longer.
qs.x: Correct: Table 1 shows that with TEA the late outward current drops from +2.0 nA to +0.3 nA, while the inward current stays at −1.2 nA. The late outward current is K⁺ leaving through voltage-gated K⁺ channels. That outflow is what brings the membrane back down (repolarization) after the Na⁺ spike. With K⁺ channels blocked, repolarization is slower, so the action potential stays up longer. Paragraph 3 says that threshold didn't change, which also fits, since threshold is set by Na⁺ channels. Why the others are wrong: blocking Na⁺ channels would abolish action potentials and wouldn't lengthen them, and the inward current didn't change; opening Na⁺ channels or slowing inactivation would enlarge the inward current, and it didn't; the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase plays little role in repolarizing within a single action potential, and TEA wasn't shown to affect it. Trap: Linking a longer action potential to Na⁺ channels because Na⁺ is the depolarizing ion.

qs.q: Compared with unmyelinated axons of equal diameter, myelinated axons conduct faster mainly because:
o: myelin increases the number of open Na⁺ channels along the internode
Not quite. Channels are concentrated at the nodes and sparse under the myelin.
myelin pumps Na⁺ out of the axon rapidly
Not quite. Myelin is an insulator. It doesn't pump ions.
action potentials regenerate only at nodes of Ranvier, and current flows passively between nodes
Correct: Action potentials regenerate only at nodes, and current spreads passively between them, so conduction is faster.
myelin lowers the resting potential to the threshold
Not quite. A resting potential at threshold would make the axon fire on its own. Myelin doesn't change resting potential.
qs.x: Correct: Myelin is a fatty insulating wrap around the axon with small gaps called nodes of Ranvier. Under the myelin, the membrane has high resistance and low capacitance, so current doesn't leak out. Depolarization spreads passively and quickly down the inside of the axon to the next node. Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are packed at the nodes, so a new action potential is regenerated there. The signal jumps from node to node (saltatory conduction), which is faster than regenerating the signal at every bit of membrane along an unmyelinated axon. Why the others are wrong: channels are concentrated at the nodes and sparse under myelin, so there aren't more open channels along the internode; myelin is an insulator, and it doesn't pump ions; lowering the resting potential to threshold would make the axon fire spontaneously. Trap: Thinking myelin speeds things up by acting on ion channels along the whole axon.

passages.title: FL01 · CARS · Passage 1
text: Translators have long been described as traitors, and the accusation rests on an assumption so familiar that it rarely receives scrutiny: that a text possesses a stable core of meaning that exists prior to any language, and that the translator's task is to carry this core across a border without spilling any of it. On this view, a good translation is a transparent window and a bad one is a smudged pane. The metaphor is attractive because it flatters the original, but it conceals more than it reveals.

Consider what a translator of a nineteenth-century novel actually confronts. A sentence may be long, its subordinate clauses stacked like crates, while the target language may prefer short declaratives. To break the sentence is to alter the rhythm that gave the narrator an air of fussy deliberation; to preserve it is to produce English that no reader would call natural. Neither choice is neutral. Fidelity to syntax and fidelity to effect pull in opposite directions, and the translator must decide which to betray. The window metaphor has no place for such a decision, since a window does not choose.

Some theorists have responded by inverting the hierarchy, arguing that translation is a form of authorship and that the translated text is a new work that merely shares a lineage with its source. This position has the virtue of honesty about the translator's labor, but it overcorrects.
