A translator who feels free to rewrite the plot, relocate the setting, or silence a troublesome character is not exercising creative license so much as abandoning an obligation. Readers who pick up a translation extend a particular kind of trust: they assume that the book in their hands answers to another book, and that its departures, where they occur, are the price of conveying something rather than the product of whim.

A more defensible account treats translation as interpretation, comparable to a pianist's reading of a sonata. No one supposes that two performances of the same sonata must be identical in order for both to be faithful, yet no one supposes that any sequence of notes counts as a performance of it either. The score constrains without determining. Similarly, the source text sets limits, so that some renderings are simply wrong, while leaving a wide field of legitimate variation. Disagreement among translators then appears not as evidence of failure but as the natural consequence of a text rich enough to sustain more than one reading.

This account also explains a curious feature of literary history: translations age faster than originals. A novel written in 1850 may still read as lively prose, while its English version from 1890 strikes us as stiff and quaint. If translation merely transferred a fixed meaning, there would be no reason for the English version to date, since the meaning has not changed. But if a translation is an interpretation shaped by the idiom and expectations of its own moment, then it will inevitably carry the marks of that moment, and later readers will perceive them as the dust of an earlier age. The original, written within the living language, is dated only in the way that all older books are; the translation is dated twice.

None of this implies that retranslation is wasteful. Each generation of translators, by making different compromises, reveals aspects of the source that earlier versions obscured. The proliferation of versions is not a sign that the work has been lost in transit but that it continues to be found.

qs.q: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?
o: Translators should be regarded as authors of new works whose obligations to the source are minimal.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 calls this authorship view an overcorrection and says translators still owe the source an obligation.
Translation is better understood as a constrained act of interpretation than as the transfer of a fixed meaning between languages.
Correct: Paragraphs 1 and 4 reject the fixed-meaning window idea and replace it with translation as constrained interpretation.
Translations inevitably betray their originals, so retranslation is largely wasteful.
Not quite. Paragraph 6 says the opposite: retranslation is not wasteful because each version reveals new aspects of the source.
Nineteenth-century novels are especially hard to translate because of their long sentences.
Not quite. Long sentences are just one example in paragraph 2, not the point of the whole passage.
qs.x: Correct: A main-idea question asks what the whole passage is arguing, not what one paragraph says. Watch how the author builds the case. Paragraph 1 attacks the idea that translation just carries a fixed meaning across, like a clear window. Paragraph 4 then offers the better account: translation is interpretation, like a pianist playing a sonata, where the source "constrains without determining." Paragraphs 5 and 6 add support. So the point is that translation is a constrained act of interpretation, not a transfer of fixed meaning. Why the others are wrong: the choice calling translators authors with minimal obligations is the view paragraph 3 says "overcorrects"; the choice saying retranslation is wasteful flips paragraph 6, which says retranslation is not wasteful; the choice about long nineteenth-century sentences is only the example in paragraph 2, a detail and not the conclusion. Trap: Picking a view because it gets lots of space. The author spends a whole paragraph on the authorship idea only to reject its extreme form.

qs.q: The author discusses the long, subordinate-clause-heavy sentence primarily to show that
o: translators must choose between competing kinds of fidelity, a feature the window metaphor cannot represent.
Correct: Paragraph 2 ends by saying the window metaphor cannot account for a choice, because a window does not choose.
readers generally prefer natural-sounding translations to literal ones, so translators should always favor fluency over fidelity
Not quite. The author never says fluency should always win. Paragraph 2 says both fidelity to syntax and to effect pull on the translator.
target languages generally prefer shorter sentences than source languages do, so long sentences are always broken up
Not quite. Paragraph 2 says a target language "may prefer" short sentences. That is a possibility, not an always-rule.
nineteenth-century prose is stylistically inferior to modern prose.
Not quite. The passage makes no comparison of old and modern prose quality. The long sentence just shows a hard choice.
qs.x: Correct: This is a function question. It asks why the author brings up the long sentence, not what the sentence says. Find the example in paragraph 2 and read what comes right after it. The author says breaking the sentence changes its rhythm, keeping it sounds unnatural, and "neither choice is neutral." Then comes the payoff: "The window metaphor has no place for such a decision, since a window does not choose." So the example exists to show that translators must pick between competing kinds of fidelity, which the window picture cannot handle. Why the others are wrong: the choice that fluency should always beat fidelity is a recommendation the author never makes, since the author says both pulls are real; the choice that target languages always break up long sentences turns one "may prefer" into an "always"; the choice that nineteenth-century prose is inferior is a value judgment the passage never offers. Trap: Turning a single illustration into a sweeping general claim instead of asking what point it serves.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward the view that translation is a form of authorship is best described as
o: qualified approval, crediting the view with one real merit while firmly rejecting its extreme conclusion.
Correct: Paragraph 3 praises the view's honesty about the translator's labor, then says it overcorrects.
neutral indifference, since the author neither credits nor criticizes the view that translators are authors
Not quite. The author does credit and criticize the view, so this isn't indifference. Paragraph 3 takes a clear position.
enthusiastic endorsement, treating translators as authors whose duties to the source text are minimal
Not quite. The author calls the view an overcorrection and says abandoning obligations to the source isn't creative license.
dismissive contempt, treating the view as having no merit whatsoever for the understanding of translation
Not quite. Too extreme. Paragraph 3 says the view has a real virtue, so the author doesn't see no merit at all.
qs.x: Correct: An attitude question asks how the author feels, so look for tone words. The authorship view shows up in paragraph 3. The author first gives it credit: it "has the virtue of honesty about the translator's labor." Then the pivot word arrives: "but it overcorrects." The rest of the paragraph explains why rewriting the plot or silencing a character abandons an obligation. So the attitude is qualified approval: one real merit credited, the extreme conclusion firmly rejected. Why the others are wrong: neutral indifference doesn't fit, because the author clearly praises and criticizes; enthusiastic endorsement ignores the "overcorrects" verdict; dismissive contempt ignores the "virtue of honesty" line, and saying there is no merit whatsoever is too extreme. Trap: Stopping at the sentence of praise and missing the "but" that follows. In CARS, what comes after the contrast word usually carries the author's real position.

qs.q: According to the passage, a translation is 'dated twice' because
o: translators of earlier eras were less skilled than modern translators, so their versions now seem clumsy and outdated
Not quite. The passage never blames translator skill. Paragraph 5 says the dating comes from the idiom and expectations of the translator's moment.
the source language changes faster than the target language, leaving the original harder to read with each decade
Not quite. Paragraph 5 never says one language changes faster than another. It talks about the translation being shaped by its own period.
the meaning of the source text changes over time while the translation stays fixed in the words of its own period
Not quite. Paragraph 5 says "the meaning has not changed." The dating comes from the translation's period, not shifting meaning.
it ages as an older book does, and it also bears the idiom and the expectations of the period in which it was made.
Correct: Paragraph 5 says the translation ages like any older book and also carries the idiom and expectations of its own moment.
qs.x: Correct: This asks for what the passage itself states, not a reason that merely sounds fair. Go to the end of paragraph 5. The author says the original is "dated only in the way that all older books are; the translation is dated twice." The paragraph explains the second layer: a translation is an interpretation shaped by "the idiom and expectations of its own moment," so it carries marks of that moment. So the two layers are ordinary age plus the period's own idiom and expectations. Why the others are wrong: the choice about translators being less skilled is an outside reason, and paragraph 5 never blames skill; the choice about the source language changing faster than the target reverses the logic, since the passage says the source meaning has not changed; the choice that the source meaning changes while the translation stays fixed also contradicts paragraph 5, which says the meaning has not changed. Trap: Supplying a believable outside explanation instead of the one the author actually gives.

qs.q: Two respected translators render a poem very differently, but one mistakes a word meaning 'river bank' for one meaning 'financial institution.' Based on the passage, the author would most likely say that
o: both renderings are equally legitimate because disagreement among respected translators is natural and the source permits many readings
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says some renderings are simply wrong, so the mistaken word is not covered by natural disagreement.
the stylistic difference is an error, but the mistaken word is acceptable creative license because translators are authors in their own right
Not quite. Paragraph 3 rejects the idea that translators have license to depart from the source. A plain mistake is not creative license.
the stylistic difference reflects legitimate variation, while the mistaken word falls outside the limits the source sets.
Correct: Paragraph 4 allows wide variation in style, but says the source sets limits, so the mistaken word is simply wrong.
both renderings fail because neither matches the original exactly, and no translation ever could
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says two faithful performances need not be identical, so exact matching is not required.
qs.x: Correct: This is an application question. You take the author's rule and apply it to a new case. The rule is in paragraph 4: the source "sets limits, so that some renderings are simply wrong, while leaving a wide field of legitimate variation," and "the score constrains without determining." In the new case there are two different things. The very different styles fall inside the field of legitimate variation. Mistaking a river bank for a financial institution is a plain error, outside the limits the source sets. Why the others are wrong: calling both renderings equally legitimate ignores the "some renderings are simply wrong" line; calling the mistaken word acceptable creative license is the authorship view that paragraph 3 says goes too far; saying both fail because neither matches the original exactly demands perfection, which paragraph 4 says faithfulness does not require. Trap: Stretching paragraph 4's point that disagreement among translators is natural to cover every difference and forgetting the limits the source still sets.

qs.q: The passage attributes which of the following assumptions to those who call translators traitors?
o: Readers who lack the source language cannot judge whether a translation is accurate, so they must simply trust the translator.
Not quite. Readers' trust comes up in paragraph 3, but it is not the assumption behind the traitor accusation in paragraph 1.
A text has a meaning that exists independently of any particular language and can be carried over intact.
Correct: Paragraph 1 says the accusation assumes a stable core of meaning, existing before any language, that can be carried across.
A translation should sound more natural to its readers than the original sounded to its first audience.
Not quite. Paragraph 1 says nothing about naturalness. The assumption is about carrying a fixed meaning across intact.
Translators generally lack sufficient knowledge of the source language to render its subtler meanings reliably.
Not quite. The passage never says translators lack language knowledge. The assumption in paragraph 1 is about meaning, not skill.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks what assumption sits behind the "traitor" accusation, so go straight to where that accusation is explained. Paragraph 1 says it rests on the assumption "that a text possesses a stable core of meaning that exists prior to any language," which the translator carries across "without spilling any of it." That matches the choice about a meaning that exists independently of any language and can be carried over intact. Why the others are wrong: the choice about readers having to trust the translator is touched on in paragraph 3, but it is about readers, not the traitor accusation; the choice about natural sound talks about fluency, which the paragraph 1 assumption never mentions; the choice that translators lack knowledge of the source language blames skill, and the passage never says that. Trap: Choosing a statement that sounds like a plausible reason to call translators traitors without checking it against what paragraph 1 actually says.

passages.title: FL01 · CARS · Passage 2
text: City planners have traditionally regarded street vending as a symptom of disorder, a residue of underdevelopment that modernization will eventually sweep away. Municipal codes in many cities reflect this assumption: vendors are licensed sparingly, confined to designated zones, or prohibited outright in commercial districts. Yet in cities around the world the number of street vendors has not declined as economies have grown; in several it has risen. This persistence is awkward for the view that vending is a transitional phenomenon, and it has prompted researchers to ask whether the planners' premise was mistaken from the start.

One line of argument holds that vending persists because it performs functions that formal retail does not. A vendor stationed outside a transit station sells to commuters at precisely the moment and place where demand peaks, in quantities as small as a single piece of fruit or a pair of batteries. Large stores cannot profitably serve such demand, because their costs of rent, staffing, and inventory presuppose bulk sales and steady foot traffic. The vendor's low overhead is not a defect of the enterprise but the source of its flexibility. Moreover, vending offers entry to people excluded from formal employment by lack of credentials, capital, or documentation. To close the street is therefore not simply to remove an eyesore; it is to remove a rung from a ladder that some residents have no other way of climbing.

Critics of vending respond that these virtues are purchased at a cost borne by others. Crowded sidewalks impede pedestrians, particularly those with disabilities; uninspected food poses health risks; and vendors who pay no taxes enjoy an advantage over shopkeepers who do. These objections deserve to be taken seriously, but they are not all of one kind. Some concern genuine harms, such as obstruction and contamination, which can in principle be addressed through regulation of where and how vending occurs. Others concern fairness among competitors, which might be addressed by bringing vendors into the tax system on terms they can afford. Only if one assumes that vending cannot be regulated, and can only be tolerated or eliminated, does the existence of these costs justify prohibition.

The experience of cities that have tried regulation is instructive but mixed. Where authorities have negotiated with vendor associations over designated spaces, standardized stalls, and modest fees, congestion has often fallen and complaints have diminished. But in other cities, formalization has produced fees and permit requirements that only the more established vendors could meet, driving the poorest out to operate illegally and thereby exposing them to harassment and confiscation. The lesson is not that regulation fails but that its design matters: rules written without the participation of those they govern tend to serve the interests of those who wrote them.

It would be a mistake, then, to treat the debate as a contest between order and chaos. The street is a shared resource whose uses compete, and every arrangement of it, including the arrangement that excludes vendors, embodies a judgment about whose needs count. Planners who recognize this are better placed to ask which combination of rules would allow pedestrians, shopkeepers, and vendors to coexist, rather than assuming that one of the three is an intruder.

qs.q: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Vendors' advantages over shopkeepers, such as lower rent and exemption from taxes, are unfair enough to justify prohibiting street vending outright.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 says the critics' costs justify prohibition only if vending cannot be regulated, so the author does not endorse a ban.
Street vending persists for reasons planners overlooked, so the productive question is how to design fair regulations rather than whether to eliminate it.
Correct: The passage argues vending persists for real reasons and ends by asking how to design rules that let all three groups coexist.
Street vending is a transitional phenomenon that will fade on its own as cities grow richer and formal retail expands, so no policy response is needed.
Not quite. This is the planners' premise from paragraph 1, which the author questions because vending has not declined.
Cities that regulate vending have consistently reduced congestion and complaints, which shows that regulation works better than tolerance or prohibition.
Not quite. Too strong. Paragraph 4 calls the experience "mixed" and says some formalization pushed the poorest out.
qs.x: Correct: A main-idea question wants the point of the whole passage. Track the moves. Paragraph 1 says vending persists despite planners' expectations, so their premise may be mistaken. Paragraph 2 gives reasons it persists. Paragraph 3 answers the critics and says their concerns can be handled by regulation. Paragraph 4 says regulation depends on its design. Paragraph 5 asks which rules let pedestrians, shopkeepers and vendors coexist. So the main idea is that vending persists for overlooked reasons, and the real question is how to design fair rules, not whether to eliminate it. Why the others are wrong: the choice calling for outright prohibition fits only one side of the critics and ignores paragraph 3's point that regulation is possible; the choice saying vending will fade on its own is the planners' old view that paragraph 1 doubts; the choice saying regulation has consistently reduced congestion ignores paragraph 4, which calls the results "mixed." Trap: Picking an extreme (ban it, or celebrate it) when the author keeps taking the middle position.

qs.q: The author mentions a single piece of fruit and a pair of batteries in order to
o: argue that small purchases are economically unimportant and therefore not worth regulating or counting.
Not quite. The author uses the small purchases as evidence of real demand, not as something unimportant.
show that vendors depend on commuters more than on any other customers, since commuters buy in small quantities.
Not quite. Paragraph 2 mentions commuters as one example. It never ranks them above other customers.
suggest that vendors' goods are of lower quality than those sold in stores, which explains their lower prices.
Not quite. Paragraph 2 says nothing about vendors' goods being worse. It credits their low overhead.
illustrate a real demand that formal stores cannot profitably serve, given the cost structures they bear.
Correct: The examples in paragraph 2 show small-quantity demand that large stores cannot profitably serve given their costs.
qs.x: Correct: This is a function question: why does the author name these two items? Find them in paragraph 2. A vendor sells to commuters "in quantities as small as a single piece of fruit or a pair of batteries." The next sentences explain that large stores "cannot profitably serve such demand," because their costs "presuppose bulk sales and steady foot traffic." So the examples show real small-quantity demand that formal stores can't profitably meet. Why the others are wrong: the choice calling small purchases unimportant says the opposite, since the author treats them as proof of a function vendors perform; the choice about commuters being the main customers stretches one example into a ranking of customers; the choice about lower quality is never raised, and the passage ties vendors' low prices to low overhead, not poor goods. Trap: Reading the examples as trivial rather than as evidence for the point the next sentence makes.

qs.q: According to the passage, the costs critics attribute to vending would justify prohibition only if
o: formal retailers could not otherwise compete with vendors who avoid rents, licenses, and taxes.
Not quite. That repeats a critic's fairness complaint. Paragraph 3 says fairness can be handled through the tax system.
pedestrian obstruction outweighed the benefits that vending provides to commuters and low-income buyers.
Not quite. The author never weighs harms against benefits to justify a ban. The stated condition is about whether vending can be regulated.
vending could not be regulated and could only be tolerated or eliminated.
Correct: Paragraph 3 says prohibition is justified only if vending cannot be regulated and can only be tolerated or eliminated.
vendors refused to pay taxes even when offered a workable way to do so.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 suggests bringing vendors into the tax system on terms they can afford, so refusal is not the stated condition.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks for a condition the author states, so look for "only if." In paragraph 3, after sorting the critics' objections, the author writes: "Only if one assumes that vending cannot be regulated, and can only be tolerated or eliminated, does the existence of these costs justify prohibition." That matches the choice about vending that could not be regulated and could only be tolerated or eliminated. Why the others are wrong: the choice about retailers being unable to compete is a critic's complaint, not the author's condition; the choice that obstruction outweighs the benefits is a weighing the author never performs, and it isn't the stated condition; the choice about vendors refusing to pay taxes ignores that the author says fairness can be addressed by bringing vendors into the tax system on affordable terms. Trap: Choosing an option that repeats a critic's complaint instead of the exact condition the author names.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the argument that vending persists because it fills roles formal retail does not?
o: Vendor numbers are highest near transit stations and other places where crowds gather at predictable hours.
Not quite. Crowds at predictable hours fit paragraph 2's point that vendors meet demand where and when it peaks.
Many vendors lack formal credentials or documentation that would qualify them for work in the formal retail sector, which is closed to them.
Not quite. This supports paragraph 2's claim that vending offers entry to people excluded from formal employment.
Most vendor sales are of the same products, in the same quantities and at the same prices as those at nearby formal stores.
Correct: If vendors sell the same things at the same prices as stores, they are not filling a role formal retail lacks.
Vendors' overhead is much lower than the rent, utilities, and licensing fees paid by formal stores selling comparable goods.
Not quite. Low overhead is exactly what paragraph 2 calls the source of the vendors' flexibility, so this strengthens the argument.
qs.x: Correct: A weaken question asks which new fact hurts the argument. First name the argument: vending persists because it does things formal retail does not (paragraph 2: serving small, peak-time demand, low overhead, entry for excluded people). The best weakener shows vendors are not doing anything different. If most vendor sales are the same products, quantities and prices as nearby stores, then vendors aren't filling a distinct role. Why the others are wrong: vendors clustering near crowds at predictable hours fits the point about meeting demand where it peaks; vendors lacking credentials for formal work supports the claim that vending offers entry to the excluded; vendors' low overhead is the very advantage paragraph 2 names. All three help the argument. Trap: Picking a fact that sounds negative about vendors, when it actually fits the argument being tested.

qs.q: The author's treatment of the critics' objections can best be described as
o: dismissive, treating the objections as pretexts for excluding the poor from public space entirely.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 says the objections deserve to be taken seriously and never calls them pretexts.
resigned, accepting that the costs of vending cannot be reduced by any regulatory design.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 says the harms can in principle be addressed through regulation, so the author is not resigned.
alarmed, because the harms to pedestrians and shopkeepers are described as severe and growing.
Not quite. The author never describes the harms as severe or growing. The tone is measured.
even-handed, granting the objections real seriousness while distinguishing carefully among them.
Correct: Paragraph 3 grants the objections real seriousness, then sorts them into harms and fairness issues.
qs.x: Correct: This asks for the author's tone toward the critics. Look at paragraph 3. The author says the objections "deserve to be taken seriously," then adds that "they are not all of one kind" and sorts them into genuine harms, which regulation can address, and fairness among competitors, which taxes can address. Taking them seriously while sorting them carefully is even-handed. Why the others are wrong: dismissive, treating them as pretexts, fails because the author says they deserve serious attention and never accuses the critics of bad motives; resigned, accepting that costs can't be reduced, contradicts paragraph 3's view that regulation can address them; alarmed, calling the harms severe and growing, is not supported, because the author never describes the harms that way. Trap: Assuming that an author who argues for vendors must be hostile to the critics.

qs.q: A city that wished to follow the passage's closing advice would most likely
o: set a fee schedule through city officials alone and enforce it strictly with fines and confiscation of goods from violators.
Not quite. Paragraph 4 warns that rules written without the people they govern serve the writers, and it describes confiscation as harmful.
convene vendors, shopkeepers, and pedestrian representatives together to draft shared rules for the use of sidewalk space.
Correct: Paragraphs 4 and 5 call for rules shaped with those they govern, treating pedestrians, shopkeepers and vendors as all belonging.
move vendors out of commercial districts to designated peripheral zones where they would not obstruct pedestrians or compete with stores.
Not quite. Paragraph 5 says to stop assuming one group is an intruder. Pushing vendors to the edges does exactly that.
stop regulating vending entirely and leave the use of sidewalk space to be settled by individual vendors and shopkeepers.
Not quite. The author says regulation's design matters, not that it should be dropped. Paragraph 3 says regulation can address the harms.
qs.x: Correct: This application question asks what a city would do if it followed the author's final advice. That advice is in paragraphs 4 and 5. Paragraph 4 says "rules written without the participation of those they govern tend to serve the interests of those who wrote them." Paragraph 5 asks which rules let "pedestrians, shopkeepers, and vendors" coexist, with none treated as an intruder. So the city would bring all three groups together to draft shared rules. Why the others are wrong: setting fees through officials alone and enforcing them with confiscation is exactly the top-down approach paragraph 4 warns about; moving vendors to peripheral zones treats vendors as the intruders, which paragraph 5 rejects; stopping regulation entirely ignores the author's view that design matters and that regulation can work. Trap: Mistaking opposition to prohibition for opposition to any regulation.

passages.title: FL01 · CARS · Passage 3
text: When photography became widely available in the nineteenth century, many commentators greeted it as a machine for preserving the past. A photograph seemed to hold a moment in suspension, immune to the fading and embellishment that corrupt the memories of those who were present. Families commissioned portraits of the dying; governments documented monuments; travelers returned with images of places their neighbors would never see. The camera, it was said, could not lie, and a civilization that possessed it would never again lose its history.

The confidence was misplaced, and the reasons are more interesting than the usual complaint that images can be manipulated. Even an unaltered photograph records a decision. Someone chose the angle, the framing, the moment, and, just as important, what to leave outside the frame. A photograph of a harvest festival may omit the debts that burdened the farmers; a photograph of a factory may show gleaming machinery and no workers. The image is accurate in what it shows and silent about what it excludes, and the silence is easily mistaken for absence. Viewers rarely ask what lay a few feet to the left. A caption adds a further layer of selection, since the words beneath an image tell viewers what to notice and what to ignore.

A subtler difficulty concerns what photographs do to the memories they were meant to protect. Psychologists have long observed that remembering is not retrieval of a stored record but reconstruction, assembled anew each time from fragments and expectations. When a photograph is available, it supplies the fragments. Over years, a person who looks repeatedly at an image of a childhood birthday may come to remember the party as the photograph depicts it, with the remembered scene acquiring the photograph's composition, its vantage point, even its colors. Events that were never photographed, meanwhile, receive no such reinforcement and may fade. The camera, in other words, does not merely preserve the past; it selects the portions of it that will survive in memory, and it does so according to what was photographed rather than what mattered.

This selective effect has consequences that extend beyond the individual. Societies, like persons, remember through the artifacts they have. An archive heavy with images of official ceremonies and light on images of ordinary labor will tend to yield a history of ceremonies. Those who were rarely photographed, because they lacked the means or the standing to commission portraits, are underrepresented in the visual record and thus easier to forget. Photography, which was supposed to democratize memory, has in many periods reproduced the hierarchies of the societies that practiced it.

None of this is an argument for discarding photographs. The remedy for a partial record is a larger and more varied one, together with a habit of reading images as evidence produced by particular people for particular purposes. A photograph read in this way becomes more informative, not less, because its omissions, once noticed, are themselves data. What is required is a shift in how we regard the medium: not as a mirror held up to the past, but as one witness among many in a continuing argument about it.

qs.q: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Early commentators were right that photography democratized historical memory.
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says photography failed to democratize memory and often reproduced the hierarchies of its societies.
Photography has damaged memory so much that archives should avoid relying on it.
Not quite. Paragraph 5 opens by saying none of this is an argument for discarding photographs.
Photographs, though once thought to preserve the past faithfully, are selective records that also shape memory and should be read critically alongside other evidence.
Correct: The passage moves from faithful preservation to selection, to shaping memory, to reading photographs critically beside other evidence.
Photographs are unreliable chiefly because they can be manipulated.
Not quite. Paragraph 2 says the reasons are more interesting than the usual complaint about manipulation, and discusses unaltered photographs.
qs.x: Correct: A main-idea question needs the whole path of the passage. Paragraph 1 describes the old belief that cameras preserve the past faithfully. Paragraph 2 says photographs are selective. Paragraph 3 says they also reshape the memories they were meant to protect. Paragraph 4 says this selectivity affects whole societies. Paragraph 5 says keep photographs but read them critically, as "one witness among many." The choice that captures all of that is the one about selective records that shape memory and should be read critically. Why the others are wrong: the choice saying early commentators were right about democratizing memory contradicts paragraph 4, which says photography often reproduced existing hierarchies; the choice saying archives should avoid photographs is rejected in paragraph 5, "None of this is an argument for discarding photographs"; the choice about manipulation is the "usual complaint" that paragraph 2 says it goes beyond. Trap: Choosing the familiar complaint (manipulation) that the author explicitly moves past.

qs.q: According to the passage, a person who repeatedly views a photograph of a childhood event may
o: come to remember the event with the photograph's composition and from the photograph's vantage point.
Correct: Paragraph 3 says the remembered scene acquires the photograph's composition, vantage point and even its colors.
forget the event entirely once the photograph has replaced the original experience in memory.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 says the photograph supplies fragments for memory. It doesn't say the event is forgotten.
recall the event more accurately than someone who has never seen the photograph, because the image fixes the details.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 says memory is reshaped to match the photograph, not that it becomes more accurate.
come to distrust the photograph because it conflicts with the person's own recollection of the day.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 describes memory absorbing the photograph, not rejecting it. Distrust is never mentioned.
qs.x: Correct: This asks what the passage says happens, so find the spot. Paragraph 3 says a person who looks repeatedly at a childhood birthday photograph "may come to remember the party as the photograph depicts it, with the remembered scene acquiring the photograph's composition, its vantage point, even its colors." That matches the choice about remembering the event with the photograph's composition and vantage point. Why the others are wrong: forgetting the event entirely is too extreme, since the photograph supplies fragments and reinforces memory; recalling more accurately because the image fixes details reverses the point, because the memory is reshaped by the photograph and not made more accurate; distrusting the photograph because it conflicts with one's recollection is never mentioned, and the passage says the photograph takes over the recollection. Trap: Assuming that reinforcement from a photograph means a more accurate memory, when the passage says it means a memory that copies the photograph.

qs.q: The author mentions a harvest festival and a factory in order to illustrate that
o: images of labor are more valuable to later historians than images of ceremonies and public celebrations.
Not quite. The examples show omission, not the relative value of labor images. The passage never ranks them for historians.
an accurate photograph can still mislead a later viewer through what it chose to leave outside the frame.
Correct: Both examples in paragraph 2 are true images that are silent about debts or workers, so they mislead through what they leave out.
photographers deliberately conceal economic hardship in order to flatter the powerful people who hired them.
Not quite. Paragraph 2 never says photographers hid hardship on purpose. It only says the frame excludes things.
governments commissioned most early photographs in order to promote official accounts of local life.
Not quite. The passage mentions governments documenting monuments in paragraph 1, but never claims they commissioned most photographs.
qs.x: Correct: This function question asks why the author gives two examples. Find them in paragraph 2: a harvest festival photo that may omit the farmers' debts, and a factory photo showing gleaming machinery but no workers. The author then states the point: "The image is accurate in what it shows and silent about what it excludes." So the examples show that an accurate photograph can still mislead through what it leaves outside the frame. Why the others are wrong: the choice about labor images being more valuable to historians is a judgment the passage never makes, though paragraph 4 touches on ordinary labor; the choice that photographers deliberately hide hardship to flatter the powerful assigns motive, but paragraph 2 only describes what a frame leaves out; the choice that governments commissioned most early photographs makes a historical claim the passage never states. Trap: Attributing intent to photographers when the passage only describes what a frame excludes.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the author's claim about how photographs affect memory?
o: Participants who repeatedly viewed photographs of an event later recalled it no differently from those who never saw them.
Correct: No difference in recall between viewers and non-viewers would contradict paragraph 3's claim that photographs reshape memory.
Participants who viewed photographs reported greater confidence in their memories of the event, though their accounts were no more detailed.
Not quite. This is about confidence, not what is remembered. It doesn't contradict the claim that photographs reshape memory content.
Participants shown a photograph afterward described the event using details that were present in the photograph and absent from other accounts.
Not quite. Using details from the photograph is what paragraph 3 predicts, so this supports the claim.
Events that were never photographed were recalled less often and less vividly than photographed ones, even after controlling for importance.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 says unphotographed events may fade, so this finding supports the author.
qs.x: Correct: A weaken question asks which finding would damage the author's claim. The claim, from paragraph 3, is that repeatedly viewing a photograph reshapes how the person remembers the event, and that unphotographed events fade. If people who repeatedly viewed photographs recalled the event no differently from people who never saw them, the photographs did not reshape recollection. That directly contradicts the claim. Why the others are wrong: greater confidence without more detail is about confidence, not about whether the content of memory changed; describing the event with details found only in the photograph supports the claim, since it shows the photograph supplying the memory; unphotographed events being recalled less often and less vividly even after controlling for importance matches paragraph 3's claim that they fade. Trap: Choosing a finding about confidence, which is not the same as the content or accuracy of memory.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward the nineteenth-century belief that the camera could not lie is best described as
o: uncertain, offering no judgment of it because the evidence is too sparse for a verdict.
Not quite. The author states a verdict in paragraph 2, calling the confidence misplaced, so this isn't uncertain.
admiring of its optimism, since it expressed hope that images could democratize knowledge.
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says photography often failed to democratize memory, so the author isn't admiring the optimism.
scornful of those who held it, regarding them as naive about the new technology.
Not quite. The author explains why the belief seemed reasonable and doesn't call people naive.
critical of the belief, though attentive to the reasons it seemed reasonable at the time.
Correct: Paragraph 2 calls the confidence misplaced, while paragraph 1 lays out why the belief seemed reasonable.
qs.x: Correct: This asks for the author's attitude toward the old belief that the camera could not lie. Look at paragraph 2, which opens: "The confidence was misplaced." That is criticism. But the author also describes why the belief felt reasonable: in paragraph 1, a photograph seemed to hold a moment "immune to the fading and embellishment" of memory. So the attitude is critical of the belief but understanding of why people held it. Why the others are wrong: uncertain, giving no judgment, ignores the plain verdict "misplaced"; admiring of its optimism about democratizing knowledge doesn't fit, since paragraph 4 says photography failed to democratize memory; scornful of the people ignores that the author explains why the belief seemed reasonable and never calls its holders naive. Trap: Confusing criticism of an idea with scorn for the people who held it.

qs.q: A historian using a town's photographic archive from 1900 would, following the author's advice, most likely
o: treat the images as the most reliable evidence available because they are unaltered records of exactly what was there at the time.
Not quite. Paragraph 2 says even unaltered photographs record choices about the frame, so they aren't the most reliable evidence.
discard the archive because it overrepresents town officials and the wealthy residents who paid for portraits and public ceremonies.
Not quite. Paragraph 5 says none of this argues for discarding photographs, and omissions are themselves data.
rely on residents' memories instead of the photographs because memories are free of the camera's selective and posed view of the town.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 says memory is reconstructed and reshaped by photographs, so memories aren't free of selectivity.
ask who made the photographs and for what purpose, note what is absent, and supplement them with other sources.
Correct: Paragraph 5 advises reading images as evidence made by particular people for particular purposes, noting omissions, and adding more sources.
qs.x: Correct: This application question asks what the author's advice would look like in practice. The advice is in paragraph 5: the remedy is "a larger and more varied" record plus "a habit of reading images as evidence produced by particular people for particular purposes," with omissions treated as data. So the historian would ask who made the photographs and why, note what is missing, and bring in other sources. Why the others are wrong: treating the images as the most reliable, unaltered evidence is the old belief the passage calls misplaced; discarding the archive because it overrepresents officials and the wealthy is rejected in paragraph 5, which says not to discard photographs; relying on residents' memories instead ignores paragraph 3, where memory is shown to be reconstructed and even shaped by photographs. Trap: Swinging from naive trust to total rejection. The author wants critical use, not abandonment.

passages.title: FL01 · CARS · Passage 4
text: Before the late nineteenth century, most towns kept their own time. Noon was the moment the sun stood highest overhead, and clocks in neighboring towns might differ by several minutes without anyone being troubled. The arrangement worked because few people needed to coordinate with anyone beyond walking distance. The railroad changed this. A train traveling between distant cities crossed many local times in a single journey, and timetables listing arrivals according to a dozen different noons were nearly useless. Railway companies therefore adopted standard time zones, and within a generation most communities had set their clocks to match.

The usual account treats this change as a triumph of practicality, a case of technology demanding rationality and rationality obliging. There is truth in this, but the account leaves out the resistance. Many towns resisted the new time, regarding it as an imposition by distant corporations on local custom. Newspaper editors complained that the railroads had presumed to alter the day itself. Some communities maintained two sets of time, one for the railway station and one for everything else, and a few clung to local time for years. That the resistance eventually faded reveals less about the persuasiveness of the arguments than about the mounting costs of standing apart: a town that kept its own time could not be conveniently reached, and so it gradually lost the commerce that depended on being reachable.

Sociologists have drawn from this episode a broader lesson about how standards spread. A standard is valuable largely because others use it, and its value to any single adopter increases with the number of adopters. Such arrangements tend to be unstable in the early period, when no one wishes to be first, and then abruptly self-reinforcing once a critical mass has been reached. Once most had adopted railway time, holdouts faced pressure not from the railways' power but from the choices of their neighbors, who preferred to deal with those whose clocks agreed with their own.

The adoption of standard time also altered how people experienced the day. When time was local and tied to the sun, it was understood as a feature of the natural world, something observed rather than set. Standard time was visibly conventional: it could be adjusted by agreement, and it applied equally to a place where the sun had risen and one where it had not. As clock time grew detached from the sun, it became easier to treat as a resource to be measured, scheduled, and allocated. Factory managers could compare hours worked; schools could divide the day into uniform periods; workers began to speak of being "on the clock." Whether these developments flowed from standard time or merely coincided with it is difficult to establish, since industrialization was proceeding for independent reasons. But the timing suggests that a shared, conventional time made certain habits of mind easier to acquire.

It would be wrong to conclude that the change was simply imposed on a passive public, or that it was freely chosen. The more accurate description lies between: individuals made rational choices, but the range of choices available to them was determined by decisions others had already made.

qs.q: Which of the following best summarizes the passage?
o: The adoption of standard time was neither simple imposition nor free choice but resulted from choices constrained by others' earlier decisions, and it may have encouraged new habits of mind.
Correct: This combines the resistance, the standards lesson, the habits-of-mind suggestion and the closing view that choices were constrained.
Standard time caused the scheduling habits of industrial society.
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says it is hard to tell whether such habits flowed from standard time or just coincided with it.
Standard time spread because communities recognized it as more rational.
Not quite. Paragraph 2 calls this the usual account and says it leaves out the resistance.
Railway companies imposed standard time on communities that had no power to resist.
Not quite. Paragraph 5 says the change was not simply imposed on a passive public.
qs.x: Correct: A summary question wants the passage's whole shape. Paragraph 1 says railways pushed towns into standard time. Paragraph 2 says the usual practical-triumph story leaves out the resistance, and that resistance faded because standing apart became costly. Paragraph 3 explains how standards spread when neighbors adopt them. Paragraph 4 says standard time may have made new habits of mind easier to acquire. Paragraph 5 concludes that the change was neither simply imposed nor freely chosen: people chose rationally, but within options shaped by others' earlier decisions. Why the others are wrong: saying standard time caused industrial scheduling habits ignores paragraph 4, which says it is difficult to establish and industrialization had independent causes; saying it spread because communities saw it as more rational is the usual account that paragraph 2 says leaves out the resistance; saying railways imposed it on powerless communities is rejected in paragraph 5. Trap: Picking a single-cause story after the author has rejected both single-cause stories.

qs.q: According to the passage, local resistance to standard time faded mainly because
o: the arguments for standard time proved persuasive to local officials and ordinary residents alike.
Not quite. Paragraph 2 says the fading reveals less about persuasive arguments than about the costs of standing apart.
railway companies directly punished towns that kept local time by withholding service and freight.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 says the pressure came not from the railways' power but from neighboring towns' choices.
keeping its own local time made a town inconvenient to reach, and so it gradually lost commerce.
Correct: Paragraph 2 says a town with its own time was hard to reach and gradually lost commerce.
newspaper editors changed their positions and began urging readers to adopt the new time.
Not quite. Editors appear in paragraph 2 only as complainers. The passage never says they changed their position.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks for the stated reason the resistance faded. Go to the end of paragraph 2. The author says the fading reveals "less about the persuasiveness of the arguments than about the mounting costs of standing apart: a town that kept its own time could not be conveniently reached, and so it gradually lost the commerce that depended on being reachable." That matches the choice about inconvenience and lost commerce. Why the others are wrong: the choice about persuasive arguments is exactly what the author says is not the explanation; the choice that railways punished towns by withholding service goes against paragraph 3, which says pressure came "not from the railways' power but from the choices of their neighbors"; the choice about editors changing sides is never mentioned, since editors appear only as complainers. Trap: Picking the persuasion answer, which matches the usual account the author is criticizing.

qs.q: The detail that some communities kept two sets of time serves to
o: suggest that dual timekeeping was a stable long-term solution.
Not quite. The passage says resistance eventually faded, so it never calls dual time a stable long-term solution.
show that railway time was less accurate than local time.
Not quite. The passage never compares accuracy. The two sets of time are listed as resistance.
illustrate the extent of the resistance to standard time.
Correct: Paragraph 2 lists the two sets of time among the ways towns resisted standard time.
demonstrate that local time was more reliable.
Not quite. Reliability is never discussed. Local time is defended as custom, not as more reliable.
qs.x: Correct: A detail question asks why a small fact is in the passage, so check where it sits. The two sets of time appear in paragraph 2, in a list of how towns resisted: editors complained, some communities "maintained two sets of time," and a few "clung to local time for years." The paragraph is about the resistance that the usual account leaves out, so this detail shows how far the resistance went. Why the others are wrong: calling dual timekeeping a stable long-term solution is never said, and the paragraph says the resistance eventually faded; saying railway time was less accurate than local time is not in the passage, which never compares accuracy; saying local time was more reliable is also never claimed, because the resistance was about custom and imposition. Trap: Reading a detail as evidence for a claim the passage never makes.

qs.q: Which situation is most analogous to the spread of standards described in the third paragraph?
o: A factory buys a new machine because it lowers costs of production, whatever other factories decide to do.
Not quite. This factory's benefit doesn't depend on what other factories do, so it lacks the rising value with adopters.
A messaging app grows more useful to each person as more friends join, so holdouts eventually sign up.
Correct: The app's value to each person grows as more friends join, and holdouts follow their neighbors, matching paragraph 3.
A restaurant grows popular after a single critic's favorable review appears in the local newspaper and draws steady crowds.
Not quite. Popularity here comes from one critic's review, not from value growing as more people adopt.
A government mandates a new currency and punishes anyone who continues to use the old one in trade.
Not quite. This works through government power. Paragraph 3 says pressure came from neighbors' choices, not power.
qs.x: Correct: An analogy question asks you to match the mechanism, not the topic. Paragraph 3 describes it: a standard "is valuable largely because others use it," its value to each adopter rises with the number of adopters, nobody wants to go first, then it becomes self-reinforcing once a critical mass is reached, and holdouts feel pressure from their neighbors. A messaging app that gets more useful to each person as more friends join, so holdouts eventually sign up, fits that exactly. Why the others are wrong: the factory buying a cost-saving machine whatever other factories do has no link to other adopters; the restaurant boosted by one critic's review works by one outside influence, not by value growing with each new user; the government mandate with punishment works by power, but paragraph 3 says the pressure did not come from power. Trap: Matching on surface features (a change of practice) instead of the mechanism of value rising with adoption.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the author's suggestion that conventional time made new habits of mind easier to acquire?
o: Industrialization proceeded faster in regions with more railways, and those regions also adopted standard time earliest and most completely.
Not quite. The author already says industrialization and standard time coincided, so this doesn't undercut the suggestion.
Regions that kept local time for decades adopted clock-based scheduling in factories and schools as quickly as standard-time regions did.
Correct: If local-time regions adopted clock scheduling just as fast, standard time wasn't what made those habits easier to acquire.
Factory managers in standard-time regions began comparing hours worked, output per shift, and wages across different plants.
Not quite. This just describes the habits of paragraph 4 appearing in standard-time regions, which fits the author's suggestion.
Most regions abandoned local time within a generation, and almost none returned to it afterward even when they were free to do so.
Not quite. This concerns how standard time spread, not whether it changed habits of mind.
qs.x: Correct: A weaken question asks which finding hurts the claim. The claim comes from paragraph 4: a shared, conventional time "made certain habits of mind easier to acquire," such as comparing hours and dividing the day into uniform periods. To weaken it, show that those habits arrived just as quickly without standard time. If regions that kept local time for decades adopted clock-based scheduling in factories and schools as fast as standard-time regions, then standard time wasn't what drove the habits. Why the others are wrong: industrialization moving faster where railways and standard time came early fits the author's own point that the two coincided, and doesn't separate cause from coincidence; managers comparing hours and output in standard-time regions simply describes the habits; regions abandoning local time and not going back is about the spread of standard time, not about habits of mind. Trap: Choosing a finding that fits the author's own account of things that coincided.

qs.q: The final paragraph primarily serves to
o: reject a choice between two extreme characterizations of how standard time was adopted.
Correct: Paragraph 5 says the change was neither simply imposed nor freely chosen, and offers a view between those extremes.
blame the railway companies for forcing communities to give up their local time.
Not quite. Paragraph 5 says it would be wrong to see the change as simply imposed, so it doesn't blame the railways.
introduce an objection to the sociologists' lesson about how standards spread through neighbors' choices.
Not quite. Paragraph 5 fits paragraph 3: choices were limited by what others had already decided.
summarize the evidence for resistance to standard time offered in the earlier paragraphs of the passage.
Not quite. The evidence for resistance is in paragraph 2. Paragraph 5 draws a conclusion rather than recapping.
qs.x: Correct: A function question asks what a paragraph does for the passage. Read paragraph 5: "It would be wrong to conclude that the change was simply imposed on a passive public, or that it was freely chosen." It then says the truth lies between, with rational choices made within a range others had set. So the paragraph rejects two extreme descriptions and offers a middle one. Why the others are wrong: blaming the railway companies for forcing the change is the imposition view the paragraph just called wrong; introducing an objection to the sociologists' lesson doesn't fit, because the closing synthesis actually matches paragraph 3, where neighbors' choices constrain holdouts; summarizing the evidence for resistance isn't what it does, since the resistance evidence is in paragraph 2 and paragraph 5 draws a conclusion. Trap: Treating a concluding synthesis as a new argument or a recap.

passages.title: FL01 · CARS · Passage 5
text: Listeners who encounter recordings made in the first decades of the twentieth century are often struck by how odd the performances sound. Violinists slide between notes with a persistence that modern players avoid; pianists roll chords and let the hands fall slightly out of synchrony; singers take liberties with tempo that a present-day conductor would not tolerate. The natural reaction is to suppose that these musicians were simply less disciplined than their successors, or that their era had not yet discovered the precision that recording would later demand.

This reaction mistakes a difference in convention for a difference in skill. The performers in question were frequently of extraordinary ability, and their departures from the written score were deliberate. In the tradition they inherited, a score was understood as a sketch rather than a specification; the performer's responsibility was to supply expressive inflection that notation could not capture, and a performance that adhered rigidly to the printed rhythm would have been considered lifeless. The modern ideal, in which the performer's task is to realize the composer's text with minimal intrusion, is itself a historical development, not an eternal standard.

Why did the ideal change? One explanation points to the recording itself. A live performance is heard once, and an idiosyncratic gesture that delights in the moment is forgotten in the next. A recording is heard again and again, and the same gesture, repeated, can begin to grate. Performers who knew their work would be preserved had reason to prefer interpretations that would withstand repetition, and listeners who could compare multiple recordings of the same piece began to notice and prize accuracy. Competition among recordings thus rewarded a kind of precision that concert halls had never demanded.

This explanation is plausible, but it is incomplete. Changes in taste were underway before recording became common, and they were driven partly by composers who grew impatient with what they regarded as performers' liberties. Several prominent composers of the period published increasingly detailed markings and issued public complaints about interpreters who altered their work. The recording industry may have accelerated the shift, but it found a movement already in progress, and it is unlikely to have created it.

There is a further irony. The performers whose styles now seem eccentric left recordings that make it possible to hear what they actually did, and the recordings reveal that written descriptions of their art can be misleading. Critics of the time praised a violinist's "restraint" or a pianist's "fidelity," words that a modern listener, hearing the recordings, would never apply. The vocabulary of praise had meant something different. Without the recordings we would have assumed that earlier musicians played much as we do and that the words meant what they mean to us. The medium that is blamed for standardizing performance has also preserved the evidence that standards were once otherwise.

That evidence invites humility. If conventions that seemed natural to one generation appear strange to the next, we have little reason to believe that our own are exempt from the same fate. Future listeners may find our scrupulous literalism as peculiar as we find the slides and rolled chords of our predecessors.

qs.q: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: Recording technology caused performers to abandon expressive freedom in favor of precision.
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says the recording explanation is plausible but incomplete, since taste was shifting before recording.
Modern performers should revive the slides and rolled chords of earlier players.
Not quite. The author never recommends reviving old practices. Paragraph 6 only suggests humility about our own conventions.
Early recordings sound odd because they reflect older performance conventions rather than lesser skill, and the later turn to literalism had several causes and is itself historically contingent.
Correct: Paragraph 2 sets convention against skill, paragraphs 3 and 4 give several causes, and paragraph 6 says our own conventions are contingent too.
Early performers were less disciplined than modern ones.
Not quite. Paragraph 2 says this reaction mistakes a difference in convention for a difference in skill.
qs.x: Correct: A main-idea question wants the whole argument. Paragraph 1 says early recordings sound odd and that people assume the musicians were less disciplined. Paragraph 2 says this "mistakes a difference in convention for a difference in skill," and calls the modern ideal "itself a historical development." Paragraphs 3 and 4 give causes for the change (recording, and earlier shifts in taste led by composers). Paragraph 6 asks for humility. That all matches the choice about older conventions rather than lesser skill, with several causes, and a later literalism that is historically contingent. Why the others are wrong: saying recording caused performers to abandon freedom is the explanation paragraph 4 calls incomplete; saying modern performers should revive slides and rolled chords is never urged, since the author only calls for humility; saying early performers were less disciplined is the reaction paragraph 2 rejects. Trap: Choosing the explanation the author presents first and then qualifies.

qs.q: According to the passage, in the tradition inherited by early twentieth-century performers a score was regarded as
o: a guide meant for composers to consult while composing rather than for performers to follow in public.
Not quite. The passage never mentions composers consulting scores while composing. Paragraph 2 is about how performers treated them.
a precise specification to be realized without alteration or any expressive addition by the performer.
Not quite. That describes the modern ideal. Paragraph 2 says the older tradition saw a score as a sketch, not a specification.
a historical document of little practical use to performers beyond establishing the notes.
Not quite. Paragraph 2 gives the score real importance as a sketch that performers filled in. It doesn't call it of little use.
an outline that the performer was expected to complete by adding expressive inflection of their own.
Correct: Paragraph 2 calls the score a sketch that the performer completed with expressive inflection notation couldn't capture.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks how the older tradition viewed a score. Paragraph 2 says: "a score was understood as a sketch rather than a specification; the performer's responsibility was to supply expressive inflection that notation could not capture." That matches the choice calling it an outline the performer completes with expressive inflection. Why the others are wrong: a guide for composers to consult while composing isn't said anywhere, and the passage is about performers; a precise specification to be realized without alteration is the modern ideal, which paragraph 2 contrasts with the older tradition; a document of little use beyond the notes goes too far, because the score was a sketch the performer built on, not something of little use. Trap: Mixing up the older convention with the modern ideal the passage sets against it.

qs.q: The author's view of the claim that recording caused the change in performance ideals is that it is
o: entirely mistaken, since recording had no effect on performance ideals whatsoever.
Not quite. Too extreme. Paragraph 4 says recording may have accelerated the shift, so it did have some effect.
fully adequate to explain the change without reference to any other cause or earlier development.
Not quite. Paragraph 4 calls the explanation incomplete and points to earlier shifts in taste and composers' complaints.
plausible but incomplete, because taste had already begun shifting before recording arrived.
Correct: Paragraph 4 says the explanation is plausible but incomplete because taste was already shifting before recording.
irrelevant to the history of performance, since technology never affects musical taste.
Not quite. The author grants that recording may have accelerated the shift, so it isn't irrelevant.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks for the author's view of the recording-caused-it theory. Paragraph 3 lays out that theory. Paragraph 4 then judges it: "This explanation is plausible, but it is incomplete. Changes in taste were underway before recording became common." It adds that recording "may have accelerated the shift" but is unlikely to have created it. So the view is plausible but incomplete. Why the others are wrong: entirely mistaken with no effect whatsoever is too extreme, because the author grants that recording may have accelerated the shift; fully adequate without any other cause is the opposite error, since the author names composers' impatience as another cause; irrelevant because technology never affects taste is also never said and clashes with the concession. Trap: Reading "incomplete" as "wrong", or ignoring the concession in "plausible."

qs.q: The author mentions critics who praised 'restraint' and 'fidelity' in order to show that
o: the vocabulary of praise meant something different then, so recordings can correct what written descriptions suggest.
Correct: Paragraph 5 says the praise words meant something different then, and recordings reveal that written descriptions can mislead.
performers of the time deliberately sought restraint, as the critics' praise indicates to modern listeners of the recordings.
Not quite. Paragraph 5 says modern listeners would never call these performances restrained. The words meant something else.
modern critics misuse words that earlier critics used correctly, so present-day reviews cannot be trusted as guides.
Not quite. The passage doesn't say modern critics misuse words. It says the meaning of the words changed over time.
critics of the time were poorly informed about music and could not hear what performers were actually doing.
Not quite. The passage never calls the critics uninformed. The issue is that the vocabulary meant something different.
qs.x: Correct: This function question asks why the author brings up critics praising "restraint" and "fidelity." Look at paragraph 5. The recordings show that these words wouldn't fit what we hear today: "The vocabulary of praise had meant something different." The author adds that without recordings we would have assumed the words meant what they mean to us. So the example shows that words meant something different then, and recordings can correct what written descriptions suggest. Why the others are wrong: saying performers deliberately sought restraint reverses it, since the recordings show playing no modern listener would call restrained; saying modern critics misuse words that earlier critics used correctly is not claimed, because the meaning simply shifted; saying earlier critics were poorly informed isn't said either, since the issue is changing vocabulary and not ignorance. Trap: Assuming the critics were wrong, when the point is that word meanings shifted.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the author's claim that changes in taste preceded the spread of recording?
o: Composers' public complaints and detailed markings appeared only after records were widely sold.
Correct: If the composers' complaints and markings came only after records sold widely, the evidence for earlier change is gone.
Listeners compared different recordings of the same piece and began to prefer the more literal performances.
Not quite. This supports the recording explanation from paragraph 3, but it doesn't show taste hadn't shifted earlier.
Some performers continued the older style on recordings made well after the new literalism had become common.
Not quite. Some performers keeping the old style doesn't say when taste began to change, so the timing claim stays.
Recordings of the same piece circulated widely by 1920, giving listeners versions to compare.
Not quite. Recordings existing by 1920 doesn't show the shift in taste came afterward, so the earlier-change claim stands.
qs.x: Correct: A weaken question asks which finding damages the claim. The claim, from paragraph 4, is that changes in taste started before recording became common, shown by composers who published detailed markings and complained about performers' liberties. If those markings and complaints appeared only after records were widely sold, the timing evidence disappears and taste no longer looks like it came first. Why the others are wrong: listeners comparing recordings and preferring literal performances is the rival recording explanation from paragraph 3 and does nothing to the timing claim; performers continuing the old style on later recordings concerns who stuck with it and doesn't touch when taste began to shift; recordings of the same piece circulating widely by 1920 only says recordings existed by then and doesn't show that the shift followed them. Trap: Picking a fact that supports the rival recording explanation without actually undermining the timing claim.

qs.q: The final paragraph suggests that the author would most likely agree that
o: future listeners will prefer the older style to the modern one once literalism has run its course.
Not quite. Paragraph 6 says future listeners may find our style peculiar, not that they will prefer the older one.
present-day performance conventions should not be assumed to be the permanent standard of correctness.
Correct: Paragraph 6 warns that our conventions are not exempt from seeming strange to later generations.
scrupulous literalism is a defect in modern performance that performers should be encouraged to abandon.
Not quite. The author doesn't call literalism a defect or urge anyone to abandon it. Paragraph 6 only asks for humility.
recordings are poor evidence of past practice because performers behaved differently before a microphone.
Not quite. Paragraph 5 says recordings preserve evidence of what performers actually did, so the author values them.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks what the author would agree with after the final paragraph. Paragraph 6 says: "If conventions that seemed natural to one generation appear strange to the next, we have little reason to believe that our own are exempt from the same fate." So the author would agree that present-day conventions should not be assumed to be the permanent standard of correctness. Why the others are wrong: predicting that future listeners will prefer the older style goes beyond the text, which only says they may find our literalism peculiar, not that they will prefer something; calling literalism a defect that performers should abandon turns a call for humility into a judgment, which the author never makes; saying recordings are poor evidence of past practice contradicts paragraph 5, which calls them valuable evidence. Trap: Turning a call for humility into a verdict against modern practice.

passages.title: FL01 · CARS · Passage 6
text: Economists often describe exchange as the trading of goods whose values the parties have compared and found equal enough to make the transaction worthwhile. On this model, a gift is an anomaly: a transfer of value without anything received in return. The standard way of handling the anomaly has been to explain it away, either by treating gifts as disguised self-interest, given to win favor or to be repaid later, or by relegating them to the private sphere of families, where market logic is held not to apply. Anthropologists who have studied societies in which gifts structure much of economic life have argued that both responses miss what gift exchange is for.

In many of these societies, giving creates a relationship rather than settling one. A gift is not equivalent to a payment because it is not meant to close an account. A person who receives a gift acquires an obligation, but the obligation is open-ended: to return something, at some later time, of a kind and amount that cannot be precisely specified. Attempting to repay at once, or with exact equivalence, is understood as an insult, a refusal of the relationship, since it announces that the recipient wishes to owe nothing. The unspecified and deferred quality of the return is not a flaw in the system but its point. Debt that remains outstanding keeps the parties bound to one another.

This analysis helps clarify why gifts and sales feel different even when the objects involved are the same. A commercial transaction is designed to leave the parties independent: after the money changes hands, neither owes the other anything and neither need meet again. A gift is designed to do the opposite. Consider the difference between handing a neighbor cash for a favor and bringing a pie after the neighbor has watched one's house. The cash may be worth more, yet it may seem faintly offensive, because it treats the neighbor as a vendor rather than as someone with whom one expects to remain in a relationship.

It would be a mistake, however, to infer that gift economies are more benevolent than markets. The obligations that bind people can also trap them. A chief who gives lavishly can place rivals under debts they cannot discharge, converting generosity into dominance. In such settings the gift is a weapon as well as a bond, and the person who cannot reciprocate is diminished rather than comforted. The open-ended character of the debt that sustains cooperation also sustains inequality.

Nor are the two systems cleanly separated in modern life. Employers speak of loyalty and offer perquisites that are not strictly wages; merchants cultivate regular customers with small unrequested favors; professionals trade courtesies that no contract requires. Each of these ordinary practices blends the logic of the market with the logic of the gift, and each depends on the ambiguity. When the gift element is made explicit as a calculated inducement, it tends to lose its force, because the recipient recognizes that the relationship being offered is itself being priced.

qs.q: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Modern life has replaced gift exchange with market exchange.
Not quite. Paragraph 5 says gift and market logic are not cleanly separated and still blend in modern life.
Gift economies are more benevolent than market economies.
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says it would be a mistake to infer that gift economies are more benevolent than markets.
Gift exchange creates and sustains relationships through open-ended obligation, distinguishing it from market exchange, although it can also sustain hierarchy and blends with market practices today.
Correct: This covers gifts creating relationships through open-ended obligation, the contrast with markets, the risk of hierarchy and the blending today.
Gifts are disguised self-interest and are best analyzed as market transactions.
Not quite. Paragraph 1 describes that as the economists' standard move, which the author says misses what gift exchange is for.
qs.x: Correct: A main-idea question wants the point that covers the whole passage. Paragraph 1 says economists treat gifts as an anomaly and explain them away. Paragraph 2 says gift giving creates a relationship through open-ended, deferred obligation. Paragraph 3 contrasts this with sales, which leave the parties independent. Paragraph 4 warns that such obligations can trap people and sustain inequality. Paragraph 5 says gift and market logic blend in modern life. The choice covering the central claim and both qualifications is the right one. Why the others are wrong: saying modern life has replaced gift exchange with market exchange contradicts paragraph 5, which says the two are not cleanly separated; saying gift economies are more benevolent is rejected at the start of paragraph 4; saying gifts are disguised self-interest is the economists' view that paragraph 1 says misses the point. Trap: Choosing the economists' view that the author sets out to criticize.

qs.q: According to the passage, immediate repayment in exact equivalence is regarded as an insult in many gift societies because it
