o: implies that the giver is wealthier than the recipient and therefore expects the recipient to repay more.
Not quite. The passage never mentions relative wealth. Paragraph 2 says the insult comes from wanting to owe nothing.
violates a rule against any return of gifts, which would be treated as an insult in itself.
Not quite. Paragraph 2 says the recipient does owe a return, later. Returning gifts isn't forbidden.
suggests that the gift was of low value and so can be matched exactly without further obligation.
Not quite. Paragraph 2 doesn't say the gift is low value. The issue is that exact, immediate repayment refuses the relationship.
signals that the recipient wishes to owe nothing further and thus refuses the relationship.
Correct: Paragraph 2 says immediate or exact repayment announces that the recipient wishes to owe nothing, refusing the relationship.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks for the stated reason immediate, exact repayment is an insult. Paragraph 2 says: "Attempting to repay at once, or with exact equivalence, is understood as an insult, a refusal of the relationship, since it announces that the recipient wishes to owe nothing." That matches the choice about the recipient wishing to owe nothing and refusing the relationship. Why the others are wrong: implying the giver is wealthier and expects more back is never mentioned; a rule against any return of gifts is the opposite of the passage, which says a return is expected later; suggesting the gift was low value is not said either, and the point is about the relationship and not the gift's worth. Trap: Assuming repayment itself is the offense, when the passage says the problem is the speed and exactness of it.

qs.q: The author's comparison of paying a neighbor cash with bringing a pie serves primarily to
o: show that treating a favor as a sale can undermine the relationship a gift would sustain.
Correct: Paragraph 3 says cash may treat the neighbor as a vendor, which can undermine the relationship a gift would sustain.
prove that cash payment is always offensive between neighbors, whatever the circumstances or amount.
Not quite. Too strong. Paragraph 3 says the cash "may seem faintly offensive," not always.
demonstrate that neighbors should never expect any payment for help, however large the favor is.
Not quite. The author makes no rule against payment. The example is about how cash can change the relationship.
show that pies are worth more than cash because they require effort and attention.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 actually says the cash may be worth more. The point is about relationship, not value.
qs.x: Correct: A function question asks why the author compares cash with a pie. In paragraph 3, the point before it is that gifts and sales feel different. The example then says that paying a neighbor cash "may seem faintly offensive, because it treats the neighbor as a vendor rather than as someone with whom one expects to remain in a relationship." So it shows that treating a favor as a sale can undermine the relationship that a gift would sustain. Why the others are wrong: proving cash is always offensive ignores the hedges "may" and "faintly"; claiming neighbors should never expect payment for any size of favor is a rule the author doesn't state; claiming pies are worth more than cash contradicts the text, which says the cash "may be worth more." Trap: Turning a hedged illustration into an absolute rule.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward the standard economic treatment of gifts is best described as
o: critical, regarding it as explaining the phenomenon of the gift away instead of explaining it.
Correct: Paragraph 1 says the standard treatment explains the gift away, and that both its responses miss what gift exchange is for.
indifferent, offering no evaluation of whether the standard economic treatment is adequate or not.
Not quite. Paragraph 1 clearly evaluates the standard treatment and finds it lacking, so the author isn't indifferent.
bitter, regarding it as dishonest and as a deliberate attempt to deceive readers about generosity.
Not quite. Too extreme. The author says the treatment misses the point and never accuses anyone of deceiving readers.
supportive, regarding it as largely adequate for explaining why people give and receive gifts.
Not quite. Paragraph 1 says both standard responses miss what gift exchange is for, so the author doesn't support them.
qs.x: Correct: An attitude question asks how the author feels about the economists' handling of gifts. In paragraph 1 the author describes the standard approach, which is to "explain it away," either as disguised self-interest or as belonging to the private sphere, and says anthropologists argue that "both responses miss what gift exchange is for." That is criticism: the treatment explains the gift away instead of explaining it. Why the others are wrong: indifferent, offering no evaluation, ignores the clear "miss what gift exchange is for" judgment; bitter and accusing economists of deliberately deceiving readers is far too strong, since the criticism is that they miss the point and nothing suggests dishonesty; supportive, calling it largely adequate, is the opposite of paragraph 1. Trap: Mistaking measured criticism for hostility.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the claim that deferred, unspecified return is essential to the way gifts bind people?
o: In some societies chiefs use lavish gifts to dominate rivals and secure the loyalty of their followers.
Not quite. Paragraph 4 already describes this, and it fits the idea that open-ended debts bind people.
People who receive gifts report feeling obligated to the giver and uneasy until they have reciprocated.
Not quite. Feeling obligated until repaying fits the claim that outstanding debt keeps parties bound, so it supports the author.
Societies that require immediate, exact repayment sustain relationships as durable as societies with open-ended debts.
Correct: If immediate, exact repayment sustains relationships just as durably, open-ended debt would not be essential to binding people.
Merchants who give small favors to regular customers retain those customers longer than other merchants do.
Not quite. Paragraph 5 makes this kind of point, that gift-like favors build ties, so it supports the author.
qs.x: Correct: A weaken question asks which finding hurts the claim. The claim, from paragraph 2, is that the deferred, unspecified return is the point of gifts, because outstanding debt keeps the parties bound. To weaken it, show that bonds can be just as durable without open-ended debt. If societies requiring immediate, exact repayment sustain relationships as lasting as those with open-ended obligations, then open-ended debt is not essential. Why the others are wrong: chiefs using gifts to dominate rivals appears in paragraph 4, and it fits the author's account of debts that bind; recipients feeling obligated and uneasy until they reciprocate matches the idea of obligation, so it supports the claim; merchants who give small favors keeping customers longer matches paragraph 5's point that gift elements build ties. Trap: Choosing a finding that the author has already worked into the argument.

qs.q: A company gives employees a bonus described as payment for meeting a quarterly target and also calls it a 'gift of appreciation.' Based on the passage, the author would predict that
o: employees will view the bonus as an insult because it is too large for the work done and implies a debt.
Not quite. Paragraph 2 says insult comes from exact, immediate repayment. Size and implied debt are not the issue here.
employees will feel stronger loyalty to the company because the bonus is generous and described as a gift.
Not quite. Paragraph 5 says an explicitly calculated inducement loses its gift force, so calling it a gift won't build loyalty.
employees will feel the bonus creates an open-ended obligation to the company that they must someday repay.
Not quite. A bonus tied to a target reads as payment, not as a gift creating open-ended debt.
employees will recognize the bonus as a calculated inducement, and its element of gift will lose its force.
Correct: Paragraph 5 says a gift made explicit as a calculated inducement tends to lose its force because the relationship is being priced.
qs.x: Correct: This application question asks you to use the author's last point. Paragraph 5 ends: "When the gift element is made explicit as a calculated inducement, it tends to lose its force, because the recipient recognizes that the relationship being offered is itself being priced." A bonus tied to a quarterly target, then called a gift of appreciation, is a calculated inducement dressed as a gift. So employees would see through it and the gift element would lose its force. Why the others are wrong: viewing it as an insult because it is too large and implies a debt is not what the passage says, since the insult in paragraph 2 comes from exact, immediate repayment; stronger loyalty because it is generous and called a gift ignores the warning that explicit inducements lose force; an open-ended obligation to repay someday doesn't fit, because the bonus is tied to a target and so reads as payment. Trap: Assuming that calling something a gift is enough to make it work as one.

passages.title: FL01 · CARS · Passage 7
text: Satire is often defended on the ground that it reforms its targets: by exposing folly to ridicule, the satirist shames people into abandoning it. The defense has a long pedigree among satirists themselves, who have routinely announced reform as their purpose. But the historical record offers little evidence that ridiculed vices diminish under ridicule, and the persistence of the very follies that satirists lampooned centuries ago suggests that something other than correction is at work.

An alternative account locates the function of satire not in its effect on its targets but in its effect on its audience. A satirical piece addresses readers who already share the satirist's judgments and invites them to enjoy the confirmation of those judgments. The pleasure is the pleasure of recognition: the reader laughs because the portrait of the pompous official or the grasping merchant matches an opinion already held. Satire, on this view, does not change minds but consolidates communities, drawing a line between the knowing, who see the joke, and the targets, who do not. A joke that required explanation would fail in just the place where it was meant to succeed.

This account explains several features that the reform theory struggles with. It explains why satire so seldom troubles its targets, who typically are not reading. It explains why the most effective satire is often the most local, depending on allusions that outsiders cannot follow, and why it ages poorly once the allusions are lost. And it explains why satirists in every age have been more popular with those who agree with them than with those they attack, a pattern that would be puzzling if the aim were to persuade the unconverted. Each of these features follows naturally from the community account, whereas the reform account must treat all of them as unfortunate accidents of circumstance.

Yet the community-building theory has its own difficulties. If satire merely confirmed existing opinion, it would be hard to explain why authorities have so frequently feared it, censoring satirists, jailing them, or banning their plays. Rulers are not generally alarmed by entertainments that leave their opponents' views unchanged. The fear suggests that satire does something more than flatter an audience, and one plausible candidate is that it makes dissent publicly speakable. A grievance that individuals harbor privately gains a different status when it is voiced aloud and met with laughter, for the laughter shows each listener that others share the grievance. The effect is not to convert but to coordinate: to turn scattered private opinions into common knowledge.

If this is right, then both traditional and revisionist accounts have captured part of the truth. Satire does not reform its targets, as the defenders claim, but neither is it merely a form of self-congratulation, as the revisionists imply. Its power lies in the space between private opinion and public expression, a space in which a society decides what it is willing to say about itself. That satirists' own stated intentions may be mistaken about this need not surprise us; writers are rarely the best theorists of what their work accomplishes.

qs.q: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?
o: Satire's power lies less in reforming targets than in making private grievances publicly speakable and so coordinating audiences.
Correct: Paragraphs 4 and 5 conclude that satire coordinates audiences by making private grievances publicly speakable, rather than reforming targets.
Satire merely flatters like-minded audiences and should not be taken seriously as a force in politics or culture.
Not quite. Paragraph 5 says satire is not merely self-congratulation, as the revisionists imply.
Authorities fear satire because it persuades their own supporters to change sides and withdraw their loyalty.
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says satire's effect is "not to convert but to coordinate," so persuading supporters to switch isn't the point.
Satire succeeds mainly by shaming its targets into reforming their conduct once their faults have been exposed.
Not quite. Paragraph 1 says there is little evidence that ridiculed vices diminish, and paragraph 5 says satire does not reform its targets.
qs.x: Correct: A main-idea question wants where the passage ends up, not a stop along the way. Paragraph 1 doubts the reform defense of satire. Paragraph 2 offers the community account, in which satire confirms the audience's views. Paragraph 3 says that account explains things reform can't. Paragraph 4 then raises a problem for it, because authorities fear satire, and suggests satire makes dissent publicly speakable and turns private opinions into "common knowledge." Paragraph 5 sums up. So the main point is that satire matters less for reforming targets than for making grievances speakable and coordinating audiences. Why the others are wrong: saying satire merely flatters and isn't a political force is the revisionist view that paragraphs 4 and 5 say is incomplete; saying authorities fear it because it persuades their supporters to switch sides contradicts paragraph 4, which says the effect is "not to convert but to coordinate"; saying satire succeeds by shaming targets into reform is the defense paragraph 1 doubts. Trap: Stopping at the revisionist account and missing the author's final coordination idea.

qs.q: According to the passage, satire tends to age poorly because
o: censors successfully suppress it before later generations have a chance to read it.
Not quite. Paragraph 4 mentions censorship only to show authorities fear satire. It is never given as why satire ages.
its targets eventually reform, which makes the satire irrelevant to readers of later periods.
Not quite. Paragraph 1 says the follies satirists mocked have persisted, so targets haven't reformed.
its audience's opinions change over time, so the satirist's positions seem foreign to later readers.
Not quite. The passage never says audiences' opinions change. Paragraph 3 says the problem is lost allusions.
its effectiveness depends on topical allusions that later readers can no longer follow.
Correct: Paragraph 3 says satire ages poorly once the local allusions it depends on are lost.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks for the reason the passage gives for satire aging poorly. Go to paragraph 3: the most effective satire "is often the most local, depending on allusions that outsiders cannot follow, and why it ages poorly once the allusions are lost." That matches the choice about topical allusions that later readers can no longer follow. Why the others are wrong: censors suppressing satire is brought up in paragraph 4 as a sign that authorities fear it, not as the reason it ages poorly; targets eventually reforming contradicts paragraph 1, which says follies persist; the audience's opinions changing over time is a believable cause, but the passage never says it. Trap: Picking a reasonable-sounding cause that the passage does not give.

qs.q: The discussion of authorities censoring satirists serves to
o: prove that satire succeeds in reforming its targets, since authorities would not censor harmless writing.
Not quite. The author doubts that satire reforms targets. Censorship is used to challenge the community account instead.
celebrate the courage of satirists who risked prison and exile to criticize the powerful.
Not quite. The passage doesn't praise satirists' courage. Paragraph 4 uses censorship as evidence in an argument.
present a difficulty for the community-building account that motivates a further hypothesis
Correct: Paragraph 4 uses authorities' fear of satire as a problem for the community account, which leads to the speakable-dissent idea.
support the claim that satire seldom troubles its targets or the officials who govern them.
Not quite. Authorities fearing and censoring satire suggests it does trouble them, which opposes this claim.
qs.x: Correct: A function question asks what the censorship discussion does. It opens paragraph 4, which begins "Yet the community-building theory has its own difficulties." The author argues that if satire merely confirmed existing opinion, it would be hard to explain why authorities so often feared it. Rulers aren't alarmed by entertainments that change no one's views. So the discussion presents a difficulty for the community account and leads to a further hypothesis, that satire makes dissent speakable. Why the others are wrong: proving satire reforms its targets contradicts the passage, which doubts reform from the start; celebrating satirists' courage is not what the paragraph does, since it uses the censorship as an argument; supporting the claim that satire seldom troubles officials runs against the point, because fear of satire suggests it does trouble authorities. Trap: Reading the example as support for the account it actually challenges.

qs.q: Which finding would most strengthen the author's final hypothesis about satire?
o: Satirists report that they intend to reform their targets and that they judge their success by whether reforms follow.
Not quite. This supports the reform defense in paragraph 1, which the author doubts, not the coordination hypothesis.
After a satirical play, audience members report greater willingness to discuss the targeted grievance openly.
Correct: Greater willingness to discuss the grievance openly shows dissent becoming publicly speakable, as paragraph 4 proposes.
Targets of satire rarely attend the performances, and those who attend are rarely moved to change.
Not quite. This fits paragraph 3's community account, but it doesn't show satire making dissent speakable.
Satirical works from past centuries remain widely read, and modern readers still recognize most of the figures they mock.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 says satire ages poorly once allusions are lost, so this goes against the passage.
qs.x: Correct: A strengthen question asks for the finding that best supports the author's final hypothesis. That hypothesis is in paragraph 4: satire makes dissent publicly speakable, and laughter shows each listener that others share the grievance, which coordinates private opinions into common knowledge. If audience members become more willing to discuss the targeted grievance openly after a satirical play, that is exactly what the hypothesis predicts. Why the others are wrong: satirists reporting an intent to reform and judging success by reforms supports the reform account, which the author doubts; targets rarely attending and rarely being moved fits the community account from paragraph 3 but says nothing about dissent becoming speakable; old satires still being read and recognized contradicts paragraph 3's point that satire ages poorly. Trap: Choosing a finding consistent with an earlier claim instead of the specific hypothesis being tested.

qs.q: The final sentence of the passage implies that satirists' stated intentions are
o: the best available evidence of what satire does and why it affects its audiences.
Not quite. The last sentence says the opposite: writers are rarely the best theorists of what their work does.
usually deliberately dishonest, since satirists wish to hide their real political aims.
Not quite. The author says satirists may be mistaken, not dishonest. Being wrong is not the same as lying.
irrelevant to literary study, which should consider only the text and its reception.
Not quite. The sentence speaks only about reliability. It never says what literary study should consider.
not a reliable guide to what their satire actually accomplishes among its readers.
Correct: The last sentence says stated intentions may be mistaken, since writers are rarely the best theorists of their work.
qs.x: Correct: The final sentence reads: "That satirists' own stated intentions may be mistaken about this need not surprise us; writers are rarely the best theorists of what their work accomplishes." So the author implies satirists' stated intentions are not a reliable guide to what their satire actually does. Why the others are wrong: calling their intentions the best available evidence says the opposite; saying they are usually deliberately dishonest changes "mistaken" into lying, and the author says only that writers are rarely the best theorists of their own work; saying intentions are irrelevant to literary study and that only text and reception count goes beyond the sentence, which comments on reliability and not on method. Trap: Reading "mistaken" as "dishonest."

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the passage's claim that satire seldom reforms its targets?
o: Rulers have often censored satirists and burned their works, sometimes imprisoning the authors for years.
Not quite. Paragraph 4 already uses censorship, and it doesn't show targets reforming.
Satire depends on local allusions that readers in other places or periods seldom recognize.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 already uses local allusions, and they say nothing about targets reforming.
Documented cases in which many satirized officials changed their conduct after reading the satire.
Correct: Documented cases of satirized officials changing their conduct would be direct evidence against the claim that satire seldom reforms targets.
Many satirical works are read mainly by people who already share the satirist's views and attitudes.
Not quite. This fits the community account in paragraph 2, so it supports rather than weakens the author.
qs.x: Correct: A weaken question asks which finding hurts the claim that satire seldom reforms its targets. That claim appears in paragraphs 1 and 3. The most direct counter would be documented cases in which many satirized officials changed their conduct after reading the satire. That is direct evidence of reform. Why the others are wrong: rulers censoring satirists appears in paragraph 4 and fits the author's view that satire has effects other than reform; satire depending on local allusions is from paragraph 3 and is part of the author's own account; satire read mostly by people who already agree is the community account in paragraph 2, which the author uses to explain why targets are rarely moved. All three fit the author's argument. Trap: Choosing a fact that the author already cites as consistent with the argument.

passages.title: FL01 · CARS · Passage 8
text: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. The aphorism is cited so often that its force has dulled, but the phenomenon it describes is real and its mechanisms deserve closer attention than the slogan suggests. Consider a school system that wishes to know whether its students are learning to read. It administers a standardized test, and scores on the test are, at first, reasonably good indicators of reading ability: students who read well tend to score well, and the correlation is strong enough to be useful. Then the system attaches consequences to the scores. Schools whose scores rise receive funding; those whose scores fall are sanctioned. The correlation between scores and ability begins to weaken, not because the test has changed but because everyone involved has begun to respond to it.

The responses take several forms. The least troubling is straightforward improvement: teachers examine the test, identify the skills it measures, and teach those skills more effectively. If the test measures reading comprehension and teachers improve comprehension instruction, the system has achieved what it hoped. But the test samples only a portion of what reading involves, and teachers under pressure have reason to concentrate on that portion. Time spent on extended writing, on sustained engagement with long books, or on discussion of ambiguous texts, none of which the test captures, may shrink. Scores may rise while the broader ability they were meant to indicate stagnates. At the far end lie practices that involve no improvement at all, such as the strategic exclusion of weak students from testing or, in documented cases, outright alteration of answer sheets.

It is tempting to treat these responses as moral failures by individuals, but this diagnosis is too convenient. Teachers who narrow the curriculum are responding rationally to the incentives they have been given. If their institution rewards a number, they will produce the number; to expect otherwise is to expect them to sacrifice their schools in the name of a purity that no one has asked of the administrators who designed the system. The failing, if there is one, belongs largely to the design.

Does this mean that measurement should be abandoned? That conclusion would be too hasty. Without measurement, resources are allocated by anecdote and influence, and the students least able to advocate for themselves are the most likely to be overlooked. The more constructive conclusion is that measures are most reliable when they are not the sole basis for consequences, when several different indicators are consulted, and when the indicators are periodically changed so that effort cannot be fixed on a single target. Even these safeguards will not eliminate distortion, but they can reduce the degree to which a measure's usefulness is destroyed by the very attention that makes it matter.

The deeper lesson is that every measure is a proxy, and the gap between proxy and purpose is where gaming takes place. The wider that gap, and the higher the stakes attached to the proxy, the greater the opportunity and the incentive to exploit it.

qs.q: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Teachers who narrow the curriculum in order to raise scores should be disciplined for gaming the tests, since their conduct harms students.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 calls blaming teachers too convenient and puts the failing largely on the design of the system.
Attaching high stakes to a measure tends to degrade its value as an indicator, but the remedy is better measurement, not abandonment.
Correct: The passage shows high stakes weakening a measure, then paragraph 4 calls abandoning measurement too hasty and recommends better safeguards.
Test scores never correlate with reading ability, which is why they should not be used to judge schools.
Not quite. Paragraph 1 says scores are at first reasonably good indicators with a strong correlation.
Standardized tests should be abandoned because they cannot capture what reading ability actually involves.
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says abandoning measurement would be too hasty, since resources would then go by anecdote and influence.
qs.x: Correct: A main-idea question wants the point of the whole passage. Paragraph 1 introduces the idea that when a measure becomes a target it stops being a good measure, and shows it with a school test. Paragraphs 2 and 3 describe the responses and say much of the fault lies in the design. Paragraph 4 asks whether measurement should be abandoned and says "That conclusion would be too hasty," recommending several, changing indicators. Paragraph 5 sums up. So the main idea is that high stakes degrade a measure, but the remedy is better measurement and not abandonment. Why the others are wrong: disciplining teachers is the moral-failure view that paragraph 3 calls "too convenient"; saying scores never correlate with reading ability contradicts paragraph 1, where scores are at first reasonably good indicators; abandoning tests is the "too hasty" conclusion of paragraph 4. Trap: Choosing the blame-the-teachers or abandon-the-test reading that the author explicitly rejects.

qs.q: According to the passage, the correlation between test scores and reading ability weakens after consequences are attached because
o: students stop reading outside school because test preparation takes up their free time.
Not quite. The passage never mentions students' free time. Paragraph 1 says everyone involved responds to the test.
schools and teachers begin to respond to the test itself, not the skill it measures.
Correct: Paragraph 1 says the correlation weakens because everyone involved begins to respond to the test.
the test becomes harder to pass as officials raise the passing standard each year.
Not quite. Paragraph 1 says the test has not changed, so no new passing standard is involved.
the test is revised to include new skills that are less closely tied to reading ability.
Not quite. Paragraph 1 says the weakening happens "not because the test has changed."
qs.x: Correct: The question asks why the correlation weakens. Go to paragraph 1, where the author says it weakens after consequences are attached "not because the test has changed but because everyone involved has begun to respond to it." That matches the choice about schools and teachers responding to the test itself and not to the skill it measures. Why the others are wrong: students stopping reading outside school is never said; the test getting harder as officials raise the passing standard is ruled out by the author, who says the test has not changed; the test being revised to include new skills is ruled out the same way. Trap: Missing the explicit statement that the test itself did not change.

qs.q: The author discusses teachers improving comprehension instruction in order to
o: show that responding to a target is not always harmful.
Correct: Paragraph 2 calls this the least troubling response, one that achieves what the system hoped, so responding to a target can be fine.
argue that the test measures all of what reading involves.
Not quite. The next sentence in paragraph 2 says the test samples only a portion of what reading involves.
claim that teachers are the main source of distortion.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 says the failing belongs largely to the design, not to teachers.
show that test tampering is rare.
Not quite. The author never says tampering is rare. Paragraph 2 only mentions it as a far-end practice.
qs.x: Correct: A function question asks why the author describes teachers improving comprehension instruction. In paragraph 2 the author calls this "the least troubling" response: teachers study the test, find the skills it measures and teach them better, and "the system has achieved what it hoped." It sits at the mild end of a range that gets worse. So it shows that responding to a target isn't always harmful. Why the others are wrong: arguing the test measures all of reading contradicts the next sentence, "the test samples only a portion of what reading involves"; claiming teachers are the main source of distortion conflicts with paragraph 3, which puts the failing largely on the design; showing that tampering is rare isn't claimed, since the author only notes that it occurs in "documented cases." Trap: Treating a mild, benign example as evidence about the test's completeness.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward teachers who narrow the curriculum is best described as
o: approving, regarding narrowing as good teaching because it focuses effort on what is measured.
Not quite. Paragraph 2 says narrowing can leave broader reading ability stagnant, so the author doesn't call it good teaching.
understanding, locating the fault chiefly in the design of the system rather than in teachers.
Correct: Paragraph 3 says teachers respond rationally to incentives and that the failing belongs largely to the system's design.
detached, offering no view of where responsibility for the narrowing of the curriculum lies.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 clearly says where responsibility lies: largely in the design.
condemnatory, treating them as morally culpable for harming students to raise their own ratings.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 calls the moral-failure diagnosis too convenient, so the author doesn't condemn the teachers.
qs.x: Correct: An attitude question asks how the author feels about teachers who narrow the curriculum. Paragraph 3 says it is tempting to see this as moral failure, but "this diagnosis is too convenient." Teachers "are responding rationally to the incentives they have been given," and "the failing, if there is one, belongs largely to the design." That is an understanding stance that puts the fault mainly on the system. Why the others are wrong: approving, calling narrowing good teaching, goes too far, because paragraph 2 says the narrowing can leave broader ability stagnant; detached, with no view on responsibility, ignores the clear statement that the fault belongs largely to the design; condemnatory, calling teachers morally culpable, is the view paragraph 3 rejects. Trap: Treating an explanation of behavior as approval of it.

qs.q: Which of the following is the best illustration of the 'gap between proxy and purpose' described in the final paragraph?
o: A city stops measuring crime rates altogether after officials conclude that police statistics cannot be trusted.
Not quite. Dropping measurement entirely isn't gaming a proxy. Paragraph 4 calls abandonment too hasty.
A company tracks sales using several different indicators so that no single figure can be manipulated.
Not quite. Using several indicators is the safeguard the author recommends in paragraph 4, not an example of the gap.
A hospital is judged on surgical survival rates, and surgeons decline to operate on the sickest patients.
Correct: The survival-rate proxy improves while the purpose, caring for patients, suffers because the sickest are turned away.
A school improves comprehension instruction after examining the test and then sees both scores and ability rise.
Not quite. Scores and ability rising together shows no gap between proxy and purpose.
qs.x: Correct: This asks you to match the idea in paragraph 5: every measure is a proxy, and "the gap between proxy and purpose is where gaming takes place." The best illustration is one where the proxy gets better while the real purpose suffers. A hospital judged on surgical survival rates, whose surgeons decline to operate on the sickest patients, improves the number (survival) while undermining the purpose (caring for patients). Why the others are wrong: a city that stops measuring crime altogether just abandons measurement, which paragraph 4 calls too hasty; a company tracking sales with several indicators is the safeguard the author recommends; a school that improves comprehension instruction and sees both scores and ability rise shows no gap, since proxy and purpose rose together. Trap: Choosing an example about measurement in general instead of one in which the proxy is exploited.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the author's suggestion that consulting several indicators and rotating them reduces distortion?
o: Schools quickly learn to raise every indicator in the rotation through the same narrow teaching practices.
Correct: If schools raise every indicator in the rotation through the same narrow practices, the safeguards don't reduce gaming.
Schools rarely exclude weak students from testing when several indicators are used, even when their ratings are at stake.
Not quite. Fewer exclusions of weak students when several indicators are used would show the safeguard helps.
Test scores are somewhat correlated with other indicators of reading ability, such as grades and teacher evaluations.
Not quite. Some correlation with grades and evaluations says nothing about whether gaming continues under several indicators.
Indicators that are never changed are gamed more heavily over time than rotated ones.
Not quite. Rotated indicators being gamed less than fixed ones supports the author's recommendation.
qs.x: Correct: A weaken question asks which finding hurts the suggestion in paragraph 4 that consulting several indicators and rotating them reduces distortion. If schools quickly learn to raise every indicator in the rotation through the same narrow teaching practices, then having several indicators and rotating them did not stop the gaming. Why the others are wrong: schools rarely excluding weak students when several indicators are used shows the safeguard working; test scores being somewhat correlated with grades and teacher evaluations just says the indicators are related and doesn't show that gaming continues; indicators that are never changed being gamed more heavily than rotated ones supports rotation. Trap: Selecting a finding that sounds critical of testing but actually backs the author's recommendation.

passages.title: FL01 · CARS · Passage 9
text: In the late twentieth century, the cleaning of several celebrated paintings provoked a controversy that revealed how little agreement exists about what a restorer is trying to restore. Conservators removed layers of aged varnish and grime, and the canvases emerged startlingly bright, their blues and reds more vivid than viewers had known. Admirers rejoiced that the artists' true colors had been recovered. Critics protested that the cleaning had stripped away subtle glazes, flattened the shadows, and produced a clarity the artists never intended.

Both sides assumed there was a determinate answer to the question of how the painting "really" looked. The admirers equated the original with the state of the painting at the moment it was finished; the critics equated it with the painting as it had come to be known and, in some cases, as the artist might have anticipated it would mature. Neither assumption is silly. Painters of earlier centuries knew that their pigments would darken and that varnish would yellow, and some applied final glazes expecting the surface to settle into a particular harmony. To remove everything added by time may therefore be to remove part of the work as its maker conceived it. At the same time, to leave a painting dimmed beneath layers that obscure its drawing and color is to deny viewers access to what the maker actually put on the canvas.

The dispute is complicated by the fact that the physical evidence is ambiguous. A conservator can distinguish original paint from later varnish under magnification and chemical analysis, but cannot always determine whether a thin, translucent layer was part of the artist's design or a later addition. In such cases the decision rests on judgment about the artist's intentions, and those intentions must be inferred from the work itself, from fragments of documentary evidence, and from comparison with other paintings, each a source of uncertainty. A restorer who claims to be merely uncovering the truth is concealing the interpretive character of the act.

This suggests that the controversy is less about technique than about what we value in old pictures. Those who prize authenticity of materials will favor minimal intervention, preferring a painting that shows its age honestly to one that has been made to look new. Those who prize the visual experience the artist designed will favor more aggressive cleaning, accepting some risk of loss for the sake of legibility. These priorities are not reducible to facts about the paint; they are commitments, and reasonable people can hold either. A restorer's decision about how far to clean is therefore a decision about which of these goods to sacrifice, and no measurement of the paint can make that decision on the restorer's behalf.

The best practice, accordingly, is probably neither bold nor timid but transparent. Restorers should document each stage of treatment, retain samples of removed material when possible, and avoid permanent measures that foreclose later reconsideration. Because the judgments embodied in any restoration will in time look as dated as the varnish they replaced, the most valuable thing a conservator can leave is the means by which a future generation can undo them.

qs.q: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Aggressive cleaning is justified because it recovers the artist's true colors, which later varnish and grime have hidden for centuries.
Not quite. This takes the admirers' side. Paragraph 2 says their assumption of one determinate original is shared by the critics too.
Restoration disputes arise because restoring involves interpretive judgments and competing values, so transparent, reversible treatment is best.
Correct: Paragraphs 3 to 5 trace the dispute to interpretive judgment and competing values, and recommend transparent, reversible treatment.
The critics of the cleaning were correct and the admirers mistaken, since the cleaned surface lacks the harmony the artist intended.
Not quite. Paragraph 2 says neither side's assumption is silly. The author doesn't declare the critics right.
Minimal intervention is always the best policy for old paintings, since any removal of material permanently destroys evidence of the artist's intentions and the work's history.
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says reasonable people can hold either priority, so no policy is declared always best.
qs.x: Correct: A main-idea question wants the whole argument. Paragraph 1 describes the cleaning controversy. Paragraph 2 says both sides wrongly assumed there was one determinate answer to how the painting "really" looked. Paragraph 3 says the physical evidence is ambiguous, so restoration rests on interpretive judgment. Paragraph 4 says the dispute is about values, and paragraph 5 recommends transparent treatment that can be undone. So the main idea is that restoration disputes come from interpretation and competing values, and transparent, reversible treatment is best. Why the others are wrong: saying aggressive cleaning is justified because it recovers true colors takes the admirers' side, which paragraph 2 says rests on an assumption; saying the critics were correct takes the other side, though the author calls neither assumption "silly"; saying minimal intervention is always best ignores paragraph 4, which says reasonable people can hold either priority. Trap: Siding with one party in the controversy when the author declines to.

qs.q: The author claims physical evidence cannot settle restoration disputes because
o: documentary evidence about artists' intentions is almost always absent from the historical record altogether.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 mentions fragments of documentary evidence, so it isn't almost always absent.
chemical analysis cannot distinguish paint from varnish at all, even with modern instruments and samples.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 says a conservator can distinguish original paint from later varnish. The trouble is only with some thin layers.
painters of earlier centuries disagreed about varnish, so no single practice can be assumed.
Not quite. The passage never says painters disagreed about varnish.
conservators cannot always tell whether a thin translucent layer was part of the artist's design.
Correct: Paragraph 3 says conservators cannot always tell whether a thin translucent layer was part of the artist's design.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks why the author says physical evidence can't settle the disputes. Look at paragraph 3. A conservator can tell original paint from later varnish, but "cannot always determine whether a thin, translucent layer was part of the artist's design or a later addition." That matches the choice about conservators being unable to tell whether a thin layer was part of the design. Why the others are wrong: documentary evidence being almost always absent overstates it, since the paragraph names "fragments of documentary evidence" as one source; chemical analysis not distinguishing paint from varnish at all contradicts the first sentence of the paragraph, which says a conservator can distinguish them; painters disagreeing about varnish is never claimed. Trap: Blowing up the ambiguity into an inability to tell any layers apart.

qs.q: The statement that painters knew pigments would darken and varnish would yellow serves to
o: suggest that earlier painters were careless about durability.
Not quite. The painters are shown anticipating aging, so they weren't careless.
prove that artists wanted their paintings to appear dark.
Not quite. Too strong. Paragraph 2 says only that some expected the surface to settle into a particular harmony.
argue that restorers have misled the public.
Not quite. Paragraph 2 says neither side's assumption is silly. It doesn't accuse restorers of misleading the public.
show that the critics' position has a reasonable basis.
Correct: Paragraph 2 uses it to show that removing time's changes may remove part of the work as conceived, giving the critics a reasonable basis.
qs.x: Correct: A function question asks why the author mentions that painters knew their pigments would darken and varnish would yellow. This appears in paragraph 2, right after the critics' view is described. The author says some painters applied final glazes "expecting the surface to settle into a particular harmony," so removing everything time added "may therefore be to remove part of the work as its maker conceived it." That shows the critics' position has a reasonable basis. Why the others are wrong: suggesting painters were careless about durability reads the opposite, since they planned for aging; proving artists wanted dark paintings overshoots, because the claim is only that they expected a particular settling; arguing that restorers have misled the public is not claimed, because the author calls both sides' assumptions not silly. Trap: Stretching a supporting detail into proof of a bigger claim.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward a restorer who claims merely to be uncovering the truth is best described as
o: skeptical, because the claim conceals the interpretive choices that restoration involves.
Correct: Paragraph 3 says the restorer's claim conceals the interpretive character of restoration, which is a skeptical, not hostile, view.
hostile, accusing the restorer of fraud and of deliberately misleading museum visitors.
Not quite. Too strong. Paragraph 3 criticizes the claim as hiding interpretation, not as fraud or deliberate deception.
admiring of the restorer's confidence in being able to recover the original surface.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 criticizes the claim rather than admiring it.
indifferent to what restorers claim, since claims have no bearing on how paintings are treated.
Not quite. The author clearly judges the claim, saying it conceals the interpretive nature of the act.
qs.x: Correct: An attitude question asks about the author's feeling toward a restorer who claims to be merely uncovering the truth. The line is in paragraph 3: such a restorer "is concealing the interpretive character of the act." That is a measured, skeptical criticism of the claim, not of the restorer's honesty. Why the others are wrong: hostile, accusing the restorer of fraud, goes far past the text, because the author says the claim hides the interpretive nature of the work and never says the restorer is deliberately deceiving visitors; admiring is the opposite of the criticism; indifferent, saying claims have no bearing on treatment, ignores that the author explicitly finds the claim misleading about what restoration is. Trap: Escalating a criticism of method into an accusation of dishonesty.

qs.q: A museum is choosing between two plans for a darkened painting. Plan X removes all later layers permanently. Plan Y removes only clearly later grime, documents each step, keeps samples, and uses reversible methods. The author would most likely favor
o: neither plan, because any intervention falsifies the work and any restoration fabricates it.
Not quite. Paragraph 5 recommends transparent restoration, so the author doesn't condemn all intervention.
Plan X, because it uncovers the painting as the artist finished it and removes every later addition.
Not quite. Paragraph 5 warns against permanent measures that foreclose later reconsideration, and Plan X is permanent.
Plan Y, because it guarantees that the original appearance will be recovered and later critics will agree.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 says the original can't be known with certainty, so no plan guarantees recovery or agreement.
Plan Y, because it preserves the means for future generations to reconsider today's judgments.
Correct: Paragraph 5 favors documentation, saved samples and reversible steps so future generations can reconsider today's judgments.
qs.x: Correct: An application question asks you to use the author's recommendation. Paragraph 5 says the best practice is "transparent": document each stage, retain samples of removed material when possible, and "avoid permanent measures that foreclose later reconsideration," because the most valuable thing a conservator can leave is the means to undo judgments. Plan Y documents steps, keeps samples and uses reversible methods, so the author would favor it because it lets future generations reconsider today's judgments. Why the others are wrong: favoring neither plan because any intervention falsifies the work goes against the passage, which accepts restoration if done transparently; favoring Plan X because it shows the painting as finished ignores that its permanent removal forecloses reconsideration, and paragraph 2 says the original may include later aging the artist expected; favoring Plan Y because it guarantees recovery of the original look is wrong, since paragraph 3 says no one can be sure what the original was. Trap: Choosing the right plan for the wrong reason, such as a guarantee of authenticity the author says doesn't exist.

passages.title: FL01 · Chem/Phys · Passage 1
text: A student studies a 0.50 kg wooden block sliding from rest down a 2.0 m long plank whose angle θ with the horizontal can be adjusted. For each angle, the student releases the block, uses photogates to measure the time needed to travel the full 2.0 m, and averages five trials. The plank surface is uniform, and separate measurements gave a coefficient of static friction of 0.25 and a coefficient of kinetic friction of 0.20 between block and plank. Use g = 9.8 m/s² and neglect air resistance. At 10° the block did not move when released, even after a gentle tap. The student reasons that the acceleration down the plank depends on both the component of gravity along the plank and the friction force opposing the motion, and she compares predictions from a free-body diagram analysis with her data. The predicted times agreed with the measured times to within 2%. Results for the other angles are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1.

qs.q: What is the acceleration of the block down the plank at an angle of 30°?
o: 3.2 m/s²
Correct: 9.8 × (0.500 − 0.20 × 0.866) = 9.8 × 0.3268 = 3.2 m/s², gravity's pull along the plank minus friction.
4.9 m/s²
Not quite. This is just g sin 30°, the pull down the plank, with friction left out entirely.
8.5 m/s²
Not quite. This is g cos 30°, the part of gravity pressing into the plank, not the part moving the block.
1.7 m/s²
Not quite. This is only the friction piece (μk g cos 30°). It still has to be subtracted from the pull.
qs.x: Correct: This is a block sliding down a ramp, so we find the net force along the plank and divide by the mass. The formula is a = g(sinθ − μk cosθ), where g is the gravity constant, θ is the plank angle, and μk is the kinetic friction coefficient (the friction number for a block that is already moving). From the passage, g = 9.8 m/s², θ = 30°, and μk = 0.20. Also sin 30° = 0.500 and cos 30° = 0.866. Plug in: a = 9.8 × (0.500 − 0.20 × 0.866). First the multiplication inside: 0.20 × 0.866 = 0.1732. Subtract: 0.500 − 0.1732 = 0.3268. Then 9.8 × 0.3268 = 3.20 m/s². The mass cancels out, which is why the 0.50 kg never gets used here. Why the others are wrong: 4.9 m/s² is g sin 30° = 9.8 × 0.5, the pull down the plank with friction left out; 8.5 m/s² is g cos 30° = 9.8 × 0.866, the part of gravity pressing into the plank, not along it; 1.7 m/s² is only the friction part, 9.8 × 0.20 × 0.866, and it never gets subtracted from the pull. Trap: Using g sinθ alone and forgetting that kinetic friction takes away from the net force along the plank.

qs.q: Which statement best explains why the block did not slide at 10°?
o: Kinetic friction exceeded the component of gravity along the plank.
Not quite. Kinetic friction only acts once the block is sliding, and it is smaller than the maximum static friction.
The normal force from the plank was zero at that angle.
Not quite. The normal force is mg cosθ, which is clearly not zero at 10°.
The component of gravity along the plank was smaller than the maximum static friction force.
Correct: At 10°, the pull along the plank is about 0.85 N, below the maximum static friction of about 1.2 N, so the block stays still.
The weight of the block was balanced by the normal force, so no net force acted on it.
Not quite. The normal force balances only the part of weight pushing into the plank. The question is about forces along the plank.
qs.x: Correct: The block stays put when the most friction the plank can offer is bigger than the pull of gravity along the plank. Static friction is the friction on a block that isn't moving, and it can grow up to a maximum of μs × N, where N is the normal force (the push of the plank straight up on the block). From the passage, m = 0.50 kg, g = 9.8 m/s², θ = 10°, and μs = 0.25. The pull along the plank is mg sinθ = 0.50 × 9.8 × 0.174 = 4.9 × 0.174 = 0.85 N. The maximum static friction is μs mg cosθ = 0.25 × 4.9 × 0.985 = 1.225 × 0.985 = 1.2 N. Since 1.2 N is bigger than 0.85 N, friction can cancel the pull completely and nothing moves (the same idea as tan 10° = 0.18 being less than 0.25). That matches Table 1, which says no motion at 10°. Why the others are wrong: kinetic friction only exists once the block is already sliding, and it is smaller than the static maximum anyway; the normal force is mg cosθ, which is not zero at 10°; the normal force cancels only the part of the weight pushing into the plank, not the full weight, so it says nothing about the direction along the plank. Trap: Saying the weight is balanced by the normal force, when the normal force only balances the part of weight perpendicular to the plank.

qs.q: What is the magnitude of the kinetic friction force on the block while it slides at 30°?
o: Not quite. This is μk × mg, which treats the full weight as the normal force. On a tilted plank it's smaller.
Not quite. This is mg sin 30°, the pull of gravity down the plank, not the friction force.
Not quite. This swaps in sin 30° where cos 30° belongs when finding the normal force.
qs.x: Correct: Kinetic friction equals the friction coefficient times the normal force, f = μk N. On a ramp the normal force is not the full weight. It is only the part of the weight pressing into the plank, N = mg cosθ. From the passage, μk = 0.20, m = 0.50 kg, g = 9.8 m/s², θ = 30°, and cos 30° = 0.866. Plug in: f = 0.20 × 0.50 × 9.8 × 0.866. Go step by step: 0.50 × 9.8 = 4.9 N (the weight). Then 4.9 × 0.866 = 4.24 N (the normal force). Then 0.20 × 4.24 = 0.85 N. Why the others are wrong: 0.98 N is 0.20 × 4.9, which treats the whole weight as the normal force, but the plank is tilted so it doesn't push back that hard; 2.5 N is mg sin 30° = 4.9 × 0.5, the pull of gravity down the plank, not a friction force; 0.49 N comes from using sin 30° = 0.5 in place of cos 30°, since 0.20 × 4.9 × 0.5 = 0.49. Trap: Using the full weight mg as the normal force on a tilted surface instead of mg cosθ.

qs.q: What is the speed of the block at the bottom of the plank when θ = 40°?
o: Not quite. This is 4.4 ÷ √2 and doesn't match any step of the motion. It likely comes from mishandling a square root.
Not quite. This is the speed after a free fall through 2.0 m, √(2gd). It ignores the plank's angle and friction.
Not quite. This is double the real final speed, from applying the factor of 2 in v = 2d ÷ t twice.
qs.x: Correct: The block starts from rest and speeds up at a constant rate, so we can use Table 1 instead of the angle. The table gives the time for 2.0 m at 40° as 0.91 s. For constant acceleration from rest, distance d = ½at², so a = 2d ÷ t². With d = 2.0 m and t = 0.91 s: a = 2 × 2.0 ÷ (0.91)² = 4.0 ÷ 0.828 = 4.8 m/s². Final speed is v = at = 4.8 × 0.91 = 4.4 m/s. There is a shortcut. Since the speed grows steadily from 0, the average speed is half the final speed, so v = 2d ÷ t = 4.0 ÷ 0.91 = 4.4 m/s. Why the others are wrong: 3.1 m/s is 4.4 ÷ √2 and has no physical basis here; 6.3 m/s is √(2gd) = √(2 × 9.8 × 2.0) = √39.2, the speed after a free fall through 2.0 m, which ignores both the plank angle and friction; 8.8 m/s is double the real answer, from applying the factor of 2 twice. Trap: Treating the average speed (d ÷ t = 2.2 m/s) as the final speed. The final speed is twice the average when starting from rest.

qs.q: What is the work done by kinetic friction on the block over the full 2.0 m at 30°?
o: Not quite. The size is right but friction points opposite to the motion, so its work is negative.
Not quite. This uses the block's weight (4.9 N) instead of the friction force, and it isn't multiplied by the distance.
Not quite. This is only the force in newtons. Work needs the force multiplied by the 2.0 m distance.
Correct: W = −f d = −(0.85 N)(2.0 m) = −1.7 J. Friction opposes the motion, so the work is negative.
qs.x: Correct: Work is force times the distance moved along the force, W = F d cosφ, where φ is the angle between the force and the motion. Friction points up the plank while the block moves down, so φ = 180° and cos 180° = −1. That makes the work negative. The kinetic friction force at 30° is f = μk m g cosθ = 0.20 × 0.50 × 9.8 × 0.866 = 0.85 N, and the distance is d = 2.0 m (the full length of the plank). Plug in: W = −(0.85 N)(2.0 m) = −1.7 J. A joule (J) is a newton times a meter, so the units work out. Negative work means friction is taking energy out of the block's motion (turning it into heat). Why the others are wrong: +1.7 J has the right size but the wrong sign, since friction opposes the motion; −4.9 J uses 4.9, which is the block's weight in newtons (0.50 × 9.8), not the friction force, and it never multiplies by the distance; −0.85 J is just the force with the 2.0 m never multiplied in. Trap: Giving the friction force in newtons as the work, or writing work done by friction with a positive sign.

passages.title: FL01 · Chem/Phys · Passage 2
text: Atherosclerotic plaque narrows arteries, and a physician models the effect with a horizontal rigid tube whose radius changes along its length. Blood is treated as an ideal, incompressible fluid of density 1060 kg/m³ with no viscosity. In the normal segment the radius is 4.0 mm and the blood speed is 0.30 m/s. Narrowed segments of smaller radius are considered one at a time. Using the continuity equation and Bernoulli's equation, the speed in each narrowed segment and the drop in pressure relative to the normal segment were calculated and are given in Table 1. Figure 1 plots speed against radius. In a real artery, viscosity cannot be ignored. For steady laminar flow of a viscous fluid in a long, narrow tube, Poiseuille's law states that the volumetric flow rate is proportional to the pressure difference across the tube and to the fourth power of the tube radius, and inversely proportional to the tube length and the fluid viscosity.

qs.q: What is the volumetric flow rate of blood through the normal segment?
o: 3.8 mL/s
Not quite. This is one quarter of the correct value, as if the area had been divided by 4.
60 mL/s
Not quite. This is four times the correct value, as if the radius were doubled.
15 mL/s
Correct: Q = Av = π(4.0 × 10⁻³ m)²(0.30 m/s) = 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ m³/s = 15 mL/s.
1.5 mL/s
Not quite. This is a factor of 10 too small, from a slip in converting m³ to mL (1 m³ = 10⁶ mL).
qs.x: Correct: Volumetric flow rate is how much volume of fluid passes per second. The formula is Q = Av, where A is the cross-sectional area of the tube and v is the speed of the blood. From the passage, the normal segment has radius r = 4.0 mm and speed v = 0.30 m/s. First change the radius to meters: 1 mm = 10⁻³ m, so r = 4.0 × 10⁻³ m. The area of a circle is A = πr² = π(4.0 × 10⁻³)². Square it: (4.0 × 10⁻³)² = 16 × 10⁻⁶ = 1.6 × 10⁻⁵ m² (squaring doubles the exponent: −3 × 2 = −6). Then A = 3.14 × 1.6 × 10⁻⁵ = 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ m². Now Q = Av = (5.0 × 10⁻⁵)(0.30) = 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ m³/s. To get mL/s: 1 m³ = 10⁶ mL, so multiply by 10⁶: 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ × 10⁶ = 1.5 × 10¹ = 15 mL/s. Why the others are wrong: 3.8 mL/s is one quarter of the right value, as if the area were divided by 4; 60 mL/s is four times the right value, as if the radius were doubled; 1.5 mL/s is a factor of 10 too small, a slip in the m³ to mL conversion. Trap: Slipping on the m³ to mL conversion, or using the radius or diameter without squaring it.

qs.q: Exercise increases the total flow rate through the model by 50% while the geometry is unchanged. What is the speed in the 2.0 mm radius segment?
o: Not quite. This multiplies by 1.5 twice, as if speed went with the square of the flow rate.
Correct: With a fixed area, speed is proportional to flow rate, so v = 1.20 × 1.5 = 1.8 m/s.
Not quite. This adds 0.30 m/s to the table speed. A 50% increase is a multiplication by 1.5.
Not quite. This divides by 1.5, which would mean the flow rate decreased.
qs.x: Correct: The tube geometry is the same, so the cross-sectional area of the 2.0 mm segment doesn't change. From Q = Av, if A is fixed, the speed is directly proportional to the flow rate Q. The flow goes up by 50%, which means the new flow is 1.5 times the old. So the speed is also 1.5 times bigger. From Table 1, the speed in the 2.0 mm radius segment before exercise is 1.20 m/s. Plug in: v<sub>new</sub> = 1.20 × 1.5 = 1.8 m/s. Why the others are wrong: 2.7 m/s multiplies by 1.5 twice (1.20 × 1.5 × 1.5), as if speed went with the square of the flow; 1.5 m/s adds 0.30 to the speed (1.20 + 0.30), when a 50% increase is a multiplication, not an addition; 0.8 m/s divides by 1.5 (1.20 ÷ 1.5), which would mean the flow went down. Trap: Treating the 50% increase as something to add, or squaring it, rather than scaling the speed in proportion.

qs.q: According to Table 1, the pressure drop in the 2.0 mm segment is 716 Pa. Approximately what is this in mmHg? (1 mmHg = 133 Pa)
o: 54 mmHg
Not quite. This is 10 times too big, with the decimal point in the wrong place.
5.4 mmHg
Correct: 716 Pa ÷ 133 Pa/mmHg = 5.4 mmHg.
0.54 mmHg
Not quite. This is 10 times too small, with the decimal point in the wrong place.
716 mmHg
Not quite. This is the pascal number with the wrong unit. No conversion was done.
qs.x: Correct: A unit conversion works by dividing by the conversion factor when you want the bigger unit. 1 mmHg = 133 Pa (given), so one mmHg is 133 Pa. To change 716 Pa into mmHg, divide by 133 Pa per mmHg: 716 ÷ 133 = 5.38, about 5.4 mmHg. The pascals cancel, leaving mmHg. A quick sense check: 133 × 5 = 665, and 133 × 5.4 = 718, so 5.4 is right. The 716 Pa pressure drop in the 2.0 mm segment comes from Table 1, and it is lower there because the blood is moving faster (1.20 m/s): Bernoulli's equation says faster fluid has more kinetic energy per volume, so the pressure is lower. Why the others are wrong: 54 mmHg and 0.54 mmHg are the same digits with the decimal point put in the wrong place, off by a factor of 10 either way; 716 mmHg is just the pascal number with a new unit label and no conversion done. Trap: Misplacing the decimal point in a unit conversion, or forgetting to convert Pa to mmHg at all.

qs.q: In a real viscous artery of fixed length and fixed pressure difference, what happens to the volumetric flow rate if the radius is cut in half?
o: It decreases by a factor of 16.
Correct: Poiseuille's law gives Q ∝ r⁴, so halving r multiplies Q by (1/2)⁴ = 1/16.
It decreases by a factor of 4.
Not quite. A factor of 4 comes from the ideal-fluid continuity relation for speed (1/r²). It ignores the r⁴ in viscous flow.
It decreases by a factor of 2.
Not quite. A factor of 2 would mean Q is directly proportional to the radius.
It increases by a factor of 4.
Not quite. A narrower tube resists the flow much more, so the flow rate falls.
qs.x: Correct: The passage says Poiseuille's law gives the flow rate Q as proportional to the pressure difference and to the fourth power of the tube radius, and inversely proportional to the length and the viscosity. In this question the length and the pressure difference are fixed, and so is the fluid, so Q is proportional to r⁴ alone. If the radius is cut in half, r becomes ½ of the old radius. Then Q is multiplied by (½)⁴ = ½ × ½ × ½ × ½ = 1/16. The flow rate drops to one sixteenth, a decrease by a factor of 16. This is why a small narrowing of an artery has such a big effect on flow. Why the others are wrong: a factor of 4 comes from the ideal-fluid continuity relation, where speed goes as 1/r² and halving the radius quadruples the speed, and it ignores the r⁴ in the viscous flow rate; a factor of 2 would mean Q is directly proportional to the radius; an increase isn't possible, since a narrower tube resists flow much more. Trap: Using the continuity-equation relation for speed (1/r²) instead of the r⁴ dependence of viscous flow.

h: Pressure drop relative to normal segment (Pa)
