passages.title: FL01 · Chem/Phys · Passage 3
text: A concentration cell is built from two copper electrodes, each immersed in its own beaker of aqueous CuSO₄, with the beakers joined by a salt bridge. The Cu²⁺ concentration in one beaker is fixed at 1.0 M, and the concentration in the other beaker is varied. At 25 °C the cell potential is given by E = (0.0592/n) log([Cu²⁺] in the concentrated half-cell ÷ [Cu²⁺] in the dilute half-cell), where n = 2 for this reaction. For each dilute concentration, the open-circuit potential was measured with a voltmeter of very high resistance. The cell was then connected across a 100 Ω resistor, and the potential difference across the resistor was measured. The results appear in Table 1, and Figure 1 plots the open-circuit potential against −log[Cu²⁺] of the dilute half-cell. The difference between the open-circuit potential and the potential across the resistor is due to the internal resistance of the cell, which behaves like a resistor in series with an ideal source.

qs.q: Which description of the electrode reactions and electron flow is correct when the cell operates?
o: Cu(s) is oxidized in the 1.0 M half-cell, and electrons flow through the wire toward the dilute half-cell.
Not quite. Oxidizing Cu in the 1.0 M cell would make the concentrations more unequal, which isn't spontaneous.
Cu(s) is oxidized in the dilute half-cell, and electrons flow through the wire toward the 1.0 M half-cell.
Correct: Cu oxidizes in the dilute cell (anode), raising its [Cu²⁺], and electrons flow through the wire to the 1.0 M cell.
Cu²⁺ is reduced in the dilute half-cell, and electrons flow through the wire toward the dilute half-cell.
Not quite. Reduction happens at the cathode, the 1.0 M cell, and electrons flow toward the cathode, not away from it.
Cu(s) is oxidized in the dilute half-cell, and electrons flow through the wire toward the dilute half-cell.
Not quite. Electrons flow from the anode to the cathode, so they can't flow toward the anode.
qs.x: Correct: A concentration cell has the same metal and ion on both sides, and the only difference is concentration. It runs because nature wants to even out the concentrations. The 1.0 M side has too much Cu²⁺, and the dilute side has too little. To even them out, the cell makes more Cu²⁺ in the dilute half-cell and uses Cu²⁺ up in the concentrated half-cell. Making Cu²⁺ means oxidation, Cu(s) → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻, so the dilute half-cell is the anode (where oxidation happens). Using up Cu²⁺ means reduction, Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu(s), so the 1.0 M half-cell is the cathode. Electrons are given off at the anode and flow through the wire to the cathode, so they travel from the dilute half-cell toward the 1.0 M half-cell. Why the others are wrong: oxidizing copper in the 1.0 M half-cell would make the concentrations more unequal, which isn't spontaneous; reduction takes place at the cathode, which is the 1.0 M half-cell, and electrons flow toward the cathode, not toward the dilute side; oxidation in the dilute half-cell is right, but electrons can't flow toward the anode, since they leave from it. Trap: Forgetting that electrons flow from the anode to the cathode through the external wire.

qs.q: What open-circuit potential is expected when the dilute half-cell is 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ M Cu²⁺?
o: Not quite. 0.059 V is the value for a dilute concentration of 0.010 M, where the log is 2.
Correct: E = 0.0296 × log(1.0 ÷ 1.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 0.0296 × 4 = 0.118 V, in line with Figure 1.
Not quite. This uses 0.0592 without dividing by n = 2.
Not quite. 0.030 V is the value for 0.10 M, where the log is 1.
qs.x: Correct: Use the equation in the passage: E = (0.0592 ÷ n) log([Cu²⁺] concentrated ÷ [Cu²⁺] dilute), with n = 2. First 0.0592 ÷ 2 = 0.0296. The concentrations: the concentrated side is 1.0 M and the dilute side is 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ M. The ratio is 1.0 ÷ 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.0 × 10⁴ (dividing by 10⁻⁴ is the same as multiplying by 10⁴). Log reads off the exponent of 10: log(10⁴) = 4. Plug in: E = 0.0296 × 4 = 0.1184 V, about 0.118 V. This follows the trend in Figure 1: each tenfold drop in dilute concentration adds 0.0296 V (0.0296 at 0.10 M, 0.0592 at 0.010 M, 0.0888 at 0.0010 M), so at 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ M (four tenfold drops) E = 4 × 0.0296 = 0.118 V. Why the others are wrong: 0.059 V is the value for a dilute concentration of 0.010 M (log = 2); 0.237 V comes from using 0.0592 without dividing by n = 2 (0.0592 × 4 = 0.237); 0.030 V is the value for 0.10 M (log = 1). Trap: Using 0.0592 without dividing by the 2 electrons transferred.

qs.q: When the dilute half-cell is 0.010 M, what is the current through the 100 Ω resistor?
o: Correct: I = V ÷ R = 0.0548 V ÷ 100 Ω = 5.5 × 10⁻⁴ A = 0.55 mA, using the voltage actually across the resistor.
Not quite. This uses the open-circuit potential (0.0592 V). Under load, the resistor gets 0.0548 V.
Not quite. This is off by a factor of 10⁴, a unit conversion error. 5.5 × 10⁻⁴ A is 0.55 mA.
Not quite. This is a factor of 10 too small.
qs.x: Correct: Ohm's law says V = IR, so the current is I = V ÷ R. The key detail is which voltage to use. When the cell is connected to the resistor, the cell has some internal resistance, and some of its voltage is lost inside the cell itself. The voltage across the resistor is what drives the current through it, so use the third column of Table 1, not the open-circuit value. For the 0.010 M row, V = 0.0548 V, and R = 100 Ω. Plug in: I = 0.0548 ÷ 100 = 0.000548 A = 5.48 × 10⁻⁴ A. To convert to milliamps: 1 mA = 10⁻³ A, so divide by 10⁻³ (move the decimal 3 places): 5.48 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ 10⁻³ = 0.548 mA, about 0.55 mA. Why the others are wrong: 0.59 mA uses the open-circuit potential, 0.0592 V ÷ 100 Ω, but that isn't the voltage across the resistor under load; 5.5 A is off by a factor of 10⁴, a unit conversion slip; 0.055 mA is a factor of 10 too small. Trap: Using the open-circuit voltage instead of the voltage across the resistor in Ohm's law.

qs.q: Based on the 0.010 M row of Table 1, what is the internal resistance of the cell?
o: Correct: The internal drop is 0.0592 − 0.0548 = 0.0044 V at I = 5.48 × 10⁻⁴ A, so r = 0.0044 ÷ 5.48 × 10⁻⁴ = 8.0 Ω.
Not quite. This is a factor of 10 too large, a slip with the exponents.
Not quite. This is a factor of 10 too small, a slip with the exponents.
Not quite. This is the total series resistance (100 Ω + 8 Ω), not the internal resistance alone.
qs.x: Correct: The passage says the cell acts like an ideal source in series with an internal resistor r. The open-circuit voltage, E = 0.0592 V (the 0.010 M row in Table 1), is the full voltage. When the cell drives the 100 Ω resistor, only 0.0548 V shows up across it. The difference is lost across the internal resistance: 0.0592 − 0.0548 = 0.0044 V. The same current flows through both resistors (they are in series): I = 0.0548 ÷ 100 = 5.48 × 10⁻⁴ A. Then Ohm's law for the internal resistance gives r = V ÷ I = 0.0044 ÷ 5.48 × 10⁻⁴. Step by step: 0.0044 = 4.4 × 10⁻³, so r = 4.4 × 10⁻³ ÷ 5.48 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.803 × 10¹ (dividing, so subtract the exponents: −3 − (−4) = +1) = 8.0 Ω. Why the others are wrong: 80 Ω and 0.80 Ω are the same digits off by a factor of 10 in the exponent; 108 Ω is the total resistance in the circuit (100 Ω load + 8 Ω internal), not the internal resistance alone. Trap: Giving the total circuit resistance instead of subtracting the 100 Ω load.

qs.q: If the cell is left connected across the resistor for a long time, what happens to the open-circuit potential?
o: It increases because Cu²⁺ accumulates in the dilute half-cell.
Not quite. Cu²⁺ does build up in the dilute cell, but that narrows the gap between the concentrations, so E falls.
It decreases toward zero as the two Cu²⁺ concentrations approach each other.
Correct: Discharge raises [Cu²⁺] in the dilute cell and lowers it in the concentrated cell, so the log term and E fall toward zero.
It remains constant because the copper electrodes are not consumed overall.
Not quite. The copper isn't consumed overall, but the potential depends on the concentration ratio, which changes.
It decreases toward zero because the copper electrodes become identical in mass.
Not quite. The potential depends on ion concentrations, not on the electrodes' masses.
qs.x: Correct: The open-circuit potential depends on the ratio of the two Cu²⁺ concentrations, E = (0.0592 ÷ 2) log([concentrated] ÷ [dilute]). The cell runs by oxidizing copper in the dilute half-cell (adding Cu²⁺ there) and reducing Cu²⁺ in the concentrated half-cell (removing Cu²⁺ there). So while the cell is connected to the resistor, the dilute side gets more concentrated and the 1.0 M side gets less concentrated. The two concentrations move toward each other, and the ratio drops toward 1. Log(1) = 0, so E falls toward zero. When the concentrations are equal, the cell has nothing left to even out, and E = 0 V. That's equilibrium, where Q = 1 and ΔG = 0. Why the others are wrong: Cu²⁺ does build up in the dilute half-cell, but this narrows the gap in concentrations, so E falls rather than rises; the copper metal is not consumed overall, but the potential depends on the concentration ratio, and that changes; it's the concentrations that move toward equal, not the electrodes becoming equal in mass, and the potential depends on ion concentrations, not electrode mass. Trap: Assuming E is fixed because the electrode material doesn't change, when it depends on the concentration ratio.

graph.title: Figure 1. Open-circuit potential versus -log[Cu²⁺] of the dilute half-cell

passages.title: FL01 · Chem/Phys · Passage 4
text: Doppler ultrasound estimates blood speed by measuring the frequency shift of echoes from moving red blood cells. A probe emits sound of frequency f₀ = 5.0 MHz into soft tissue, in which sound travels at c = 1540 m/s. For blood moving at speed v much less than c, with the beam making an angle θ with the flow direction, the magnitude of the frequency shift is Δf = 2f₀v cosθ / c. A technician tests a phantom in which fluid flows at a constant 0.50 m/s, varying the angle between the probe and the flow. The measured shifts agree with the equation and are shown in Table 1. In a separate measurement through deep tissue, the echo returning from a boundary had an intensity equal to one-thousandth of the intensity of the transmitted pulse. The technician reports attenuation in decibels, where the change in sound level is β = 10 log(I₂/I₁). Assume sound is a longitudinal wave in all media discussed.

qs.q: At θ = 0°, what frequency shift would be measured for blood flowing at 0.80 m/s?
o: Not quite. This is about half the right value and doesn't come from the formula. Δf rises with speed, so it should be larger than 3247 Hz.
Not quite. This is the Table 1 value for 0.50 m/s. The blood here is faster, so the shift must be larger.
Not quite. This multiplies by 1.6 twice, as if Δf grew with v². It grows in direct proportion to v.
Correct: Δf is proportional to v, so 3247 Hz × (0.80 ÷ 0.50) = 3247 × 1.6 = 5195 Hz, about 5200 Hz.
qs.x: Correct: The passage gives Δf = 2f₀v cosθ ÷ c, where f₀ is the probe frequency, v is the blood speed, θ is the beam angle and c is the speed of sound in tissue. Everything stays the same here except v, so Δf is directly proportional to v (double the speed, double the shift). Table 1 says that at θ = 0° and v = 0.50 m/s the shift is 3247 Hz. The new speed is 0.80 m/s, so the ratio is 0.80 ÷ 0.50 = 1.6. Multiply: Δf = 3247 Hz × 1.6 = 5195 Hz, which rounds to about 5200 Hz. You can check this with the formula: at 0°, cos 0° = 1, so Δf = 2 × (5.0 × 10⁶ Hz) × 0.80 ÷ 1540 = 8.0 × 10⁶ ÷ 1540 = 5195 Hz. Why the others are wrong: 2600 Hz is about half of the right answer, 5195 Hz, and doesn't fit any step of the work; 3250 Hz is the table value for 0.50 m/s, with the faster flow ignored; 8300 Hz is 3247 × 1.6 × 1.6, as if Δf grew with v². Trap: Squaring the speed ratio, even though the shift is linear in v.

qs.q: Why does the equation for Δf contain a factor of 2?
o: The ultrasound travels to the blood and back, doubling the wavelength.
Not quite. The round trip is longer, but it doesn't double the wavelength. The shift comes from the motion of the cells.
Blood cells move in both directions along the vessel, so two shifts add together.
Not quite. Blood moves one way along the vessel. Motion in opposite directions would give shifts of opposite sign, not added ones.
Sound waves in tissue have both longitudinal and transverse components, each shifted once.
Not quite. The passage says sound is longitudinal in all media, so there are no transverse parts to shift.
The blood cells first act as moving receivers of the transmitted wave and then as moving sources of the reflected wave, so the shift occurs twice.
Correct: The moving cell first acts as a moving receiver, then as a moving source of the echo, so the shift happens twice.
qs.x: Correct: A Doppler shift is a change in the frequency you hear when the source or the listener is moving. In this setup the sound shifts twice. First, the red blood cell is moving, so as a receiver it meets the waves at a different rate than the probe sent them, and it "hears" a shifted frequency. Then the cell scatters (reflects) that sound back, so now it acts as a moving source sending out the shifted frequency. The probe then receives a frequency shifted a second time by almost the same amount. Two nearly equal shifts add up, which gives the factor of 2 in Δf = 2f₀v cosθ ÷ c. Why the others are wrong: the round trip makes the sound travel farther, but it does not double the wavelength, and distance has nothing to do with the shift; blood in a given vessel flows one way, and shifts from opposite directions would have opposite signs and cancel rather than add; the passage states sound is a longitudinal wave in all media, so there are no transverse parts to add in. Trap: Blaming the 2 on the sound going there and back, when it comes from the Doppler effect happening twice.

qs.q: What is the wavelength of the 5.0 MHz ultrasound in soft tissue?
o: 3.1 mm
Not quite. The digits are right but the decimal is one place too far right. Recheck the m to mm conversion.
Not quite. The digits are right but the decimal is one place too far left. Recheck the m to mm conversion.
7.7 mm
Not quite. This multiplies by 5.0 where you should divide: 1540 × 5.0 ÷ 10⁶ = 7.7 × 10⁻³ m = 7.7 mm. Wavelength is c ÷ f.
qs.x: Correct: For any wave, the speed equals frequency times wavelength, so the wavelength is λ = c ÷ f, where c is the speed of sound and f is the frequency. From the passage, c = 1540 m/s and f₀ = 5.0 MHz. The prefix M (mega) means a million, 1 MHz = 10⁶ Hz, so 5.0 MHz = 5.0 × 10⁶ Hz. Plug in: λ = 1540 m/s ÷ (5.0 × 10⁶ Hz). First 1540 ÷ 5.0 = 308. Then 308 ÷ 10⁶ = 308 × 10⁻⁶ m = 3.08 × 10⁻⁴ m (moving the decimal two places left adds 2 to the exponent: −6 + 2 = −4). That rounds to 3.1 × 10⁻⁴ m. To get millimeters, remember 1 mm = 10⁻³ m, so divide by 10⁻³: 3.1 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ 10⁻³ = 3.1 × 10⁻¹ mm = 0.31 mm. Why the others are wrong: 3.1 mm and 0.031 mm are the same digits with the decimal in the wrong place, a slip when converting m to mm; 7.7 mm comes from multiplying by 5.0 where you should divide (1540 × 5.0 ÷ 10⁶ = 7.7 × 10⁻³ m). Trap: Losing a power of 10 when converting MHz to Hz or meters to millimeters.

qs.q: What is the attenuation, in decibels, of the echo described in the passage relative to the transmitted pulse?
o: 20 dB
Not quite. 20 dB means a factor of 100 in intensity. One-thousandth needs three factors of 10.
3 dB
Not quite. This is just the exponent, 3. The formula multiplies the log by 10 to get decibels.
30 dB
Correct: β = 10 log(10⁻³) = 10 × (−3) = −30 dB, so the echo is 30 dB below the transmitted pulse.
300 dB
Not quite. 300 dB would mean a factor of 10³⁰. One-thousandth is 10⁻³, giving 30 dB.
qs.x: Correct: Sound level change is β = 10 log(I₂ ÷ I₁), where I₂ is the echo intensity and I₁ is the transmitted intensity. The echo is one-thousandth of the transmitted pulse, so I₂ ÷ I₁ = 1/1000 = 10⁻³. Plug in: β = 10 log(10⁻³). The log just reads off the exponent of 10, so log(10⁻³) = −3. Then β = 10 × (−3) = −30 dB. The negative sign means the echo is weaker, so the attenuation (the loss) is 30 dB. A good habit: every factor of 10 in intensity is 10 dB, and 1000 is three factors of 10, which gives 30 dB. Why the others are wrong: 20 dB is a factor of 100 (10 log 10⁻² = −20), not 1000; 3 dB is just the exponent, with the 10 never multiplied in (and 3 dB really means about a factor of 2); 300 dB would be a factor of 10³⁰, far too big. Trap: Reading the exponent (3) as the decibel value and forgetting to multiply by 10.

passages.title: FL01 · Chem/Phys · Passage 5
text: Technetium-99m (Tc-99m) is a metastable nuclear isomer widely used for diagnostic imaging. It is obtained from a generator in which molybdenum-99 (atomic number 42) undergoes β⁻ decay, producing Tc-99m. Tc-99m then decays to the ground state of technetium-99 by emitting a γ photon of energy 140 keV. A technician isolates a sample of pure Tc-99m and measures its activity in a dose calibrator every 6.0 hours for one day. The data in Table 1 show that the activity is halved during each 6.0 hour interval. Figure 1 plots the natural logarithm of the activity against time. Use hc = 1240 eV·nm. A decay constant λ and the half-life t½ are related by t½ = ln 2/λ, where ln 2 = 0.693. Radioactive decay is a first-order process, so the activity A at time t obeys A = A₀e^(−λt), and a plot of ln A against t is a straight line with slope −λ. Because the γ photon carries no charge and no mass, the emission leaves the nucleus with the same numbers of protons and neutrons that it had before the transition. Clinically, the short half-life limits the radiation dose to the patient.

qs.q: What is the decay constant of Tc-99m?
o: Not quite. This is 1 ÷ 6.0 with the ln 2 left out. The formula needs ln 2 in the top.
Correct: λ = ln 2 ÷ t½ = 0.693 ÷ 6.0 h = 0.12 h⁻¹, matching the slope magnitude in Figure 1.
Not quite. This is t½ ÷ ln 2, the relationship flipped. The decay constant should be small for a 6 h half-life.
Not quite. This multiplies 6.0 by 0.693. The formula divides ln 2 by the half-life.
qs.x: Correct: The passage gives the link between half-life and decay constant: t½ = ln 2 ÷ λ, so λ = ln 2 ÷ t½. The decay constant λ is the fraction of the sample that decays per unit time. From the passage, ln 2 = 0.693, and Table 1 shows the activity halves every 6.0 h, so t½ = 6.0 h. Plug in: λ = 0.693 ÷ 6.0 h = 0.1155 h⁻¹, which rounds to 0.12 h⁻¹. Check against Figure 1: ln A goes from 5.99 at 0 h to 3.22 at 24 h, so the slope is (3.22 − 5.99) ÷ 24 = −2.77 ÷ 24 = −0.115 h⁻¹. The magnitude of the slope is λ, and it matches. Why the others are wrong: 0.17 h⁻¹ is 1 ÷ 6.0, which skips the ln 2; 8.7 h⁻¹ is 6.0 ÷ 0.693, with the relationship flipped upside down; 4.2 h⁻¹ is 6.0 × 0.693, multiplying where the formula divides. Trap: Using 1 ÷ t½ as the decay constant and forgetting ln 2.

qs.q: If the sample were measured again 30 hours after the first measurement, what activity would be expected?
o: 6.3 MBq
Not quite. This is six half-lives, which would be 36 h. At 30 h there have been only five.
25 MBq
Not quite. This is the Table 1 value at 24 h, four half-lives. Thirty hours is one more halving.
12.5 MBq
Correct: 30 h ÷ 6.0 h = 5 half-lives, so A = 400 ÷ 2⁵ = 400 ÷ 32 = 12.5 MBq.
50 MBq
Not quite. This is the Table 1 value at 18 h, three half-lives. More time has passed than that.
qs.x: Correct: Each half-life cuts the activity in half. The sample is measured at time zero, so 30 hours after the first measurement is t = 30 h. Count the half-lives: number of half-lives = t ÷ t½ = 30 h ÷ 6.0 h = 5. The starting activity from Table 1 is A₀ = 400 MBq. After 5 halvings, A = A₀ ÷ 2⁵. Work out 2⁵ = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32. So A = 400 ÷ 32 = 12.5 MBq. You can also halve step by step: 400 → 200 → 100 → 50 → 25 → 12.5. That is five halvings, and the table already gives the first four. Why the others are wrong: 25 MBq is the measured value at 24 h, only four half-lives; 50 MBq is the value at 18 h, three half-lives; 6.3 MBq is six half-lives, which is 36 h (400 ÷ 64 = 6.25). Trap: Miscounting the half-lives, or just grabbing the nearest number from the table.

qs.q: Which statement correctly describes the decay of Tc-99m to Tc-99?
o: The nucleus emits a β⁻ particle, increasing the atomic number by 1.
Not quite. β⁻ decay is how Mo-99 turns into Tc-99m. Tc-99m to Tc-99 keeps the same element.
The nucleus emits a γ photon and moves to a lower energy state, with its mass number and atomic number unchanged.
Correct: An isomeric transition releases extra nuclear energy as a γ photon, so protons and neutrons are unchanged.
The nucleus emits an α particle, decreasing the mass number by 4.
Not quite. α emission would drop the mass number by 4 and change the element. The product here is Tc-99.
The nucleus captures an inner electron, decreasing the atomic number by 1.
Not quite. Electron capture would lower the atomic number by 1, giving molybdenum. The product is still technetium.
qs.x: Correct: The passage says Tc-99m is a metastable isomer. That means it has the same protons and neutrons as Tc-99, just with extra energy stored in the nucleus (the "m" stands for metastable). It gets rid of that extra energy by emitting a γ photon (a gamma ray, a packet of light with no mass and no charge), and ends up in the ground state, Tc-99. Look at the passage's sentence about the photon: because it carries no charge or mass, the nucleus keeps the same numbers of protons and neutrons. So both the atomic number (43) and the mass number (99) stay the same. Why the others are wrong: β⁻ emission would raise the atomic number by 1, but β⁻ is the decay that made Tc-99m out of Mo-99, and the product here is still technetium; α emission would drop the mass number by 4, giving a mass-95 nucleus, not Tc-99; electron capture would lower the atomic number by 1 and give molybdenum, but the passage says the product is Tc-99. Trap: Mixing up the β⁻ decay that forms Tc-99m with the γ emission by which it decays.

qs.q: What is the wavelength of the 140 keV γ photon?
o: 8.9 nm
Not quite. The digits are right, but 8.9 nm is 1000 times too big. The answer is 8.9 × 10⁻³ nm.
Not quite. This is a factor of 10 too small. Recheck the division by 1.40 × 10⁵ and the nm to pm step.
89 pm
Not quite. This is a factor of 10 too large, a slip with the power of 10.
8.9 pm
qs.x: Correct: A photon's wavelength comes from its energy: E = hc ÷ λ, so λ = hc ÷ E. The passage gives hc = 1240 eV·nm and the photon energy is 140 keV. The prefix k (kilo) means 1000, so 140 keV = 140 × 10³ eV = 1.40 × 10⁵ eV. Plug in: λ = 1240 eV·nm ÷ (1.40 × 10⁵ eV). The eV units cancel and leave nm. 1240 ÷ 1.40 = 885.7, and dividing by 10⁵ gives 885.7 × 10⁻⁵ nm = 8.86 × 10⁻³ nm (the decimal moves two places left, so the exponent goes up by 2: −5 + 2 = −3). Now change to picometers. 1 pm = 10⁻³ nm, so 1 nm = 1000 pm, and we multiply by 1000: 8.86 × 10⁻³ nm × 1000 = 8.86 pm, which rounds to 8.9 pm. Why the others are wrong: 8.9 nm and 0.89 pm are the same digits with the unit or the decimal slipped, off by a factor of 1000 and a factor of 10; 89 pm is 10 times too big, from a slip in the power of 10. Trap: Losing track of the factor of 1000 between nanometers and picometers.

passages.title: FL01 · Chem/Phys · Passage 6
text: Colligative properties depend on the number of dissolved particles rather than their identity. A student measures the freezing-point depression, ΔTf, of aqueous solutions that are each 0.50 molal. The van't Hoff factor i is defined as the measured ΔTf divided by the ΔTf expected if the solute did not dissociate (Kf = 1.86 °C·kg/mol for water). The ideal values of i are 1 for glucose, 2 for NaCl, 3 for CaCl₂, and 2 for MgSO₄. Results are given in Table 1. For comparison, the boiling-point elevation constant of water is Kb = 0.512 °C·kg/mol. For osmotic pressure, Π = iMRT, with R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K). Assume that for these dilute solutions the molarity is approximately equal to the molality, and that measured i values at 0.50 m apply at 25 °C. The student also notes that all measurements used the same pure solvent, that the solutes are non-volatile, and that the measured values differ from the ideal ones for some salts because interactions between ions in solution reduce their effective independence. Molar masses should be taken from a periodic table when needed.

qs.q: What freezing-point depression is expected for a 0.20 m aqueous glucose solution?
o: Not quite. This is the 0.50 m value from Table 1. The solution here is more dilute, so the drop is smaller.
Not quite. This doubles the answer as if glucose split into two ions. It doesn't, so i = 1.
Correct: Glucose does not dissociate, so ΔTf = 1 × 1.86 × 0.20 = 0.37 °C.
Not quite. This is half of the right value, and nothing in the formula calls for halving.
qs.x: Correct: Freezing-point depression is how many degrees the freezing point drops when you dissolve something. The formula is ΔTf = i Kf m, where i is the van't Hoff factor (the number of particles each unit of solute makes), Kf is the freezing-point constant and m is the molality (moles of solute per kg of water). Glucose doesn't split into ions, so i = 1, and Table 1 confirms it with a measured i of 1.00. Kf = 1.86 °C·kg/mol and m = 0.20 mol/kg. Plug in: ΔTf = 1 × 1.86 × 0.20. 1.86 × 0.20 = 0.372, so ΔTf = 0.37 °C. Why the others are wrong: 0.93 °C is the Table 1 value at 0.50 m, with the lower concentration ignored; 0.74 °C doubles the answer as if glucose made two ions; 0.19 °C is half of 0.37 with no reason to halve it. Trap: Using a van't Hoff factor above 1 for a nonelectrolyte (a solute that does not break into ions).

qs.q: Which explanation best accounts for the van't Hoff factor of MgSO₄ being much lower than 2?
o: MgSO₄ is a molecular compound that does not dissociate in water.
Not quite. MgSO₄ is an ionic salt, and its measured i of 1.18 is above 1, so it does dissociate.
Mg²⁺ ions react with water to form Mg(s) and H₂.
Not quite. Water doesn't reduce Mg²⁺ to magnesium metal under these conditions, and that wouldn't explain a lower i anyway.
The sulfate ion is much larger than chloride, so it lowers the freezing point of water less per ion.
Not quite. Colligative properties depend on how many particles there are, not how big each one is.
The highly charged Mg²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ ions associate into ion pairs, reducing the effective number of independent particles.
Correct: The 2+ and 2− ions attract strongly and form ion pairs, which reduces the number of independent particles.
qs.x: Correct: The van't Hoff factor counts how many independent particles each formula unit gives in solution. MgSO₄ could ideally make 2 (one Mg²⁺ and one SO₄²⁻), but Table 1 shows the measured i is only 1.18. The reason is that both ions carry a 2+ or 2− charge, so they pull on each other strongly. Some of them stay stuck together as ion pairs, and a stuck pair counts as one particle. That cuts the number of independent particles and lowers i. The passage says this directly: interactions between ions reduce their effective independence. Why the others are wrong: MgSO₄ is an ionic salt, and a measured i of 1.18 is above 1, so it does dissociate, just not fully; magnesium metal and H₂ are not formed, since Mg²⁺ is not reduced by water; ion size doesn't matter, because colligative properties depend on how many particles there are, not what they are. Trap: Thinking colligative effects depend on the size or identity of the ions instead of the particle count.

qs.q: Approximately what osmotic pressure would a 0.50 M NaCl solution have at 25 °C, using the measured i from Table 1?
o: 12 atm
Not quite. This uses i = 1 and ignores that NaCl splits into ions. The measured i is 1.94.
37 atm
Not quite. This uses i = 3, the ideal value for CaCl₂. NaCl makes two ions, and its measured i is 1.94.
48 atm
Not quite. This is about double the right answer, as if i were nearly 4. The measured i for NaCl is 1.94.
24 atm
Correct: Π = iMRT = 1.94 × 0.50 × 0.0821 × 298 = 23.7 atm, about 24 atm.
qs.x: Correct: Osmotic pressure is the pressure needed to stop water from flowing into a solution through a membrane. The passage gives Π = iMRT, where i is the van't Hoff factor, M is the molarity, R is the gas constant and T is the temperature in kelvin. Values: i = 1.94 (measured for NaCl in Table 1), M = 0.50 mol/L, R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K), and T = 25 °C + 273 = 298 K. Plug in: Π = 1.94 × 0.50 × 0.0821 × 298. Go one step at a time: 1.94 × 0.50 = 0.97. Then 0.0821 × 298 = 24.47. Then 0.97 × 24.47 = 23.7 atm, about 24 atm. Why the others are wrong: 12 atm uses i = 1, so it pretends NaCl doesn't split into ions (0.50 × 24.47 = 12.2); 37 atm uses i = 3, which belongs to CaCl₂ (3 × 0.50 × 24.47 = 36.7); 48 atm is about double the right answer, as if i were about 4. Trap: Leaving out the van't Hoff factor, or using the wrong number of ions.

qs.q: What is the boiling point of the 0.50 m glucose solution at 1 atm?
o: Not quite. This lowers the boiling point. A dissolved solute raises it.
Not quite. This uses the freezing-point depression (0.93 °C from Kf) instead of the boiling-point constant Kb.
Not quite. This doubles the change, as if glucose broke into two particles. Glucose stays whole, so i = 1.
Correct: ΔTb = 1 × 0.512 × 0.50 = 0.26 °C, so the boiling point rises from 100.00 °C to 100.26 °C.
qs.x: Correct: Dissolving a non-volatile solute raises the boiling point. The formula is ΔTb = i Kb m, where Kb is the boiling-point constant, m is molality, and i is the van't Hoff factor. Glucose doesn't dissociate, so i = 1 (Table 1 gives a measured i of 1.00). The passage gives Kb = 0.512 °C·kg/mol, and the solution is 0.50 m. Plug in: ΔTb = 1 × 0.512 × 0.50 = 0.256 °C, which rounds to 0.26 °C. Pure water boils at 100.00 °C at 1 atm, and the solution boils higher, so add: 100.00 + 0.26 = 100.26 °C. Why the others are wrong: 99.74 °C subtracts 0.26 instead of adding it, but a solute raises the boiling point; 100.93 °C uses the freezing constant Kf (1.86 × 0.50 = 0.93) instead of Kb; 100.51 °C doubles ΔTb, as if glucose made two particles. Trap: Using the freezing-point constant Kf in a boiling-point problem.

qs.q: What mass of CaCl₂ (molar mass 110.98 g/mol) should be dissolved in 500 g of water to prepare a 0.50 m solution?
o: Not quite. That is 0.50 mol, the amount for a full 1.0 kg of water. Only 0.500 kg is used here.
Not quite. That is 0.125 mol, only enough for 250 g of water. The solution has 500 g.
Correct: 0.50 mol/kg × 0.500 kg = 0.25 mol, and 0.25 mol × 110.98 g/mol = 27.7 g.
Not quite. That is a full mole, which would make 2.0 m in 500 g of water.
qs.x: Correct: Molality (m) is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent, so moles = molality × kg of water. From the question, m = 0.50 mol/kg and the water is 500 g. Convert grams to kilograms: 1 kg = 1000 g, so divide by 1000: 500 g ÷ 1000 = 0.500 kg. Plug in: moles of CaCl₂ = 0.50 mol/kg × 0.500 kg = 0.25 mol. Now convert moles to grams with the molar mass, 110.98 g/mol: mass = 0.25 mol × 110.98 g/mol = 27.7 g (a quarter of 110.98 is 27.745). Why the others are wrong: 55.5 g is 0.50 mol, enough for a full 1.0 kg of water; 13.9 g is 0.125 mol, only enough for 250 g of water; 111 g is a full mole, which in 500 g of water would be 2.0 m. Trap: Using the full kilogram of solvent when only 500 g is used.

passages.title: FL01 · Chem/Phys · Passage 7
text: A student compares boiling points to evaluate the role of intermolecular forces. Table 1 lists four compounds of nearly equal molar mass but different functional groups, along with their normal boiling points. Figure 1 shows the normal boiling points of the straight-chain alkanes from methane (C₁) to hexane (C₆). Pentane and diethyl ether are both volatile liquids that cannot donate hydrogen bonds to themselves. Butanone has a carbonyl group but no O–H bond. 1-Butanol has an O–H group. The student notes that a boiling point reflects the energy needed to overcome intermolecular attractions in the liquid, such as London dispersion forces, dipole–dipole interactions, and hydrogen bonding. London dispersion forces generally increase with the number of electrons and with the surface area available for contact between molecules. The student hypothesizes that the functional group matters more than molar mass when molar masses are similar. The boiling points in the table were measured at 1 atm. The student expects that, among compounds of similar size and shape, the strongest net intermolecular attractions will produce the highest boiling point, and she will test this idea against both datasets.

qs.q: Which intermolecular force best explains why 1-butanol has the highest boiling point in Table 1?
o: Stronger London dispersion forces because 1-butanol has a larger molar mass than pentane
Not quite. Pentane (72 g/mol) and 1-butanol (74 g/mol) are almost the same mass, so dispersion forces can't explain an 81 °C gap.
Hydrogen bonding between O–H groups of neighboring molecules, in addition to dispersion forces
Correct: The O–H group lets 1-butanol molecules hydrogen bond to each other, much stronger than the forces in the others.
Covalent bonding between neighboring 1-butanol molecules
Not quite. Covalent bonds are inside a molecule. The attractions between separate molecules are not covalent.
Ion–dipole interactions between 1-butanol molecules
Not quite. Ion–dipole forces need an ion, and pure 1-butanol has none.
qs.x: Correct: A boiling point tells you how hard it is to pull molecules apart from each other in the liquid. Table 1 shows 1-butanol boils at 117 °C, far above the others (pentane 36 °C, diethyl ether 35 °C and butanone 80 °C in the table), even though all four have nearly the same molar mass. The passage says 1-butanol has an O–H group. An O–H group can form a hydrogen bond, which is a strong attraction between the H on one molecule's O–H and the lone pair on the oxygen of a neighbor. Each 1-butanol molecule can both give and receive these, so the molecules cling to each other much more tightly, and it takes extra heat to separate them. Why the others are wrong: dispersion forces depend on electron count and surface area, and 1-butanol (74 g/mol) is only 2 g/mol heavier than pentane (72 g/mol), which cannot explain an 81 °C gap (117 − 36 = 81); covalent bonds hold atoms inside one molecule and aren't what holds separate molecules together in the liquid; ion–dipole forces need an ion, and pure 1-butanol has none. Trap: Blaming a big boiling point gap on molar mass when the masses are almost identical.

qs.q: Diethyl ether has a polar C–O–C bond, yet its boiling point is almost the same as that of pentane. What is the best explanation?
o: Diethyl ether is nonpolar, so its only intermolecular force is dispersion, unlike pentane.
Not quite. Diethyl ether is polar. Its dipole is just small, not zero.
Pentane forms hydrogen bonds that offset its lack of a dipole.
Not quite. Pentane has no oxygen or other electronegative atom, so it can't form hydrogen bonds.
Diethyl ether has only a weak net dipole and cannot hydrogen bond to itself, so dispersion forces dominate in both liquids.
Correct: Ether has only a weak dipole and no O–H, so dispersion forces dominate in both, and both boil near 35 °C.
Diethyl ether forms hydrogen bonds with itself, but these are canceled by its larger molar mass.
Not quite. Ether has no H on its oxygen, so it can't form hydrogen bonds with itself.
qs.x: Correct: Diethyl ether has an oxygen between two carbons (the C–O–C unit), and the bend in this arrangement gives the molecule a small dipole, meaning one end is a little negative and the other a little positive. But the passage says it cannot donate hydrogen bonds to itself, because its oxygen has no H attached. So its dipole–dipole attraction is weak. Pentane has no polar bonds at all, so only dispersion forces hold it together. Their sizes are nearly the same (74 versus 72 g/mol), so their dispersion forces are alike, and the small extra dipole in ether barely matters. Table 1 shows 35 °C for ether and 36 °C for pentane, nearly equal. Why the others are wrong: diethyl ether isn't nonpolar, it has a modest dipole that is just small; pentane has no electronegative atom, so it can't hydrogen bond; ether has no H on oxygen, so it cannot form hydrogen bonds with itself at all. Trap: Assuming any molecule that contains oxygen can hydrogen bond with itself.

qs.q: Based on the trend in Figure 1, which value is the most reasonable estimate of the boiling point of heptane (C₇)?
o: About 70 °C
Not quite. About 70 °C is nearly the same as hexane at 69 °C, but each added carbon has raised the boiling point by 33 °C or more.
About 130 °C
Not quite. About 130 °C needs a jump of about 61 °C, larger than the recent jumps, which are shrinking.
About 40 °C
Not quite. About 40 °C is below hexane (69 °C). Boiling points rise with chain length.
About 100 °C
Correct: The jumps are shrinking (73, 47, 41, 37, 33 °C), so the next is about 30 °C: 69 + 30 ≈ 100 °C.
qs.x: Correct: Figure 1 shows the boiling point rising each time a carbon is added, because a longer chain has more electrons and more surface, so stronger dispersion forces. But the jumps get smaller. Work out the jump for each step using the figure's values: methane to ethane, −89 − (−162) = 73 °C; ethane to propane, −42 − (−89) = 47 °C; propane to butane, −1 − (−42) = 41 °C; butane to pentane, 36 − (−1) = 37 °C; pentane to hexane, 69 − 36 = 33 °C. The jumps keep shrinking by a few degrees, so the next one (hexane to heptane) should be about 30 °C. Add it to hexane's value: 69 + 30 = 99, so about 100 °C. Why the others are wrong: 70 °C would mean heptane boils almost the same as hexane at 69 °C, but each added carbon has raised the boiling point; 130 °C needs a jump of 61 °C, bigger than the last several jumps; 40 °C is below hexane, the wrong direction. Trap: Extending the trend as if each jump were constant or growing, instead of shrinking.

qs.q: Butanone boils about 44 °C higher than pentane despite the same molar mass. What is the best explanation?
o: Butanone has a permanent dipole from its polar C=O bond, adding dipole–dipole attractions to dispersion forces.
Correct: The polar C=O gives butanone a real dipole, so dipole–dipole attractions add to dispersion forces.
Butanone forms hydrogen bonds between carbonyl oxygens and C–H bonds as strongly as an alcohol does.
Not quite. Butanone has no H on oxygen, so it can't hydrogen bond to itself the way an alcohol does.
Butanone has a much larger surface area than pentane.
Not quite. The two molecules are similar chains of similar shape, so surface area isn't what differs.
Butanone has more electrons than pentane, so its dispersion forces are far stronger.
Not quite. Butanone has about the same number of electrons as pentane (40 versus 42), so dispersion is not much stronger.
qs.x: Correct: Butanone and pentane have almost the same size and shape (both 72 g/mol), so their dispersion forces are close. What differs is the carbonyl group (C=O) in butanone. Oxygen pulls electrons toward itself harder than carbon does, so the C=O bond is polar, and the whole molecule gets a clear dipole (one end partly negative, one end partly positive). Butanone molecules line up so the positive end of one meets the negative end of the next. This dipole–dipole attraction is extra on top of dispersion, and it raises the boiling point to 80 °C versus pentane's 36 °C (80 − 36 = 44 °C higher). Why the others are wrong: a hydrogen bond needs an H bonded to O, N or F, and butanone has no O–H, so it can't match an alcohol like 1-butanol at 117 °C; the shapes and surface areas are similar, so surface area doesn't explain the gap; butanone actually has slightly fewer electrons (40) than pentane (42), so dispersion is not stronger. Trap: Treating any compound with oxygen as a hydrogen-bond donor.

graph.title: Figure 1. Boiling point of straight-chain alkanes

passages.title: FL01 · Chem/Phys · Passage 8
text: A student analyzes an over-the-counter tablet mixture containing ibuprofen, aspirin, caffeine, and acetaminophen. Thin-layer chromatography (TLC) is run on silica gel plates with an ethyl acetate/hexane mobile phase. In 50% ethyl acetate, the solvent front traveled 8.0 cm, and the spot distances are in Table 1. Figure 1 shows the retention factor (Rf) of each compound as the percentage of ethyl acetate in the mobile phase changes. Silica gel is a polar stationary phase. In a separate experiment, the student extracts an aqueous caffeine solution with dichloromethane (DCM). The partition coefficient K for caffeine is 4.0, defined as the concentration in DCM divided by the concentration in water. To separate ibuprofen (a carboxylic acid with pKₐ ≈ 4.4) from caffeine, the student dissolves the mixture in diethyl ether and shakes it with aqueous sodium bicarbonate (pH ≈ 8.3), then separates the layers. The two layers are immiscible, and the student assumes that the extraction reaches equilibrium each time the layers are shaken together. Spots are visualized under ultraviolet light, since all four compounds absorb UV.

qs.q: In a repeat run with 50% ethyl acetate, the solvent front travels 10.0 cm. How far will the aspirin spot travel?
o: 4.0 cm
Not quite. This is the spot distance from the first run, when the solvent front only went 8.0 cm.
6.3 cm
Not quite. This is 10.0 ÷ 1.6, which isn't a step in the Rf calculation.
8.0 cm
Not quite. This is the solvent front from the first run, not a spot distance.
5.0 cm
Correct: Rf stays 0.50 for this system, so the spot travels 0.50 × 10.0 cm = 5.0 cm.
qs.x: Correct: Rf (retention factor) is the distance the spot traveled divided by the distance the solvent front traveled, Rf = spot distance ÷ solvent front distance. It describes how a compound behaves in a given plate and solvent system, so it stays the same when the plate is longer or shorter, as long as the solvent mix is the same. From Table 1, aspirin has Rf = 0.50 in 50% ethyl acetate (check: 4.0 cm ÷ 8.0 cm = 0.50). In the repeat run the solvent front is 10.0 cm. Rearrange: spot distance = Rf × solvent front. Plug in: 0.50 × 10.0 cm = 5.0 cm. Why the others are wrong: 4.0 cm is the aspirin distance in the first run, when the front went only 8.0 cm; 6.3 cm is 10.0 ÷ 1.6, which has no meaning here; 8.0 cm is the solvent front from the first run, not a spot distance. Trap: Assuming the spot distance stays the same when the solvent front distance changes. It is the ratio that stays fixed.

qs.q: Why does acetaminophen have the lowest Rf in Table 1?
o: It is the least polar, so it dissolves poorly in the mobile phase.
Not quite. A less polar compound sticks to silica less and travels farther, like ibuprofen. Acetaminophen is the most polar, not the least.
It has the lowest molar mass and so diffuses the slowest.
Not quite. Rf depends on how strongly a compound sticks to each phase, not on molar mass or diffusion speed.
It forms covalent bonds with the silica gel.
Not quite. Sticking to silica comes from reversible attractions like hydrogen bonds, not covalent bonds.
It is the most polar of the four compounds, so it adsorbs most strongly to the polar silica and is carried least by the mobile phase.
Correct: It is the most polar, so it hydrogen bonds to the polar silica the most and the solvent carries it the least.
qs.x: Correct: In TLC, a compound moves up the plate carried by the mobile phase (the solvent), but it can also stick to the stationary phase (the silica on the plate). Silica gel is polar, as the passage says, and it holds on to polar compounds by hydrogen bonding. The more a compound sticks to the silica, the less the solvent carries it, so it travels a shorter distance and has a lower Rf. Acetaminophen has an OH group on a benzene ring and an amide group, both good at hydrogen bonding, so it is the most polar of the four and sticks hardest. Table 1 shows it has the smallest Rf, 0.20 (1.6 cm out of 8.0 cm). Why the others are wrong: the least polar compound would be the one that moves farthest, like ibuprofen at 0.80, so this has it backward; molar mass and diffusion speed are not what sets Rf, which depends on how strongly the compound is attracted to each phase; sticking to silica is reversible, since covalent bonding would trap the compound and chromatography couldn't separate anything. Trap: Thinking polar compounds travel farthest on a polar stationary phase.

qs.q: Which mobile phase composition in Figure 1 gives the greatest difference in Rf between aspirin and acetaminophen?
o: 50% ethyl acetate
Correct: The gaps are 0.20 at 20%, 0.30 at 50% and 0.25 at 80%, so 50% separates the two best.
20% ethyl acetate
Not quite. At 20% the gap is 0.25 − 0.05 = 0.20, the smallest of the three.
80% ethyl acetate
Not quite. At 80% the gap is 0.70 − 0.45 = 0.25, smaller than the 0.30 gap at 50%.
The difference is identical at all three compositions.
Not quite. The gaps are 0.20, 0.30 and 0.25. They are not the same.
qs.x: Correct: We want the mobile phase where the two spots are farthest apart, meaning the biggest difference in Rf. Read Figure 1 for aspirin and acetaminophen at each composition and subtract. At 20% ethyl acetate: aspirin 0.25 and acetaminophen 0.05, so 0.25 − 0.05 = 0.20. At 50%: aspirin 0.50 and acetaminophen 0.20, so 0.50 − 0.20 = 0.30. At 80%: aspirin 0.70 and acetaminophen 0.45, so 0.70 − 0.45 = 0.25. The biggest gap is 0.30 at 50% ethyl acetate. Why the others are wrong: 20% gives a gap of only 0.20, because both spots barely move in such a weak solvent; 80% gives 0.25, smaller than at 50%, since the strong solvent pushes both spots up the plate together; the gaps are 0.20, 0.30 and 0.25, so they are not identical. Trap: Choosing the composition where the spots travel farthest, instead of where they are farthest apart from each other.

qs.q: After the ether solution is shaken with aqueous NaHCO₃, which species is found mainly in the aqueous layer?
o: Ibuprofen as its carboxylate anion
Correct: At pH 8.3, well above its pKₐ of 4.4, ibuprofen loses H⁺ and becomes a water-soluble carboxylate ion.
Caffeine as its protonated cation
Not quite. Caffeine is only a very weak base, so at pH 8.3 it stays neutral and stays in the ether.
Ibuprofen in its neutral acid form
Not quite. Neutral ibuprofen prefers ether, but at this pH it has been turned into its ionic form.
Both ibuprofen and caffeine in their neutral forms
Not quite. Only the ionized compound moves into water, so the two end up in different layers.
qs.x: Correct: Water and ether don't mix, so whatever dissolves better in water goes to the bottom aqueous layer, and charged species like water. Ibuprofen is a carboxylic acid (RCOOH) with pKₐ ≈ 4.4. The pKₐ is the pH where half of the acid has lost its proton. The bicarbonate solution has pH ≈ 8.3, which is far above 4.4, so the ibuprofen loses its H⁺ and becomes a carboxylate anion (RCOO⁻). That anion is an ion, so it is attracted to water and moves into the aqueous layer. Caffeine isn't acidic and stays neutral at this pH, so it stays in the ether. That is how the two get separated. Why the others are wrong: caffeine is only a very weak base, and at pH 8.3 it isn't protonated, so it stays in the ether; neutral ibuprofen would prefer the ether, but the base has already turned it into the ion; if both stayed neutral, nothing would be separated, but only the ionized one moves into water. Trap: Forgetting that removing a proton from an acid makes it an ion, and ions dissolve in water.

qs.q: A 100 mL aqueous caffeine solution is shaken once with 50 mL of DCM. What fraction of the caffeine is extracted into the DCM?
o: Not quite. 80% is K ÷ (K + 1), which only works when the two volumes are equal. Here they are 50 mL and 100 mL.
Not quite. 50% would mean equal moles in each layer. With K = 4.0 and these volumes, more caffeine goes into the DCM.
Not quite. 33% is the fraction left in the water. The question asks for the fraction extracted.
Correct: K = (n<sub>DCM</sub> ÷ 50) ÷ (n<sub>aq</sub> ÷ 100) = 4.0 gives n<sub>DCM</sub> ÷ n<sub>aq</sub> = 2.0, so the fraction extracted is 2 ÷ 3 = 67%.
qs.x: Correct: The partition coefficient is K = [caffeine in DCM] ÷ [caffeine in water] = 4.0, where the brackets mean concentration (moles per volume). Let n<sub>DCM</sub> be the moles of caffeine in the DCM and n<sub>aq</sub> the moles left in the water. The volumes are 50 mL of DCM and 100 mL of water. Concentration is moles divided by volume, so K = (n<sub>DCM</sub> ÷ 50) ÷ (n<sub>aq</sub> ÷ 100) = 4.0. Rearrange: n<sub>DCM</sub> ÷ n<sub>aq</sub> = 4.0 × (50 ÷ 100) = 4.0 × 0.5 = 2.0. So there are 2 parts in the DCM for every 1 part in the water, and 2 + 1 = 3 parts in total. The fraction extracted is 2 ÷ 3 = 0.67, or 67%. Why the others are wrong: 80% is K ÷ (K + 1) = 4 ÷ 5, which only works if both volumes are equal; 50% would need n<sub>DCM</sub> ÷ n<sub>aq</sub> = 1, but K = 4.0 favors DCM more than that; 33% is 1 ÷ 3, the fraction left in the water, not the fraction extracted. Trap: Ignoring that the volumes differ and using K ÷ (K + 1), or reporting the fraction left behind.

passages.title: FL01 · Chem/Phys · Passage 9
text: A student examines how the structure of an alkyl bromide affects its rate of nucleophilic substitution. In one set of experiments, each alkyl bromide reacts with sodium iodide in acetone, a polar aprotic solvent, under conditions that favor a bimolecular mechanism (SN2). In a second set, the same alkyl bromides are allowed to react with a solvent of aqueous ethanol (solvolysis), under conditions that favor a unimolecular mechanism (SN1). Approximate relative rates, set to 1 for ethyl bromide in the SN2 series and for methyl bromide in the SN1 series, are shown in Table 1. In addition, the student treats optically pure (R)-2-bromobutane with sodium iodide in acetone and analyzes the product with a polarimeter. A second experiment compares the rate of the reaction of iodide with 1-bromobutane in acetone with the rate in water, a polar protic solvent. The student also plans to double the concentration of nucleophile in the solvolysis reaction of tert-butyl bromide. Throughout, the leaving group is bromide, and temperature is held constant. The student's goal is to connect each observation to the mechanism by which the reaction proceeds, and to the effects of substrate structure, solvent, and nucleophile on the rate.

qs.q: Why does tert-butyl bromide react so much faster than methyl bromide under SN1 conditions?
o: The tert-butyl carbon is less hindered, so the nucleophile attacks more easily.
Not quite. The tertiary carbon is the most crowded, which is why it is slowest in SN2.
Bromide is a better leaving group from tertiary carbons because it is more basic there.
Not quite. Bromide is the leaving group in every case in Table 1, so it can't explain the difference between them.
The rate-determining step forms a tertiary carbocation, which is stabilized by electron donation from three alkyl groups.
Correct: The slow step forms a carbocation, and three alkyl groups stabilize the positive charge best.
The tert-butyl group can donate a proton to the solvent, which accelerates the reaction.
Not quite. The mechanism is carbocation formation then capture, not proton donation to the solvent.
qs.x: Correct: SN1 is a two-step reaction. The slow step is the leaving group falling off by itself to leave a carbocation (a carbon with a positive charge). Then the nucleophile (the electron-rich attacker) grabs it in a fast step. Since the slow step makes the carbocation, the more stable the carbocation, the faster the whole reaction. Alkyl groups (carbon chains) push electron density toward the positive carbon, which spreads out the charge and steadies it. A tertiary carbon, like tert-butyl, has three alkyl groups, so it makes the most stable carbocation. Methyl has none, so its carbocation is very unstable. That matches Table 1: the SN1 rate goes from 1 for methyl to 1 × 10⁸ for tert-butyl. Why the others are wrong: the tert-butyl carbon is the most crowded, not the least, which is exactly why it is slowest in SN2; bromide is the leaving group every time, so it can't be better only on tertiary carbons, and a better leaving group is a weaker base anyway; the mechanism is carbocation formation and capture, with no proton donation by the alkyl group. Trap: Reasoning with steric hindrance, which controls SN2, instead of carbocation stability, which controls SN1.

qs.q: What is the major product of the reaction of (R)-2-bromobutane with NaI in acetone?
o: (R)-2-iodobutane
Not quite. Keeping R would need a front-side attack or two inversions. A single SN2 step inverts the center.
A racemic mixture of 2-iodobutane
Not quite. A racemic mixture comes from SN1 through a flat carbocation. This reaction is SN2.
(S)-2-iodobutane
Correct: SN2 attacks from the back side and inverts the stereocenter, so (R) becomes (S).
(S)-2-iodobutane and 1-iodobutane in equal amounts
Not quite. Iodide replaces the bromine on the same carbon. Nothing makes 1-iodobutane.
qs.x: Correct: Sodium iodide in acetone (a polar aprotic solvent) favors SN2, as the passage says. In SN2, the nucleophile (here I⁻) attacks the carbon from the side opposite the leaving group (the back side), in one smooth step. As iodide comes in on one side, bromide leaves from the other, and the three other groups flip over like an umbrella in the wind. This is called inversion of configuration: the 3D arrangement is mirrored. The starting material is (R). With the other priorities unchanged (iodine, like bromine, is still the highest priority group), the flipped arrangement is read as (S). So the product is (S)-2-iodobutane. Why the others are wrong: (R)-2-iodobutane would mean the 3D arrangement was kept, which needs a front-side attack or two inversions, not one SN2 step; a racemic mixture (equal R and S) is what you'd see from SN1 with a flat carbocation, which this is not; iodide replaces the bromine on the same carbon, so 1-iodobutane doesn't form. Trap: Predicting racemization for every substitution at a stereocenter, when SN2 gives inversion.

qs.q: How would the rate of the SN2 reaction of iodide with 1-bromobutane change when the solvent is changed from acetone to water?
o: It would increase, because water is more polar and stabilizes the transition state more.
Not quite. Polar solvents help SN1, but in SN2 water would tie up the nucleophile and slow the reaction.
It would increase, because water can donate protons to the nucleophile.
Not quite. Adding a proton to a nucleophile makes it less nucleophilic, not more.
It would decrease, because water hydrogen bonds to iodide and lowers its nucleophilicity.
Correct: Water hydrogen bonds to iodide and surrounds it, making it a weaker nucleophile, so the SN2 rate drops.
It would not change, because the substrate is the same.
Not quite. The solvent changes how reactive the nucleophile is, even when the substrate is the same.
qs.x: Correct: In SN2 the nucleophile has to get to the carbon, so how reactive the nucleophile is controls the rate. Acetone is a polar aprotic solvent, meaning it is polar but has no O–H or N–H bonds to hydrogen bond with. It leaves the iodide ion mostly bare and ready to attack. Water is a polar protic solvent: its O–H bonds form hydrogen bonds with the negative iodide ion and wrap it in a shell of water molecules. That shell holds the iodide in place and makes it harder for it to reach the carbon, so the nucleophile is less reactive and the SN2 rate drops. Why the others are wrong: more polar solvents help SN1 by stabilizing the ions that form, but in SN2 the loss of nucleophile reactivity wins out; water donating protons to iodide would make it HI, a worse nucleophile, not a better one; the substrate being the same doesn't matter, since the solvent changes how strong the nucleophile is. Trap: Assuming a more polar solvent always speeds up substitution.

qs.q: If the concentration of nucleophile is doubled in the solvolysis of tert-butyl bromide under SN1 conditions, how will the rate change?
o: It will double because the rate depends on both substrate and nucleophile.
Not quite. That's the SN2 answer, where the rate is first order in both reactants. This is SN1.
It will not change appreciably, since the rate-determining step does not involve the nucleophile.
Correct: The slow step is ionization of the C–Br bond, which doesn't involve the nucleophile, so rate = k[RBr] and doesn't change.
It will quadruple because the rate is second order in nucleophile.
Not quite. Neither mechanism is second order in nucleophile, so the rate wouldn't quadruple.
It will decrease because the added nucleophile competes with the solvent.
Not quite. Extra nucleophile doesn't slow the ionization step, which sets the rate.
qs.x: Correct: The rate of a reaction depends only on what is in the slow step (the rate-determining step). For tert-butyl bromide under SN1 conditions, the slow step is the C–Br bond breaking to make a carbocation and bromide. The nucleophile isn't involved yet. It attacks afterward in a fast step. That makes the rate law rate = k[RBr], where k is the rate constant and [RBr] is the concentration of the alkyl bromide. The nucleophile concentration isn't in it. So doubling the nucleophile doesn't change the rate. Compare SN2, where the nucleophile attacks in the one and only step, and so rate = k[RBr][Nu] and doubling the nucleophile would double the rate. Why the others are wrong: doubling the rate is the SN2 answer, first order in each reactant; quadrupling would need second order in nucleophile, which neither mechanism has; added nucleophile doesn't slow the ionization step, so the rate won't decrease. Trap: Applying the SN2 rate law, with nucleophile in it, to an SN1 reaction.

passages.title: FL01 · Chem/Phys · Passage 10
text: A chemist studies the unimolecular isomerization of a compound in solution. The reaction is first order, and its rate constant k was measured at four temperatures, giving the data in Table 1. Figure 1 plots ln k against 1/T, where T is in kelvin, and the points fall on a straight line. The Arrhenius equation, k = A exp(−Ea/RT), describes the data, and R = 8.314 J/(mol·K). The overall reaction has ΔH° = −40 kJ/mol and ΔS° = −100 J/(mol·K), and both values are assumed to be independent of temperature over the range studied. In a second experiment, the chemist adds a catalyst that provides an alternative pathway for the same reaction, and she observes that the rate constant at 300 K increases substantially. The chemist reasons that the catalyst changes the kinetics of the reaction but not its thermodynamics. She also notes that the rate constant of a first-order reaction has units of inverse time, and that the half-life of such a reaction does not depend on the starting concentration. The same sample volume and solvent were used for all runs, and the temperature of each run was held constant by a thermostatted bath.

qs.q: The slope of the line in Figure 1 is approximately −7.2 × 10³ K. What is the activation energy of the reaction?
o: 7.2 kJ/mol
Not quite. This only converts the slope's number and never multiplies by R. The slope is −Ea/R, so Ea needs R.
0.87 kJ/mol
Not quite. This divides the slope by R. Since slope = −Ea/R, you multiply by R to get Ea.
120 kJ/mol
Not quite. This is double the correct value, from a factor of 2 that isn't in the Arrhenius relation.
60 kJ/mol
Correct: Slope = −Ea/R, so Ea = (7.2 × 10³ K)(8.314 J/mol·K) = 6.0 × 10⁴ J/mol = 60 kJ/mol.
qs.x: Correct: The Arrhenius equation is k = A exp(−Ea/RT). Take the natural log of both sides and you get ln k = ln A − (Ea/R)(1/T). That has the form y = b + mx, with ln k as y and 1/T as x. So a plot of ln k against 1/T, as in Figure 1, is a straight line whose slope is −Ea/R. Here Ea is the activation energy (the energy hill the molecules must climb to react) and R is the gas constant. The question gives the slope as −7.2 × 10³ K, and the passage gives R = 8.314 J/(mol·K). Rearrange: Ea = −slope × R = (7.2 × 10³ K)(8.314 J/(mol·K)). Multiply: 7.2 × 8.314 = 59.86, so Ea ≈ 59.9 × 10³ J/mol = 6.0 × 10⁴ J/mol. Then 1 kJ = 1000 J, so divide by 1000: 6.0 × 10⁴ ÷ 10³ = 60 kJ/mol. Why the others are wrong: 7.2 kJ/mol only changes units on the slope and never multiplies by R; 0.87 kJ/mol comes from dividing 7.2 × 10³ by R (7200 ÷ 8.314 = 866 J) instead of multiplying; 120 kJ/mol is twice the right answer, with an extra factor of 2 that isn't in the equation. Trap: Dividing the slope by R instead of multiplying, or forgetting that the slope is −Ea/R.

qs.q: What is the half-life of the compound at 320 K?
o: Not quite. This is 1 ÷ k with the ln 2 left out. Half-life needs 0.693 in the top.
Not quite. This multiplies 0.693 by k. The formula divides ln 2 by k.
Not quite. This is double the right value, an extra factor of 2 the formula doesn't have.
qs.x: Correct: For a first-order reaction the half-life (the time for half of the compound to react) is t½ = ln 2 ÷ k, where k is the rate constant. The nice thing is that it does not depend on how much compound you start with, as the passage points out. Using ln 2 = 0.693, and from Table 1, k at 320 K is 4.50 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Plug in: t½ = 0.693 ÷ (4.50 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹). Dividing by 10⁻³ is the same as multiplying by 10³ (subtract the exponent −3, so −(−3) = +3): 0.693 ÷ 4.50 = 0.154, and 0.154 × 10³ = 154 s. Why the others are wrong: 222 s is 1 ÷ k = 1 ÷ 0.0045, which leaves out ln 2; 3.1 × 10⁻³ s is 0.693 × k, multiplying where the formula divides; 308 s is twice the right half-life. Trap: Using 1 ÷ k as the half-life and leaving out the ln 2.

qs.q: How does the catalyst affect the reaction?
o: It lowers ΔG° of the reaction, making the products more stable.
Not quite. A catalyst doesn't change the energies of reactants or products, so ΔG° stays the same.
It lowers the activation energy and leaves ΔG° and the equilibrium constant unchanged.
Correct: A catalyst lowers Ea and speeds the forward and reverse reactions equally, so ΔG° and K are unchanged.
It increases the equilibrium constant by increasing the forward rate only.
Not quite. A catalyst speeds the reverse reaction equally, so K doesn't change.
It raises the energy of the reactants so they are closer to the transition state.
Not quite. A catalyst lowers the transition state's energy. It doesn't raise the reactants' energy.
qs.x: Correct: A catalyst is a helper that offers the reaction a different route with a lower activation energy Ea (a smaller hill to climb). A lower hill makes the reaction faster. But it does not change where the reactants and products sit on the energy diagram, only the hill in between. So ΔG° (the overall free energy change, which says how favorable the reaction is), ΔH°, and the equilibrium constant K all stay the same. The lower hill helps the forward and reverse reactions equally, so the system reaches the same equilibrium sooner. This matches the chemist's reasoning in the passage that the catalyst changes kinetics but not thermodynamics. Why the others are wrong: lowering ΔG° and making products more stable would change the energies of reactants and products, which a catalyst doesn't touch; raising K by speeding up only the forward reaction is impossible since the reverse speeds up too; raising the reactants' energy isn't how it works, the catalyst lowers the transition state's energy instead. Trap: Believing a catalyst makes a reaction more spontaneous by changing ΔG°.

qs.q: What is ΔG° for the reaction at 300 K?
o: −10 kJ/mol
−70 kJ/mol
Not quite. This comes from a sign slip: −40 − 30. Subtracting a negative term (−30) is adding.
+10 kJ/mol
Not quite. This has the wrong sign. ΔG° is negative here, so the reaction is spontaneous.
−30 kJ/mol
Not quite. This uses only the 30 kJ/mol from TΔS° and drops ΔH°, or mixes up the temperature.
qs.x: Correct: Gibbs free energy change tells you whether a reaction is favorable at a given temperature. The formula is ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°, where ΔH° is the enthalpy change, T is the temperature in kelvin and ΔS° is the entropy change. From the passage, ΔH° = −40 kJ/mol, ΔS° = −100 J/(mol·K), and the question gives T = 300 K. The units don't match yet, so convert ΔS° to kJ: 1 kJ = 1000 J, so divide by 1000: −100 J/(mol·K) ÷ 1000 = −0.100 kJ/(mol·K). Plug in: ΔG° = −40 − (300)(−0.100). First 300 × (−0.100) = −30. Then subtracting a negative is adding, so −40 − (−30) = −40 + 30 = −10 kJ/mol. Negative means the reaction is spontaneous at 300 K. Why the others are wrong: −70 kJ/mol comes from a sign slip, −40 − 30 instead of −40 + 30; +10 kJ/mol flips the sign of the whole answer; −30 kJ/mol uses only the TΔS° term, or skips the −40. Trap: Mishandling the negative sign of ΔS° or forgetting to convert J to kJ.

passages.title: FL01 · Psych/Soc · Passage 1
text: Researchers examined the effect of acute sleep restriction on working memory. 60 healthy adults aged 19 to 30 were randomly assigned to one of two groups. The control group slept 8 hours in the laboratory, and the restricted group was allowed only 4 hours. The next morning, each participant completed a computerized 2-back task, in which letters appear one at a time and the participant indicates whether the current letter matches the one shown two items earlier. Accuracy and mean reaction time on correct trials were recorded. The experimenters who scored the task did not know each participant's group, but participants knew how long they had been allowed to sleep. Group means were compared with independent-samples t-tests, using a significance threshold of p < 0.05. Results are shown in Table 1. In a separate sample of sleep-restricted adults, functional imaging showed reduced activation of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex during the same task, relative to well-rested adults. The investigators concluded that a single night of short sleep impairs the ability to hold and update information over a few seconds.

qs.q: Random assignment of participants to the two sleep conditions primarily served to:
o: ensure that every participant would respond identically to the 2-back task regardless of sleep condition.
Not quite. People differ in how sensitive they are to sleep loss, and randomizing doesn't remove those differences.
make the results generalize to all adults regardless of age, sex, or baseline sleep habits.
Not quite. Generalizing depends on how people were sampled into the study, not on how they were assigned to groups.
eliminate the need for a statistical test of the group difference in 2-back accuracy.
Not quite. Chance can still leave small group differences, so a statistical test of the accuracy gap is still needed.
distribute pre-existing differences, such as baseline memory ability, roughly equally across groups.
Correct: Chance assignment spreads baseline differences, like memory ability, about evenly across the two groups.
qs.x: Correct: Random assignment means chance, not the researchers, decides who lands in the sleep-restricted group and who lands in the control group. That matters because people already differ before the study starts. Some have sharper working memory, some are naturally better rested, some just like letter games. With 60 people split by chance, those differences tend to spread out about evenly across both groups, so the groups start out comparable on average. Then a gap in 2-back accuracy afterward (Table 1) is more likely to come from the sleep manipulation. Why the others are wrong: people still differ in how much sleep loss hurts them, and randomization doesn't erase that; generalizing to all adults depends on how the 60 people were picked (sampling), not how they were split into groups; you still need the t-test because chance can leave small leftover differences between groups. Trap: Mixing up random assignment (who goes in which group, which supports cause and effect) with random sampling (who gets into the study, which supports generalizing).

qs.q: Relative to the control group mean, the percent decrease in accuracy in the restricted group was closest to:
o: Not quite. 8 is the gap in percentage points. A relative percent change divides that gap by the control mean.
Not quite. This divides 8 by the restricted mean, 76. The baseline should be the control mean, 84.
Correct: (84 − 76) ÷ 84 = 8 ÷ 84 ≈ 0.095, which is about 9.5% lower than control.
Not quite. This doesn't come from dividing 8 by either group mean. 8 ÷ 84 is about 0.095.
qs.x: Correct: Percent change = (change ÷ starting value) × 100. The starting value is the control mean, since the question says relative to the control group. From Table 1, control accuracy = 84% and restricted accuracy = 76%. The change is 84 − 76 = 8 percentage points. Plug in: 8 ÷ 84. Simplify by dividing top and bottom by 4: 8 ÷ 84 = 2 ÷ 21. Now 2 ÷ 21 is about 0.095 (21 × 0.095 = 1.995, which is almost 2). Multiply by 100 to turn it into a percent: 0.095 × 100 = 9.5%. Why the others are wrong: 8% is just the raw gap in percentage points, and it never gets divided by the baseline; 10.5% divides by the wrong number (8 ÷ 76 = 0.105), using the restricted mean as the baseline; 12.0% doesn't come from dividing 8 by either mean. Trap: Dividing by the wrong baseline, or calling a percentage-point gap a percent change.

qs.q: The imaging finding in the sleep-restricted adults is most consistent with the idea that the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex:
o: encodes new declarative memories into long-term storage after a delay.
Not quite. Storing new long-term declarative memories relies mainly on the hippocampus and temporal lobe, not the DLPFC.
controls the release of cortisol and other hormones during stress.
Not quite. Cortisol release is controlled by the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, which has nothing to do with the 2-back task.
supports the maintenance and manipulation of information in working memory.
Correct: The DLPFC supports holding and updating information in working memory, which is what the 2-back task demands.
coordinates the timing and sequencing of voluntary movements of the limbs.
Not quite. Timing of voluntary limb movement involves the cerebellum and basal ganglia, not the DLPFC.
qs.x: Correct: The passage says imaging showed less activity in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC, a part of the front of the brain) while sleep-restricted adults did the 2-back task. That task makes you hold letters in mind and keep updating them, which is working memory. The DLPFC is a core region for exactly that kind of holding and juggling of information over a few seconds. So less activity there fits worse 2-back accuracy in Table 1, and it fits the investigators' conclusion in the last sentence of the paragraph. Why the others are wrong: storing new long-term declarative memories mostly depends on the hippocampus and nearby temporal lobe; releasing cortisol is run by the hypothalamus, pituitary and adrenal glands (the stress axis); timing and sequencing of limb movements involve the cerebellum and basal ganglia. Trap: Blaming the hippocampus for every memory problem, even when the task is short-term holding and updating rather than storing long-term memories.

qs.q: Which feature of the design most weakens the conclusion that sleep loss alone caused the group difference in accuracy?
o: The scorers of the task did not know the group assignments of the participants.
Not quite. Scorers who don't know the groups reduces experimenter bias. That's a strength, not a weakness.
Both groups completed the same 2-back task in the morning under identical conditions of testing.
Not quite. Same task, same time of day, same setting keeps testing conditions equal. That's a strength.
Participants knew their sleep condition, so expectations or effort could have differed between groups.
Correct: Because participants knew their condition, expectations or effort could differ between groups, muddying the sleep effect.
Participants were randomly assigned to the sleep-deprived or the rested group before any testing began.
Not quite. Random assignment balances pre-existing differences and strengthens the causal claim.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks what weakens the claim that sleep loss alone caused the gap. The passage says participants knew how long they had been allowed to sleep. Someone told they got only 4 hours might expect to do badly, or just try less hard. That would lower their score for reasons other than sleep loss itself (these are called demand characteristics, meaning people act the way they think the study expects). You can't really hide sleep time from people, so this threat stays. Why the others are wrong: the scorers not knowing the groups (blind scoring) cuts down experimenter bias, so it's a strength; giving both groups the same task in the morning keeps testing conditions equal, also a strength; random assignment helps balance pre-existing differences, again a strength. Trap: Picking a design feature just because it sounds technical, when the question wants a weakness.

qs.q: The reaction-time results in Table 1 indicate that the restricted group:
o: responded faster but less accurately, showing a speed-accuracy trade-off in the sleep-deprived group.
Not quite. Faster responding would mean a lower mean RT, but the restricted group's mean RT is higher (668 vs 612 ms).
was slower and less accurate, so the deficit is not a speed-accuracy trade-off.
Correct: RT rose from 612 to 668 ms (p = 0.01) while accuracy fell, so the group was worse on both measures.
showed no reliable difference from controls in either measure because the SDs are large.
Not quite. Both p-values (0.01 and < 0.001) are below 0.05, so the differences are significant despite the SDs.
was more accurate on trials with longer reaction times, as expected for a speed-accuracy trade-off.
Not quite. Table 1 gives only group means. It says nothing about accuracy on slower versus faster trials.
qs.x: Correct: Table 1 shows reaction time (RT) went up from 612 ms in the control group to 668 ms in the restricted group, with p = 0.01. Since 0.01 is below the 0.05 cutoff given in the passage, that slowing is statistically significant. Accuracy also dropped from 84% to 76% (p < 0.001). So the restricted group was slower and less accurate. A speed-accuracy trade-off would mean going faster and making more mistakes, or going slower and making fewer, and that isn't what happened. Why the others are wrong: responding faster is wrong because the restricted RT is higher, not lower; saying there was no reliable difference in either measure is wrong since both p-values are under 0.05, even if the standard deviations (SDs) look big; Table 1 only gives group averages, so it can't tell you whether accuracy rose on slow trials. Trap: Thinking that overlapping SDs automatically mean a result isn't significant. The p-value is what tells you that.
