passages.title: FL01 · Psych/Soc · Passage 2
text: Dark adaptation was measured in two groups of observers. Each observer first viewed an intense light for 5 minutes. The room was then darkened, and at set intervals the dimmest flash that the observer could detect was determined. The flash was a small dim 500-nm spot presented 10 degrees away from the point of fixation. Threshold is expressed in log units, where a lower value indicates greater sensitivity. Group N contained 10 observers with normal vision, and Group V contained 10 observers with a dietary deficiency of vitamin A. Mean thresholds are plotted in Figure 1. Normal observers reported that the flash appeared colorless at the later time points, although it appeared faintly colored at early time points. Observers in Group V had normal visual acuity under daylight conditions and did not differ from Group N in the size of the initial threshold elevation immediately after the bright light. In Group V, a clinical examination showed no damage to the optic nerve or to the cornea. The researchers wished to link the shape of each curve to the photoreceptor populations of the retina and to the photopigment that each population uses.

qs.q: The second downward phase of Group N's curve, after about 10 minutes, most likely reflects:
o: regeneration of rhodopsin in rods, which are more sensitive than cones in dim light.
Correct: Once rod rhodopsin has regenerated, rods become more sensitive than cones, so thresholds keep falling after the break.
regeneration of cone photopigment, which is more sensitive than rhodopsin in dim light.
Not quite. Cones adapt quickly and explain the early phase. Cone pigment isn't more sensitive than rhodopsin in dim light.
dilation of the pupil to its maximum diameter.
Not quite. Pupil dilation happens within seconds and can't explain a drop that continues over 30 minutes.
recovery of horizontal cells in the fovea.
Not quite. The fovea has cones and no rods, so it can't explain the late rod-driven phase.
qs.x: Correct: Figure 1 shows Group N's threshold falling fast in the first few minutes, leveling off around 3.4 to 3.2 log units, then dropping again after about 10 minutes, to 1 by 30 minutes. Lower threshold means the eye can see dimmer flashes. The early drop is the cones, which adapt quickly. The late drop is the rods, which take longer because their pigment, rhodopsin, has to rebuild after the bright light bleached it. Once rhodopsin is back, rods are more sensitive than cones in dim light, so the threshold keeps falling. Why the others are wrong: cones account for the early plateau, and cone pigment isn't more sensitive than rhodopsin in dim light; pupil dilation takes seconds, so it can't explain a change over 30 minutes; the fovea has cones but no rods, so horizontal cells there can't explain a rod-driven phase. Trap: Swapping the roles. Fast early phase is cones, slow late phase is rods.

qs.q: Which explanation best accounts for the flat later portion of Group V's curve?
o: Without enough vitamin A, retinal cannot be supplied to regenerate rhodopsin in the rods.
Correct: Retinal comes from vitamin A and is needed to rebuild rhodopsin, so deficient rods stay insensitive (night blindness).
Vitamin A deficiency destroys the cones first, so the early phase of dark adaptation does not occur.
Not quite. Group V's early phase matches Group N's, so the cones are working.
Vitamin A is needed for transmission of visual signals across the optic chiasm to the cortex.
Not quite. The exam showed no optic nerve damage, and vitamin A isn't what carries signals across the optic chiasm.
The deficiency prevents the cornea and lens from refracting incoming light onto the retina.
Not quite. The cornea was normal, and poor refraction wouldn't cause a deficit specific to the rods.
qs.x: Correct: Group V's curve in Figure 1 matches Group N's for the first 10 minutes or so (the cone part), then stays flat near 3.2 to 3.5 instead of dropping again. That means the cones are working but the rods never catch up. Rods need rhodopsin, and rhodopsin is made from retinal, which the body gets from vitamin A. With a vitamin A deficiency, there isn't enough retinal to rebuild rhodopsin after the bright light, so rods stay stuck at low sensitivity. This is the classic cause of night blindness. Why the others are wrong: destroyed cones would wipe out the early phase, but Group V's early phase looks normal; the passage says no optic nerve damage was found, and vitamin A isn't a signal carrier across the optic chiasm; the cornea was normal, and bending light wouldn't cause a rod-specific problem anyway. Trap: Assuming any vision problem must be in the optic nerve or lens, when the clue (flat late phase) points to the photopigment.

qs.q: At 30 minutes, the threshold for Group V is higher than that for Group N by 2.2 log units. Group V therefore needed a flash that was approximately how many times more intense?
o: 2.2 times
Not quite. 2.2 is the difference in log units, not the ratio of intensities. The ratio is 10 raised to 2.2.
160 times
Correct: Ratio = 10²·² = 100 × 1.6 ≈ 160 times more intense.
16 times
Not quite. 16 is about 10¹·². The exponent here is 2.2, not 1.2.
1,000 times
Not quite. 1,000 is 10³, which would be a 3.0 log unit difference, not 2.2.
qs.x: Correct: A log unit is a power of 10, so a difference of 2.2 log units means a ratio of 10 raised to the power of 2.2. Read the values from Figure 1 at 30 minutes: Group V = 3.2 log units and Group N = 1 log unit. The difference is 3.2 − 1 = 2.2 log units, which matches the question. Split the exponent: 10²·² = 10² × 10⁰·². Multiplying powers of 10 means adding the exponents, so this split is fine. 10² = 100. 10⁰·² is about 1.6 (because 1.6⁵ is about 10, and 0.2 = 1/5). So 100 × 1.6 = 160. Group V needed a flash about 160 times as intense. Why the others are wrong: 2.2 times treats the log difference as if it were the ratio; 16 times comes from using 10¹·² and not 10²·²; 1,000 times is 10³, a 3.0 log unit difference. Trap: Treating a difference in log units as a difference in the original units, instead of a ratio of powers of 10.

qs.q: The test flash was presented 10 degrees from fixation and appeared colorless at the later time points. These observations are best explained by the fact that:
o: cones, concentrated outside the fovea, contain three pigments and signal only brightness at low light.
Not quite. Cones are concentrated in the fovea, and their three types are what allow color vision.
the fovea contains the highest density of rods, so peripheral light is not detected by the eye.
Not quite. The fovea has cones and no rods. That is the opposite of what this choice says.
rods, concentrated outside the fovea, contain a single photopigment and thus do not signal color.
Correct: Rods are concentrated outside the fovea and have one pigment, so the late flash they detected looked colorless.
color is encoded only after the signal reaches the optic nerve, not in the photoreceptors.
Not quite. Color coding starts in the retina, with different cone types, long before the optic nerve.
qs.x: Correct: The flash was shown 10 degrees away from the point of fixation, which puts it in the periphery of the retina. Rods are packed in the periphery, while the fovea (the center) is full of cones. The flash was detected in the late phase, which Figure 1 shows is rod territory (after about 10 minutes). Rods all contain one pigment, rhodopsin, so they can only report 'how much light', not which color. That's why the flash looked colorless later and faintly colored early on, when cones were still doing the work. Why the others are wrong: cones sit mostly in the fovea, not outside it, and the three cone types are what allow color; the fovea has no rods, so that choice reverses the facts; color coding starts in the retina with the different cone types and opponent processing, not at the optic nerve. Trap: Putting rods in the fovea. The fovea is all cones, and rods live in the periphery.

passages.title: FL01 · Psych/Soc · Passage 3
text: Stress responses were studied in 48 undergraduates using a 2 × 2 between-subjects design with 12 participants per cell. Participants were randomly assigned to perform either a stressful task (an unrehearsed, videotaped speech judged by a panel) or a non-stressful control task (reading aloud in an empty room). Within each task, participants waited beforehand either alone or with a supportive friend who was allowed to talk with them but who did not take part in the task. Saliva samples were collected 20 minutes after the task ended, and cortisol was measured. Participants also rated their anxiety on a 10-point scale. Mean cortisol is shown in Table 2. A two-way analysis of variance showed a significant main effect of task (p < 0.001), a significant main effect of support (p = 0.002), and a significant task by support interaction (p = 0.01). Anxiety ratings paralleled cortisol results. In a post-study questionnaire, participants in the speech task who waited with a friend reported being more confident that they could cope with the speech than did those who waited alone. Cortisol was sampled in the afternoon in all conditions.

qs.q: The hormone measured in this study is released as the final step of an axis in which:
o: the hypothalamus releases CRH, the anterior pituitary releases ACTH, and the adrenal cortex releases cortisol.
Correct: Hypothalamic CRH signals the anterior pituitary to release ACTH, and ACTH makes the adrenal cortex release cortisol.
the posterior pituitary releases ACTH, which then stimulates the adrenal medulla to release cortisol directly into the blood.
Not quite. ACTH comes from the anterior pituitary, and it acts on the adrenal cortex. The medulla makes epinephrine and norepinephrine.
the adrenal medulla releases cortisol directly in response to sympathetic input.
Not quite. The adrenal medulla releases epinephrine and norepinephrine, not cortisol.
the thyroid releases cortisol in response to TSH from the hypothalamus.
Not quite. TSH drives the thyroid, a different axis. The thyroid doesn't release cortisol.
qs.x: Correct: The passage says cortisol was measured in saliva, so the question is about the cortisol stress axis (the HPA axis). It runs in a chain. The hypothalamus releases CRH. CRH tells the anterior pituitary to release ACTH. ACTH travels in the blood to the adrenal cortex (the outer layer of the adrenal gland), which releases cortisol, a steroid hormone that helps the body handle stress. Why the others are wrong: ACTH comes from the anterior pituitary, not the posterior one, and it acts on the cortex rather than the medulla; the adrenal medulla (the inner core) makes epinephrine and norepinephrine, not cortisol, and it responds to sympathetic nerves; the thyroid is part of a different axis (TSH makes it release thyroid hormone) and it doesn't make cortisol. Trap: Mixing up the adrenal cortex (cortisol, hormonal axis) with the adrenal medulla (epinephrine, nerve-driven).

qs.q: The significant task by support interaction indicates that:
o: the speech task raised cortisol equally whether or not a friend was present.
Not quite. In the speech task, cortisol was 14.0 alone but 9.5 with a friend, so the effect of the friend was not the same.
the presence of a friend had no effect on cortisol in any condition tested.
Not quite. The main effect of support was significant (p = 0.002), so a friend did matter overall.
anxiety ratings caused the cortisol differences between the friend and no-friend groups.
Not quite. Anxiety ratings only paralleled cortisol. This design can't show that anxiety caused the cortisol difference.
the effect of a friend on cortisol depended on whether the task was stressful.
Correct: A friend cut cortisol by 4.5 nmol/L in the speech task but only 0.2 in reading, so the friend's effect depends on stress.
qs.x: Correct: An interaction means the effect of one factor changes depending on the level of the other factor. Here the factors are task (speech or reading) and support (alone or with friend). From Table 2, in the speech task a friend lowered cortisol from 14.0 to 9.5 nmol/L, a drop of 14.0 − 9.5 = 4.5 nmol/L. In the reading task a friend lowered it from 6.0 to 5.8, a drop of 6.0 − 5.8 = 0.2 nmol/L. A 4.5 drop versus a 0.2 drop is different, so the friend's effect depends on whether the task is stressful. That matches the significant interaction (p = 0.01). Why the others are wrong: the speech task raised cortisol more when alone (14.0) than with a friend (9.5), so it wasn't equal; a significant main effect of support (p = 0.002) means the friend did matter; the anxiety ratings only paralleled cortisol, and this design can't show that one caused the other. Trap: Mixing up a main effect (one factor's overall effect) with an interaction (one factor's effect changing across the other factor).

qs.q: The post-study confidence ratings are most consistent with which view of how support reduced the stress response?
o: The James-Lange theory: support directly changed bodily arousal, which was then labeled as calm by the participant.
Not quite. James-Lange starts with body arousal. Here the first thing that changed was confidence, a thought.
Cognitive appraisal: support raised participants' perceived ability to cope, lowering perceived threat.
Correct: A friend raised perceived ability to cope, so the speech looked less threatening and the stress response dropped.
Classical conditioning: the friend became a conditioned stimulus for cortisol release.
Not quite. Nothing paired a neutral stimulus with cortisol release, and the friend lowered cortisol.
Learned helplessness: friends taught participants that outcomes are uncontrollable.
Not quite. Learned helplessness would predict more stress, not less, because outcomes feel uncontrollable.
qs.x: Correct: The passage says speech-task participants who waited with a friend felt more confident they could cope. That is a change in how they sized up the situation, not a direct change in the body. Cognitive appraisal theory says stress depends on how you judge the demand against your resources for coping. A friend adds to your resources, so the same speech feels less threatening and the stress response (cortisol, Table 2) shrinks. Why the others are wrong: James-Lange says the body's arousal comes first and the emotion follows, but here the thing that changed first was confidence, a thought; classical conditioning would need a neutral stimulus paired with cortisol release, and nothing like that was set up (and the friend lowered cortisol); learned helplessness would predict more stress, because it comes from feeling outcomes can't be controlled. Trap: Picking a famous theory because the name is familiar, without checking what happened first in the data (confidence, then lower stress).

qs.q: In the speech condition, the reduction in mean cortisol associated with waiting with a friend, expressed as a percentage of the 'alone' mean, was closest to:
o: Not quite. 4.5 is the drop in nmol/L. To get a percent, divide it by the 'alone' mean.
Not quite. This divides 4.5 by 9.5, the 'friend' mean. The baseline should be the 'alone' mean, 14.0.
Not quite. 68% is what's left (9.5 ÷ 14.0), not the reduction.
qs.x: Correct: Percent reduction = (reduction ÷ 'alone' mean) × 100. The question says to use the 'alone' mean as the baseline. From Table 2, speech 'alone' = 14.0 nmol/L and speech 'with friend' = 9.5 nmol/L. The reduction is 14.0 − 9.5 = 4.5 nmol/L. Plug in: 4.5 ÷ 14.0. Multiply top and bottom by 10 to get rid of the decimal: 45 ÷ 140. Divide top and bottom by 5: 9 ÷ 28, which is about 0.32 (28 × 0.32 = 8.96). Multiply by 100: 0.32 × 100 = 32%. Why the others are wrong: 4.5% is the raw drop in nmol/L treated as if it were a percent; 47% comes from dividing by the 'friend' mean (4.5 ÷ 9.5 = 0.47), the wrong baseline; 68% is the fraction left over (9.5 ÷ 14.0 = 0.68), not the fraction lost. Trap: Dividing by the after-treatment mean, or reporting what remains instead of what was reduced.

passages.title: FL01 · Psych/Soc · Passage 4
text: Researchers studied observational learning in 90 children aged 4 to 6 (45 boys, 45 girls). Each child watched a short film of an adult model who played with an inflatable doll by hitting it. Children were randomly assigned, within sex, to one of three versions of the film's ending: the model was praised and given candy (rewarded), the model was scolded and spanked (punished), or nothing happened (no consequence). There were 15 children per sex per condition. Each child was then taken to a playroom containing the same doll and other toys and observed through a one-way mirror for 10 minutes. Observers who did not know which film the child had seen counted the number of imitative aggressive acts. The mean counts are given in Table 3 and Figure 2. In a second phase, every child was told that they would get a sticker for each action by the model that they could reproduce, and almost all children, regardless of condition, then reproduced many of the model's aggressive acts. A statistical analysis showed significant main effects of condition (p < 0.01) and sex (p < 0.05), and no interaction.

qs.q: The lower imitation in the 'punished' condition is best explained by:
o: negative reinforcement: the film removed an aversive stimulus from the children after the behavior.
Not quite. Negative reinforcement means your own behavior removes something unpleasant. That didn't happen here.
vicarious punishment: the model's observed consequences reduced the children's tendency to act.
Correct: Watching the model get punished made the children less likely to act. That's vicarious punishment.
classical conditioning of fear to the doll through direct pairing of the doll with spanking of the child.
Not quite. The children were never spanked. Only the model was, so there was no direct pairing for the child.
habituation to the film after repeated viewing, reducing the children's attention to the model.
Not quite. Each child saw the film once, so habituation to repeated viewing doesn't apply.
qs.x: Correct: In the punished version, the children watched the model get scolded and spanked. They weren't punished themselves. Social learning theory says watching a model's consequences changes how likely you are to copy the behavior. Seeing someone punished lowers that chance, and this is called vicarious punishment (vicarious means you feel it through someone else). Table 3 fits: boys copied 3.2 acts after punishment versus 6.8 with no consequence, and girls 1.7 versus 4.4. Why the others are wrong: negative reinforcement means your own behavior takes away something unpleasant, and that didn't happen; classical conditioning of fear through spanking would need the children to be spanked, but only the model was; habituation would need repeated viewings, and each child saw the film once. Trap: Treating consequences the child only watched as if the child had experienced them directly.

qs.q: Among boys, the decrease in mean aggressive acts from the 'no consequence' condition to the 'punished' condition, as a percentage of the 'no consequence' mean, was closest to:
o: Not quite. 3.6 is the drop in acts. A percent decrease divides that by the 'no consequence' mean.
Not quite. This divides 3.6 by 7.6, the boys' rewarded mean. The baseline should be the no-consequence mean, 6.8.
Not quite. This divides the girls' drop (2.7) by the boys' rewarded mean (7.6), mixing groups.
qs.x: Correct: Percent decrease = (drop ÷ 'no consequence' mean) × 100. From Table 3, boys in 'no consequence' = 6.8 acts and boys in 'punished' = 3.2 acts. The drop is 6.8 − 3.2 = 3.6 acts. Plug in: 3.6 ÷ 6.8. Multiply top and bottom by 10: 36 ÷ 68. Divide both by 4: 9 ÷ 17, which is about 0.529 (17 × 0.53 = 9.01). Multiply by 100: 0.529 × 100 = 52.9%, which rounds to about 53%. Why the others are wrong: 3.6% is the raw drop in acts, with no division; 47% divides 3.6 by 7.6, the boys' rewarded mean, instead of the no-consequence mean the question names; 35% divides the girls' drop (4.4 − 1.7 = 2.7) by the boys' rewarded mean (2.7 ÷ 7.6 = 0.355), which mixes two different groups. Trap: Dividing by the wrong condition when you compute a relative decrease.

qs.q: Why is the observed sex difference a weaker basis for a causal claim than the condition difference?
o: Children cannot be randomly assigned to sex, so other differences in upbringing may be confounded with it.
Correct: Sex can't be randomly assigned, so differences in upbringing or other traits may be mixed up with it.
Sex was measured with less precision than the film condition, which weakens the internal validity of the whole study.
Not quite. Sex is easy to measure. The weakness is the lack of random assignment, not poor precision.
Observers knew each child's sex, but not each child's film condition, so scoring was blind to film.
Not quite. Whether observers knew the child's sex doesn't solve the problem, since sex is still not a manipulated variable.
The sex difference was non-significant, so no conclusion about it can be drawn from these data.
Not quite. The passage says the main effect of sex was significant (p < 0.05).
qs.x: Correct: The passage says children were randomly assigned, within sex, to one of the three film endings. So film ending was a variable the researchers controlled, and random assignment spreads other differences evenly. Sex can't be assigned. Boys and girls may differ in how they were raised, what toys they play with, or what adults expect of them, and any of those could be mixed up (confounded) with sex. So the significant sex effect (p < 0.05) shows a difference, but it can't pin the cause on sex itself. Why the others are wrong: sex is easy to measure, so precision isn't the problem; the problem is no random assignment; whether observers knew the child's sex doesn't fix the causal issue, since sex is still not manipulated; the passage says the sex effect was significant, so the claim that no conclusion can be drawn is wrong. Trap: Assuming that any significant factor in an ANOVA is a cause, even one the researchers didn't manipulate.

qs.q: In the second phase, children in all conditions reproduced the model's behavior once they were offered stickers. This finding suggests that:
o: the children in the punished condition had not learned the behavior during the first phase.
Not quite. If they hadn't learned the acts, they couldn't have reproduced them when asked.
stickers acted as punishment and suppressed imitation in the second phase.
Not quite. Stickers are positive reinforcement. They increased imitation instead of suppressing it.
observational learning requires direct reinforcement of the observer in order to be acquired.
Not quite. Observational learning happens without rewarding the observer. The model's consequences affect performance.
the punished children had learned the behavior but were less likely to perform it spontaneously.
Correct: The punished children had learned the acts but were less likely to do them unprompted. Learning and performance differ.
qs.x: Correct: In the second phase, every child was told they'd get a sticker for each model action they could reproduce, and almost all of them did, including the punished group. You can only reproduce what you've learned. So the children in the punished condition had learned the aggressive acts by watching, but the model's punishment made them less likely to show those acts on their own (the lower numbers in Table 3). This is the difference between learning (acquiring the behavior) and performance (actually doing it). Why the others are wrong: if they hadn't learned it, they couldn't have copied it on request; stickers are a reward, so they raise behavior, not suppress it; observational learning doesn't need the observer to be rewarded, since the model's consequences mainly affect performance. Trap: Thinking that not doing something means not having learned it.

qs.q: Neural activity in premotor and inferior frontal regions that fires both when an individual performs an action and when the individual observes the same action performed by another is most closely associated with:
o: place cells.
Not quite. Place cells are in the hippocampus and fire for a specific location, not for watching actions.
Purkinje cells.
Not quite. Purkinje cells are output neurons of the cerebellum involved in coordinating movement.
grid cells.
Not quite. Grid cells are in the entorhinal cortex and map space in a repeating pattern.
mirror neurons.
Correct: Mirror neurons fire both when you perform an action and when you watch someone else perform it.
qs.x: Correct: The question describes neurons in premotor and inferior frontal areas that fire both when you do an action and when you watch someone else do it. Those are mirror neurons. They are thought to help with imitation and with understanding other people's actions, which ties right into this passage about children copying a model. Why the others are wrong: place cells are in the hippocampus and fire when you are in a particular spot in space; Purkinje cells are big output neurons of the cerebellum that help coordinate movement; grid cells are in the entorhinal cortex and fire in a repeating pattern that maps space. Trap: Choosing a cell type with a familiar name that sounds brain-related, instead of matching the clue (fires both when doing and when watching).

passages.title: FL01 · Psych/Soc · Passage 5
text: A laboratory study examined how the number of people who witness an emergency affects helping. Participants (n = 200) were told they were in a study of reactions to a noisy office. Each sat in a cubicle and completed a questionnaire. After several minutes, they heard what appeared to be a worker in the next room dropping a shelf and crying out in pain. In the 'alone' condition, the participant was by himself or herself. In the other three conditions, the participant was in a room with one, two, or four other people who were research assistants instructed to continue working and to show no concern. There were 50 participants in each of the four conditions, and all conditions had the same distribution of age and sex. The experimenters recorded whether the participant left the cubicle to help within 2 minutes and the time to respond. Results are summarized in Table 4 and Figure 3. A χ² test of helping (yes or no) by condition was significant (p < 0.001). In interviews afterward, many non-helping participants said that the emergency 'did not seem that serious' because the others seemed calm.

qs.q: The decline in helping as group size increased is best explained by:
o: social loafing, in which individuals reduce effort when they believe their output cannot be individually evaluated.
Not quite. Social loafing is about less effort on a shared task, not about reacting to an emergency.
deindividuation, in which anonymity within a crowd raises aggression.
Not quite. Deindividuation means losing self-awareness in a crowd. These people were in separate cubicles.
diffusion of responsibility, in which each person feels less personally obligated to act when others are present.
Correct: Diffusion of responsibility means each person feels less obligated to act when others are present, so helping drops.
group polarization, in which discussion makes the group's view more extreme.
Not quite. Group polarization needs a group discussion. There was none here.
qs.x: Correct: Table 4 and Figure 3 show helping falling as more people were in the room: 84% alone, 64% with two people, 48% with three, and 34% with five. This is the bystander effect. The best-known reason is diffusion of responsibility, meaning each person feels less personally on the hook to act when others are around ('someone else will do it'). The passage adds that the research assistants kept working calmly, which also hinted that nothing needed doing. Why the others are wrong: social loafing is about people putting in less effort on a shared task when their own work can't be singled out, not about reacting to an emergency; deindividuation is losing your sense of self inside a crowd, but these people sat in separate cubicles; group polarization needs a group discussion that pushes views to an extreme, and nobody discussed anything here. Trap: Choosing a different famous group effect just because it sounds close.

qs.q: Across all 200 participants, the overall percentage who helped within 2 minutes was:
o: Not quite. 52.5% would mean 105 helpers, but the counts add up to 115.
Not quite. 62.5% would mean 125 helpers, but the counts add up to 115.
Not quite. 58.0% would mean 116 helpers. The total is 115.
qs.x: Correct: Overall percent = (total helpers ÷ total participants) × 100. From Table 4, the helpers in the four conditions were 42, 32, 24 and 17. Add them in steps: 42 + 32 = 74, then 74 + 24 = 98, then 98 + 17 = 115 helpers. The passage says n = 200 participants (50 in each of 4 conditions). Plug in: 115 ÷ 200. Dividing by 200 is the same as dividing by 2 then by 100: 115 ÷ 2 = 57.5, and 57.5 ÷ 100 = 0.575. Multiply by 100: 0.575 × 100 = 57.5%. As a check, the average of the four percents is (84 + 64 + 48 + 34) ÷ 4 = 230 ÷ 4 = 57.5, which agrees because the groups are the same size. Why the others are wrong: 52.5% would need 105 helpers; 62.5% would need 125 helpers; 58.0% would need 116 helpers, and the total is 115. Trap: Mis-adding the four helper counts, which lands you one of the near-miss answers.

qs.q: Participants' statements that the event 'did not seem that serious' because others seemed calm best illustrates:
o: normative social influence driven by a desire for approval from the group.
Not quite. Normative influence is conforming to gain approval. These participants said they reinterpreted the event itself.
the foot-in-the-door technique, in which a small request precedes a larger one.
Not quite. Foot-in-the-door is a small request followed by a larger one. That didn't happen here.
social facilitation of a well-learned response in the presence of others.
Not quite. Social facilitation is about task performance when others are present, not judging an unclear situation.
informational social influence leading to pluralistic ignorance.
Correct: They used others' calm as information that it wasn't an emergency, and those others weren't really informed (pluralistic ignorance).
qs.x: Correct: The passage says many non-helpers told the interviewer the emergency 'did not seem that serious' because the others seemed calm. So they used other people's calm as information about whether it was a real emergency. That's informational social influence: you copy others because you think they know something you don't. But those others were research assistants told to show no concern, so they weren't actually informed. When everyone assumes the others know better and nobody reacts, you get pluralistic ignorance (everyone wrongly thinks everyone else sees no problem). Why the others are wrong: normative influence is going along to be accepted or liked, but these people said they changed their reading of the event; foot-in-the-door is a small request followed by a bigger one, and nothing like that happened; social facilitation is about how being watched changes performance on a task, not about judging an unclear situation. Trap: Treating all conformity as normative influence, when this one is about using others as information.

qs.q: A χ² test was an appropriate choice for the analysis of helping because:
o: the outcome was a continuous variable with an approximately normal distribution within each group.
Not quite. A continuous, normally distributed outcome would call for a t-test or ANOVA. Helping was yes or no.
the outcome (helped or not) is categorical and was compared across independent groups.
Correct: Helped or not is a categorical outcome, and χ² compares counts of it across independent groups.
the same participants were measured repeatedly in all four conditions of the experiment.
Not quite. Each condition had different participants, so measurements were independent, not repeated.
the study compared the means of exactly two independent groups.
Not quite. Four groups were compared, and χ² works with counts, not means.
qs.x: Correct: A chi-square (χ²) test compares counts in categories. Here the outcome for each person is 'helped' or 'did not help'. That's a category, not a number on a scale. And the 200 people were split into four separate groups of 50, with each person in only one group. So the test checks whether the share who helped differs more across the four conditions than chance would allow (the passage reports p < 0.001). Why the others are wrong: a continuous, roughly normal outcome would call for a t-test or ANOVA, and 'helped or not' isn't that; the same people weren't measured in all four conditions, since each condition had its own participants; there were four groups, not two, and χ² compares counts, not means. Trap: Picking a test by counting groups without first asking what kind of outcome you measured.

passages.title: FL01 · Psych/Soc · Passage 6
text: A study examined whether a reminder about group stereotypes affects performance in a domain that is important to the test-taker's identity. 96 undergraduates who rated mathematics as highly important to their self-concept were recruited: 64 women and 32 men. Women were randomly assigned to one of two conditions. In the 'threat' condition, they were told before a difficult 20-item math test that the test had shown gender differences in the past. In the 'no threat' condition, they were told that the test showed no gender differences. All 32 men received the 'threat' instructions. Participants were tested individually and then rated their anxiety during the test on a 7-point scale. Results are summarized in Table 5. Scores of the women in the 'threat' condition were significantly lower than those of women in the 'no threat' condition (p < 0.01), and the 'no threat' women and men did not differ significantly. A statistical mediation analysis found that test anxiety accounted for part of the effect of the instructions on women's scores. Prior math achievement, measured by self-reported scores on a college entrance exam, did not differ between the two groups of women.

qs.q: The lower scores of women in the threat condition are best interpreted as an example of:
o: stereotype threat, in which fear of confirming a negative group stereotype impairs performance.
Correct: Being reminded of a negative group stereotype in a domain they care about raised anxiety and lowered scores.
the self-serving bias, in which people credit their own successes to internal causes.
Not quite. The self-serving bias is about how people explain their successes and failures, not a drop caused by a reminder.
the Pygmalion effect, in which the high expectations of others raise a person's performance over time.
Not quite. The Pygmalion effect is high expectations raising performance, which is the opposite of this pattern.
the fundamental attribution error, in which others' behavior is attributed to disposition.
Not quite. The fundamental attribution error is about explaining other people's behavior by disposition, not a change in scores.
qs.x: Correct: Women who were told the test had shown gender differences scored lower (11.2 out of 20) than women told it showed none (13.6), and they reported more anxiety (4.1 vs 3.0 in Table 5). Math mattered a lot to them, and they were reminded of a negative stereotype about their group. Worrying about confirming that stereotype can eat up attention and push performance down. That is stereotype threat. Why the others are wrong: the self-serving bias is about crediting yourself for successes and blaming outside things for failures, and no one was explaining results here; the Pygmalion effect is when other people's high expectations raise your performance, which is the opposite direction; the fundamental attribution error is about explaining other people's behavior by their character, not about a score drop. Trap: Grabbing an attribution bias because the scenario involves explaining performance.

qs.q: Using the pooled standard deviation of the two groups of women, the effect size (Cohen's d) for the difference between the threat and no threat conditions is closest to:
o: Not quite. 2.4 is the raw difference in points. Cohen's d divides it by the pooled SD.
Not quite. 0.3 would match a mean gap of about 1 point, not 2.4.
Not quite. 1.3 would need a pooled SD of about 1.8, but it is about 3.25.
qs.x: Correct: Cohen's d = (mean difference) ÷ (pooled SD). From Table 5, women no threat = 13.6 with SD 3.1, and women threat = 11.2 with SD 3.4. Both groups have n = 32, so the pooled SD is the square root of the average of the two variances: pooled SD = √((3.4² + 3.1²) ÷ 2). Square each SD: 3.4² = 11.56 and 3.1² = 9.61. Add: 11.56 + 9.61 = 21.17. Divide by 2: 21.17 ÷ 2 = 10.585. Square root: √10.585 is about 3.25 (3.25² = 10.56). The mean difference is 13.6 − 11.2 = 2.4 points. Plug in: d = 2.4 ÷ 3.25 = 0.74, closest to 0.7. Why the others are wrong: 2.4 is the raw gap in points, not divided by an SD; 0.3 would mean a gap of only about 1 point; 1.3 would need a pooled SD of only about 1.8. Trap: Reporting the raw difference as an effect size, or dividing by the wrong spread.

qs.q: What was the main purpose of including the group of men?
o: To serve as a group that was randomly assigned to the 'no threat' condition for comparison with women.
Not quite. All the men got the 'threat' instructions. None were assigned to 'no threat'.
To test whether the anxiety measure is reliable across the threat and no-threat conditions.
Not quite. One administration of the anxiety scale in one group can't test its reliability.
To show that the 'threat' instructions alone do not reduce performance, so the effect depends on the stereotype.
Correct: Men heard the same threat instructions but scored like 'no threat' women, so the instructions alone don't hurt performance.
To increase the sample size so that the sex difference in the main comparison would be significant.
Not quite. The men were a comparison control, not extra people added to make a result significant.
qs.x: Correct: The passage says all 32 men got the 'threat' instructions. Table 5 shows they scored 14.0, about the same as the 'no threat' women (13.6), and the passage says those two groups did not differ significantly. So hearing 'this test has shown gender differences' didn't hurt the men. That tells us the instructions themselves aren't the problem. The drop for women in the threat condition depends on the stereotype that applies to them. The men act as a control group that heard the same words. Why the others are wrong: no man was in the 'no threat' condition, so they weren't randomized to it; one group taking the anxiety scale once can't test whether the scale is reliable; the aim was a comparison group, not extra people to make the sex difference reach significance. Trap: Thinking a comparison group is there to boost sample size, when it is there as a control.

qs.q: Participants were chosen because mathematics was highly important to their self-concept. This selection criterion was most likely used because:
o: people who do not care about math cannot take a math test or be affected by its context in any way.
Not quite. Someone who doesn't care about math can still take the test. The point is how much is at stake personally.
self-concept is determined only by performance feedback received from other people.
Not quite. Self-concept comes from several sources, such as self-perception and social comparison, not only others' feedback.
identity is formed entirely during adolescence and is unchanging in adulthood.
Not quite. Identity keeps developing in adulthood, so it is not fixed after adolescence.
stereotype threat is expected to be stronger when the domain is central to identity.
Correct: Stereotype threat is expected to be stronger when the domain is central to identity, since more is at stake.
qs.x: Correct: The passage says only students who rated math as highly important to their self-concept were recruited. Stereotype threat bites hardest when the subject matters to who you are, because then a negative stereotype about your group puts something you care about at risk. If a person doesn't care about math, a math stereotype stings much less, and the effect would be hard to see. So choosing math-identified students gives the threat the best chance to show up. Why the others are wrong: people who don't care about math can still take a math test, so that claim is too extreme; self-concept comes from many sources, like self-perception and comparing yourself to others, not only feedback from others; identity keeps developing in adulthood, so 'formed entirely in adolescence' is false. Trap: Choosing a sweeping claim about development or identity that sounds like psychology but doesn't explain the selection rule.

passages.title: FL01 · Psych/Soc · Passage 7
text: Researchers examined how implicit and explicit measures of attitudes toward an out-group predict behavior. A total of 120 participants completed an Implicit Association Test (IAT), in which faster pairing of out-group faces with negative words yields a higher D score, and a self-report scale on explicit attitudes toward the out-group, in which higher scores indicate more negative attitudes. Participants were told that the study concerned computer tasks and that a member of the out-group, who was a trained confederate, would join them for a second task. While the participant waited, the researchers measured how far (in cm) the participant placed his or her chair from the confederate's chair. Correlations among the measures are given in Table 6. Figure 4 plots a random subset of 8 participants' IAT scores against seating distance. The researchers argued that implicit attitudes reflect automatic associations that are less open to deliberate control. They also noted that participants were told the study was not about attitudes and that explicit responses were anonymous, but that the sample was drawn only from an undergraduate psychology subject pool.

qs.q: The proportion of variance in seating distance that is shared with IAT D scores is closest to:
o: Not quite. 34% is r written as a percent. Variance shared is r squared.
Not quite. 3% comes from squaring 0.18, the IAT-explicit correlation, not the 0.34 for seating distance.
Not quite. 58% is the square root of 0.34. You need to square r, not take its root.
Correct: r² = 0.34² = 0.1156, so about 12% of the variance is shared.
qs.x: Correct: The share of variance in one variable that is shared with another is r², called the coefficient of determination. From Table 6, the correlation between IAT D score and seating distance is r = 0.34. Square it: 0.34² = 0.34 × 0.34. First 34 × 34 = 1,156 (34 × 30 = 1,020, and 34 × 4 = 136, so 1,020 + 136 = 1,156). With two decimals each, that's four decimal places: 0.1156. Multiply by 100 to make a percent: 0.1156 × 100 = 11.56%, which is about 12%. So IAT scores account for about 12% of the differences in how far people sat. Why the others are wrong: 34% is just r written as a percent, with no squaring; 3% comes from squaring 0.18, which is the IAT-explicit correlation, not the one asked about; 58% is the square root of 0.34 (about 0.58), which goes the wrong way. Trap: Reading r as the percent of variance explained, instead of r².

qs.q: Which statement is best supported by Table 6?
o: Implicit negative attitudes cause people to sit farther from out-group members in a waiting room.
Not quite. A correlation doesn't show cause. A third variable or the reverse direction could explain it.
Implicit attitudes were more strongly related to seating distance than were explicit attitudes.
Correct: Seating distance correlated significantly with IAT scores (0.34, p < 0.001) but not with explicit attitudes (0.12, p = 0.19).
Explicit attitudes are unrelated to implicit attitudes in the general population of adults.
Not quite. The implicit-explicit correlation was 0.18 (p = 0.05), weak but not zero, and the sample can't speak for all adults.
Seating distance is a valid measure of explicit attitudes.
Not quite. Seating distance's correlation with explicit attitudes was not significant, so Table 6 doesn't show it measures them.
qs.x: Correct: Table 6 gives two correlations with seating distance. For the IAT D score, r = 0.34 with p < 0.001, so it's clearly significant. For the explicit attitude score, r = 0.12 with p = 0.19, which is above 0.05, so it's not significant. So the implicit measure was more strongly related to how far people sat than the explicit one. Why the others are wrong: a correlation can't show cause, so you can't say implicit attitudes make people sit farther; some third factor, or the reverse direction, could be at play; the implicit-explicit correlation was 0.18 (p = 0.05), which is weak but not 'unrelated', and a sample of 120 college students can't speak for all adults anyway; the table shows seating distance did not correlate significantly with explicit attitudes, so it can't be called a measure of them. Trap: Reading cause into a correlation coefficient, however small its p-value.

qs.q: Explicit self-reports of attitudes toward out-groups are often weaker predictors of behavior than implicit measures, most likely because explicit reports are:
o: subject to social desirability bias and limited introspective access.
Correct: Social desirability bias and limited self-insight can make explicit reports differ from automatic evaluations.
unaffected by participants' awareness of what is being measured by the questionnaire.
Not quite. Explicit measures are affected by awareness of what's being measured. That is the weakness.
determined only by genetic factors rather than by learning and experience.
Not quite. Attitudes come from learning and social experience, not only from genes.
only reliable when the scale has few items and a simple response format.
Not quite. How many items a scale has doesn't address the reporting bias.
qs.x: Correct: Explicit measures are just what people tell you on a questionnaire. People may not want to say they hold negative views of a group, so they answer in a way that looks good (social desirability bias). Some also don't fully know their own automatic reactions (limited introspective access, meaning limited ability to look inward and see what's driving you). So what they report can differ from what shows up in their quick reactions and their behavior. The passage hints at this, noting that responses were anonymous and the study was framed as not being about attitudes. The IAT is harder to fake because it relies on speed. Why the others are wrong: saying explicit reports aren't affected by awareness gets it backward, since awareness is the problem; attitudes are shaped by learning and social experience, not only genes; the number of items on a scale doesn't address the reporting bias. Trap: Forgetting that wanting to look good is a threat to self-report validity.

qs.q: The chair-placement behavior, if driven by negative attitudes toward the out-group, is best classified as:
o: prejudice.
Not quite. Prejudice is the attitude that the IAT and scale measured, not the chair placement.
a stereotype.
Not quite. A stereotype is a belief about a group, not an action.
a self-fulfilling prophecy.
Not quite. A self-fulfilling prophecy needs a belief that leads to behavior that makes the belief come true. That isn't described.
discrimination.
Correct: Discrimination is behavior, and keeping distance by seat placement is a behavior.
qs.x: Correct: Social psychology splits this into three pieces. A stereotype is a belief or generalization about a group (thinking). Prejudice is the feeling or attitude toward a group (feeling). Discrimination is how you actually act toward people because of their group (doing). The IAT and the explicit scale measure attitudes, which is the prejudice piece. But picking a chair farther from the out-group member is an action, so if negative attitudes drove it, that's discrimination (avoidance). Why the others are wrong: prejudice is the attitude the IAT and scale tapped, not the seat choice; a stereotype is a belief about a group, not a behavior; a self-fulfilling prophecy needs a belief that makes people act in a way that makes the belief come true, and the passage doesn't describe that loop. Trap: Mixing up the three parts: stereotype (thought), prejudice (feeling), discrimination (action).

qs.q: Based on the line connecting the lowest and highest IAT points in Figure 4, the approximate increase in seating distance per 0.5 unit increase in IAT D score is:
o: 37 cm
Not quite. 37 cm is the change for a full unit of D score. The question asks about half a unit.
18 cm
Correct: Slope = (108 − 60) ÷ (1.3 − 0) ≈ 37 cm per unit, so 0.5 unit gives about 18 cm.
9 cm
Not quite. 9 cm would need a slope of only about 18 cm per unit.
48 cm
Not quite. 48 cm is the whole rise across the full 1.3 units.
qs.x: Correct: Slope = rise ÷ run = (change in seating distance) ÷ (change in IAT D score). Read the lowest and highest IAT points in Figure 4: (0, 60) and (1.3, 108), in the form (D score, cm). Rise = 108 − 60 = 48 cm. Run = 1.3 − 0 = 1.3 units. Plug in: slope = 48 ÷ 1.3. Multiply top and bottom by 10: 480 ÷ 13 = about 36.9, so roughly 37 cm per 1.0 unit of D score. The question asks about 0.5 unit, which is half a unit, so multiply by 0.5: 36.9 × 0.5 = 18.5, which is about 18 cm. Why the others are wrong: 37 cm is the change for a full unit, not half; 9 cm would come from a slope of only about 18 cm per unit; 48 cm is the whole rise across 1.3 units. Trap: Using the whole rise (or the per-unit slope) instead of the amount for the 0.5 interval the question asks about.

passages.title: FL01 · Psych/Soc · Passage 8
text: A variation of a classic conformity study examined the conditions under which individuals yield to a group. Each of 100 participants was seated with five confederates and judged which of three comparison lines matched a standard line. On 12 critical trials, all five confederates gave the same incorrect answer. Participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions (n = 25 each). In the 'unanimous' condition, participants answered aloud after hearing all confederates. In the 'ally' condition, one confederate gave the correct answer on every critical trial, and the other four gave the incorrect answer. In the 'dissenter' condition, one confederate gave a different incorrect answer, and the other four gave a common incorrect answer. In the 'private' condition, there were five unanimous confederates, but the participant wrote the answer on paper, without it being seen by others. The outcome was the number of conformist (incorrect) responses, out of 12. Results are shown in Table 7. When the lines are presented alone, participants make fewer than 1% errors. Afterwards, participants were fully debriefed about the deception.

qs.q: The lower conformity in the 'private' condition relative to the 'unanimous' condition suggests that:
o: conformity was due entirely to informational influence, because participants doubted their own perception.
Not quite. If conformity were purely informational, answering privately wouldn't cut it so much, since the group's information would still be there.
participants in the private condition had better vision.
Not quite. Participants were randomly assigned, so vision should be about equal across conditions.
much of the conformity was due to normative influence, a desire to avoid disapproval from the group.
Correct: Answering privately cut conformity from 4.2 to 1.4, which points to normative influence, the wish to avoid group disapproval.
conformity occurs only when the group is larger than 10 people.
Not quite. Every condition had five confederates. The data say nothing about a threshold of 10 people.
qs.x: Correct: Compare the means in Table 7. In the unanimous condition people answered out loud and gave 4.2 conformist answers out of 12. In the private condition, where they wrote their answers on paper and no one saw them, the mean fell to 1.4. The group's wrong answers were still heard in both cases, so any information the group provided was still there. What changed was whether the participant had to face the group. So a lot of the conformity was normative influence, which means going along to avoid disapproval or to fit in. Why the others are wrong: if it were purely informational (doubting your own eyes), writing privately wouldn't cut it so much; participants were randomly assigned to conditions, so vision should be about the same across groups; group size was five confederates in every condition, so the data say nothing about a threshold of 10. Trap: Assuming any drop in conformity means people doubted what they saw, instead of feeling social pressure.

qs.q: The 'dissenter' condition was included to determine whether:
o: participants will conform less when the majority is correct than when it is incorrect.
Not quite. The majority gave an incorrect answer in every condition.
a correct answer from an ally is necessary in order to reduce conformity to the majority.
Not quite. The result shows an ally isn't required. A wrong dissenter also lowered conformity.
confederates are more convincing in groups than when they respond alone.
Not quite. The dissenter condition doesn't compare confederates in groups with confederates alone.
breaking the unanimity of the majority reduces conformity even if the dissenter is wrong.
Correct: A wrong dissenter still lowered conformity (4.2 to 1.8), so breaking unanimity matters even without correct information.
qs.x: Correct: In the dissenter condition, one confederate gave a different wrong answer, while the other four gave a common wrong answer. So the dissenter didn't offer the correct answer. They just broke up the unanimous front. Table 7 shows conformist answers fell from 4.2 (unanimous) to 1.8 (dissenter). So conformity dropped even though the dissenter gave no correct information, which means a group that isn't unanimous is easier to resist. Why the others are wrong: the majority was wrong in every condition, so this wasn't a test of correct versus incorrect majorities; the result shows an ally isn't required, since a wrong dissenter also lowered conformity; the dissenter condition doesn't compare confederates in groups with confederates alone. Trap: Assuming support only counts when the dissenter is right.

qs.q: Relative to the 'unanimous' condition, the percent decrease in mean conformist responses in the 'ally' condition was closest to:
o: Not quite. 3.1 is the raw drop in responses. A percent decrease divides it by the unanimous mean.
Not quite. 26% is the fraction left (1.1 ÷ 4.2), not the fraction lost.
Not quite. 57% is the decrease for the dissenter condition (2.4 ÷ 4.2), not the ally condition.
qs.x: Correct: Percent decrease = (drop ÷ unanimous mean) × 100. From Table 7, unanimous mean = 4.2 and ally mean = 1.1 conformist responses. The drop is 4.2 − 1.1 = 3.1. Plug in: 3.1 ÷ 4.2. Multiply top and bottom by 10: 31 ÷ 42. That's about 0.738 (42 × 0.738 = 30.996, almost 31). Multiply by 100: 0.738 × 100 = 73.8%, which rounds to about 74%. Why the others are wrong: 3.1% is the raw drop in responses, not divided by anything; 26% is the fraction left over (1.1 ÷ 4.2 = 0.26), not the part that went away; 57% is the drop for the dissenter condition ((4.2 − 1.8) ÷ 4.2 = 2.4 ÷ 4.2 = 0.571), a different condition. Trap: Giving the fraction remaining instead of the fraction lost.

qs.q: Which of the following is a feature of the study that addresses an ethical concern raised by the deception?
o: Participants were randomly assigned to the four conditions.
Not quite. Random assignment supports internal validity. It doesn't address the ethics of deception.
The sample contained 25 participants per condition.
Not quite. Sample size relates to statistical power, not to the deception.
The outcome was recorded as the number of errors.
Not quite. How the outcome was recorded has no bearing on the ethics of deception.
Participants were fully debriefed after the study.
Correct: Full debriefing explains the deception and purpose afterward, the standard remedy when deception is needed.
qs.x: Correct: The passage says the study used deception, because participants thought they were just judging lines and didn't know the confederates were acting. Deception raises an ethical worry, since people have been misled. The standard fix is debriefing: after the study, you tell participants what was really going on and why, and let them ask questions. The passage's last sentence says participants were fully debriefed. Why the others are wrong: random assignment to the four conditions is about internal validity (making groups comparable), not ethics; 25 per condition is about statistical power (the ability to detect an effect), not the deception; recording the number of errors is just how the outcome was measured, and has nothing to do with the ethics of misleading people. Trap: Mistaking a good research design feature for an ethical safeguard.

passages.title: FL01 · Psych/Soc · Passage 9
text: A public health department compared mortality in four neighborhoods grouped by median household income quartile, from lowest (Q1) to highest (Q4). Each group contained 250,000 residents. The department reviewed death certificates for one calendar year and also computed the period life expectancy at birth for each group. The data are shown in Table 8, and life expectancy is plotted in Figure 5. Residents in the lowest-income neighborhoods were more likely to live near major highways and industrial sites, and fewer had employer-provided health insurance. Residents in the highest-income neighborhoods were more likely to have completed a college degree. The report noted that the analysis was cross-sectional, so each resident's income and health were measured at one time only, and that the data were aggregated by neighborhood. The department's authors stated that every step up the income ladder was associated with longer life, not only the step out of poverty, and discussed the idea that higher socioeconomic status gives people more flexible resources, such as money, knowledge, power, and social connections, that can be used to avoid risks and to benefit from new health advances.

qs.q: The crude death rate in the Q1 neighborhoods, per 1,000 residents, was:
o: Not quite. A rate of 1 per 1,000 would mean 250 deaths, but Q1 had 2,500.
Not quite. A rate of 100 per 1,000 would mean 25,000 deaths, far above 2,500.
Not quite. A rate of 0.1 per 1,000 would mean only 25 deaths.
qs.x: Correct: Death rate per 1,000 = (deaths ÷ population) × 1,000. From Table 8, Q1 had 2,500 deaths in the year and a population of 250,000 residents. Plug in: (2,500 ÷ 250,000) × 1,000. Simplify the fraction by dividing top and bottom by 2,500: 2,500 ÷ 2,500 = 1 and 250,000 ÷ 2,500 = 100, so the fraction is 1 ÷ 100 = 0.01. Multiply by 1,000: 0.01 × 1,000 = 10. So the Q1 crude death rate is 10 deaths per 1,000 residents. Why the others are wrong: 1 per 1,000 would mean only 250 deaths; 100 per 1,000 would mean 25,000 deaths; 0.1 per 1,000 would mean 25 deaths. Each of those just slides the decimal point. Trap: Misplacing a decimal when turning a proportion into a rate per 1,000.

qs.q: According to Figure 5, the gap in life expectancy between the highest and lowest income quartiles is:
o: 8.2 years
Correct: The gap is 82.3 − 74.1 = 8.2 years between the highest and lowest quartiles.
5.5 years
Not quite. 5.5 years is the Q1-to-Q3 gap (79.6 − 74.1), not the Q1-to-Q4 gap.
5.3 years
Not quite. 5.3 years is the Q2-to-Q4 gap (82.3 − 77.0).
2.7 years
Not quite. 2.7 years is the Q3-to-Q4 gap (82.3 − 79.6).
qs.x: Correct: The gap is the highest value minus the lowest value. Figure 5 and Table 8 give life expectancy at birth by income quartile: Q1 (lowest) = 74.1 years and Q4 (highest) = 82.3 years. Plug in: 82.3 − 74.1. Subtract the whole numbers first: 82 − 74 = 8. Then the decimals: 0.3 − 0.1 = 0.2. Put them together: 8.2 years. So people in the highest-income neighborhoods are expected to live 8.2 years longer than those in the lowest. Why the others are wrong: 5.5 years is the Q3 minus Q1 gap (79.6 − 74.1); 5.3 years is the Q4 minus Q2 gap (82.3 − 77.0); 2.7 years is the Q4 minus Q3 gap (82.3 − 79.6). Each uses the wrong pair of bars. Trap: Reading the wrong two bars from the graph.

qs.q: Because the study was cross-sectional, which alternative to the conclusion that low income causes poor health must be considered?
o: Poor health may reduce a person's ability to work and earn income (reverse causation).
Correct: With one time point, direction is unclear. Poor health can lower a person's ability to earn (reverse causation).
Mortality was measured in only four income groups, which is too few for any comparison.
Not quite. Four groups are enough to compare. The number of groups doesn't address which way causation runs.
Residents of all neighborhoods have the same health risks regardless of income.
Not quite. The report describes different exposures, like highways and insurance, so risks aren't the same.
Life expectancy is measured in years and income in dollars, so the two cannot be compared.
Not quite. Different units for life expectancy and income don't create a causal alternative.
qs.x: Correct: The report says it was cross-sectional, meaning income and health were each measured at one point in time. With one snapshot, you can see that low income and short life go together, but you can't tell which came first. The usual story is that low income leads to worse health. The other direction is also possible: being sick can make it hard to work and earn, which drags income down (reverse causation, also called health selection). So you have to keep that alternative in mind before saying low income causes poor health. Why the others are wrong: having four groups is plenty for a comparison, and the number of groups says nothing about which way the cause runs; the passage says exposures differed (highways, industrial sites, insurance), so health risks aren't the same everywhere; years and dollars being different units doesn't create a causal alternative. Trap: Treating a link measured at one time as proof of which way the cause runs.

qs.q: The authors' idea that higher socioeconomic status provides flexible resources that can be used to avoid health risks and to gain from new advances is most consistent with:
o: the demographic transition model of population change.
Not quite. The demographic transition model describes how birth and death rates shift with industrialization.
symbolic interactionism as applied to everyday interaction.
Not quite. Symbolic interactionism is about meanings created in everyday interaction, not health inequality.
the strain theory of deviance proposed by Merton.
Not quite. Strain theory explains deviance as a gap between goals and the means to reach them.
the fundamental cause theory of health inequality.
Correct: Fundamental cause theory says SES gives flexible resources, so health inequality persists as specific mechanisms change.
qs.x: Correct: The authors say higher socioeconomic status (SES) gives people flexible resources (money, knowledge, power, social connections) that they can use in many ways to avoid health risks and to get the most from new health advances. That's the core of fundamental cause theory. It says SES keeps producing health gaps even when the specific diseases or treatments change, because people with more resources always find a way to use them. That fits the passage's point that every step up the income ladder, not just out of poverty, goes with longer life (Table 8). Why the others are wrong: the demographic transition model is about birth and death rates changing as countries industrialize; symbolic interactionism is about the meanings people build in everyday interactions; Merton's strain theory is about deviance coming from a gap between goals and the means to reach them. Trap: Picking a sociology theory by name instead of matching it to what the authors actually argue.

qs.q: The conclusion that any individual resident of a Q1 neighborhood will die earlier than any resident of a Q4 neighborhood would be an example of:
o: a placebo effect, because participants expected the neighborhood to affect their health.
Not quite. A placebo effect is a response to an inert treatment, which doesn't apply here.
an ecological fallacy, because group-level data may not apply to individuals.
Correct: Neighborhood data describe groups. Individual outcomes vary, so you can't apply the pattern to every person.
regression to the mean, because extreme neighborhood values drift toward the average.
Not quite. Regression to the mean is about extreme values drifting toward average when measured again.
a type II error, because a true difference between neighborhoods was missed.
Not quite. A type II error is failing to reject a false null hypothesis. The statement isn't about a missed difference.
qs.x: Correct: The data in Table 8 are about whole neighborhoods. They give averages for groups (life expectancy of 74.1 years for Q1, 82.3 for Q4). The statement says that any one person from Q1 will die before any one person from Q4. That takes a pattern in groups and applies it to every single person, which is an ecological fallacy. Inside each neighborhood, people vary a lot. Plenty of Q1 residents will outlive plenty of Q4 residents, so the group pattern says nothing certain about an individual. Why the others are wrong: a placebo effect is a response to an inert treatment, which isn't happening; regression to the mean is when extreme values move toward average on a second measurement; a type II error means missing a real difference by failing to reject a false null hypothesis, and this statement is not about a missed difference. Trap: Jumping from a group-level pattern to a sure claim about every individual.

passages.title: FL01 · Psych/Soc · Passage 10
text: Researchers followed a national sample of 2,000 adults, each with documented family income during childhood, and recorded the income quintile of each adult at age 40. Parents' income quintiles were assigned from tax records when the participants were children. The researchers also recorded whether each participant earned a college degree. Table 9 shows, for each parental income quintile, the percentage of adult children who ended up in the bottom and top quintiles of the adult income distribution, and the percentage who earned a degree. In interviews with a subset of the participants, children from top-quintile families more often described receiving help from parents in selecting colleges, guidance on how to interact with admissions officers and employers, and introductions to professional contacts. Children from bottom-quintile families more often reported that they were the first in their families to apply to college and that they did not know how to ask for financial aid. The authors framed the results as showing both movement and persistence in social class position across generations, and discussed competing explanations from functionalist and conflict perspectives.

qs.q: The interview findings regarding parents' guidance and professional contacts are best described by which concept?
o: Cultural and social capital, which are passed on within families and advantage high-income children.
Correct: Cultural and social capital are knowledge and networks families pass on, advantaging high-income children.
Anomie, a breakdown of social norms in times of rapid social change or upheaval.
Not quite. Anomie is normlessness during rapid social change, not advantage passed down in families.
Relative deprivation, the perception of being worse off than other comparable people or groups.
Not quite. Relative deprivation is feeling worse off than a comparison group, not a difference in family resources.
The looking-glass self, in which self-concept reflects imagined evaluations by other people.
Not quite. The looking-glass self explains how self-concept forms, not how class is reproduced.
qs.x: Correct: The interviews say top-quintile children got help picking colleges, coaching on how to deal with admissions officers and employers, and introductions to professional contacts. In sociology (Bourdieu), the know-how, habits and manners families pass on are cultural capital, and the useful connections are social capital. Families with more of both can hand them to their kids, which helps keep class position in the family from one generation to the next. This fits the passage's point about persistence in Table 9. Why the others are wrong: anomie (Durkheim) is normlessness during rapid social change, not passed-down advantage; relative deprivation is feeling worse off than a comparison group; the looking-glass self is how we form self-concept from imagined views of others, not how class is reproduced. Trap: Choosing a famous sociology term that doesn't match the evidence given.

qs.q: The probability that a child from a top-quintile family reaches the top quintile, compared with a child from a bottom-quintile family, is about:
o: 30 times as high
Not quite. 30 is the difference in percentage points (38 − 8), not a ratio.
4.75 times as high
Correct: 38% ÷ 8% = 4.75, so the top-quintile child is about 4.75 times as likely to reach the top.
0.21 times as high
Not quite. 0.21 is 8 ÷ 38, the ratio flipped. It compares bottom to top.
3.2 times as high
Not quite. 3.2 doesn't follow from the table. 38 ÷ 8 is 4.75.
qs.x: Correct: To say one probability is 'times as high' as another, divide them. Read the 'Child in top quintile (%)' column of Table 9. A child from a top-quintile family: 38%. A child from a bottom-quintile family: 8%. Plug in: 38 ÷ 8. 8 × 4 = 32, and 38 − 32 = 6 is left over, which is 6 ÷ 8 = 0.75 of another 8. So 38 ÷ 8 = 4 + 0.75 = 4.75. A top-quintile child is about 4.75 times as likely to reach the top. Why the others are wrong: 30 is the difference in percentage points (38 − 8), and a difference is not a 'times as high' ratio; 0.21 is 8 ÷ 38, the ratio flipped upside down; 3.2 doesn't come from these numbers. Trap: Subtracting percentages when the question asks for a ratio.

qs.q: Which interpretation of Table 9 is most consistent with a conflict perspective?
o: Unequal rewards motivate the most talented people to fill the most functionally important positions.
Not quite. That's the functionalist (Davis-Moore) argument that unequal rewards draw talent to important positions.
Advantaged groups use their resources to preserve their position, which limits mobility for others.
Correct: Conflict theory sees advantaged groups using their resources to protect their position and limit others' mobility.
Class position has no effect on adult income once education is held constant.
Not quite. Table 9 shows adult outcomes strongly tied to parental quintile, so this is contradicted.
Social stratification is beneficial because it promotes social stability and cohesion.
Not quite. Praising stratification for stability and cohesion is a functionalist claim.
qs.x: Correct: Conflict theory sees society as a contest over limited resources. Groups with more power use what they have to protect their position, and that makes it harder for others to move up. Table 9 fits: children from the top quintile are much more likely to land in the top quintile as adults (38%, compared with 8% for bottom-quintile children) and to earn a degree (75% vs 18%). The interviews add that those children got extra help and contacts. Why the others are wrong: the idea that unequal rewards draw talented people into important jobs is the functionalist (Davis-Moore) argument; saying class has no effect on adult income once education is held constant is contradicted by the strong link between parent quintile and adult outcome in the table; saying stratification is good because it keeps society stable is also functionalist. Trap: Picking the functionalist claim when the question asks for the conflict view.

qs.q: The study compares the class position of adults with that of their parents. This type of change is called:
o: intragenerational mobility.
Not quite. Intragenerational mobility compares one person's own status at different times in life.
structural mobility.
Not quite. Structural mobility comes from economic shifts that move many people at once.
social reproduction.
Not quite. Social reproduction is class persisting across generations, not the term for change.
intergenerational mobility.
Correct: Intergenerational mobility compares children's class position with their parents'.
qs.x: Correct: The study compares adults' class position at age 40 with their parents' class position. That's a change across generations (parents to children), called intergenerational mobility. 'Inter' means between, so between generations. Why the others are wrong: intragenerational mobility ('intra' means within) would compare one person's own position at different times in their life, and this study compares children with parents; structural mobility is movement caused by big shifts in the economy that move many people at once, which isn't what is being described; social reproduction is the opposite idea, class staying the same across generations, so it is not the name for the change. Trap: Mixing up inter (between generations) and intra (within one lifetime).
