questions.q: At pH 7.4, in a native gel electrophoresis experiment, a protein with an isoelectric point of 9.5 will most likely migrate toward:
o: the anode, because the protein has a net positive charge
Not quite. A positively charged protein moves toward the cathode, not the anode.
the cathode, because the protein has a net negative charge
Not quite. The protein isn't negative. pH 7.4 is below its pI of 9.5.
neither electrode, because the net charge is zero
Not quite. Net charge is zero only when the pH equals the pI (9.5), not at 7.4.
the cathode, because the protein has a net positive charge
Correct: pH 7.4 is below the pI of 9.5, so the protein is net positive and moves toward the negative electrode, the cathode.
questions.x: Correct: The isoelectric point (pI) is the pH at which a protein has no net charge. Above the pI the protein has lost more protons and is negative, and below the pI it is carrying extra protons and is positive. Here the pI is 9.5 and the gel buffer is pH 7.4, which is below the pI, so the protein is on the positive side. In an electric field, a positive particle moves toward the negative electrode, which is the cathode. A handy way to remember it: cations go to the cathode. The gel is native, so no SDS is covering the charge. Why the others are wrong: a net positive protein heading to the anode (the positive electrode) would be attracted to a charge like its own; a net negative protein would go to the anode, but this one isn't negative; and a protein has zero net charge only when the pH equals the pI, which would be pH 9.5, not 7.4. Trap: Mixing up which electrode attracts positive charge, or misreading whether the pH is above or below the pI.

questions.q: A purified antibody migrates at 150 kDa on SDS-PAGE without a reducing agent. With β-mercaptoethanol, bands are seen at 50 kDa and 25 kDa. These data are most consistent with an antibody composed of:
o: one 50 kDa and one 25 kDa chain linked by hydrogen bonds
Not quite. One of each chain adds up to 75 kDa, and SDS disrupts hydrogen bonds anyway.
two heavy and two light chains linked by disulfide bonds
Correct: Reducing breaks disulfides, and 2 × 50 + 2 × 25 = 150 kDa. Two heavy and two light chains are held by disulfide bonds.
three 50 kDa chains linked by disulfide bonds
Not quite. Three 50 kDa chains would not give a 25 kDa band.
one 150 kDa chain with internal peptide bonds cleaved
Not quite. β-mercaptoethanol doesn't cleave peptide bonds.
questions.x: Correct: SDS-PAGE separates proteins by size. SDS strips a protein of its shape but does not break disulfide bonds (S–S bonds between cysteines) unless a reducing agent such as β-mercaptoethanol is added. Without the reducing agent, the antibody runs as one 150 kDa band, so all its pieces are still tied together. With the reducing agent the S–S bonds break, and two bands appear at 50 kDa and 25 kDa. Add up the pieces. Four chains fit: 2 × 50 + 2 × 25 = 100 + 50 = 150 kDa. That is the classic antibody layout, two heavy chains (50 kDa each) and two light chains (25 kDa each) held by disulfide bonds. Why the others are wrong: one 50 and one 25 kDa chain would add up to only 75 kDa, and SDS disrupts hydrogen bonds anyway; three 50 kDa chains would give 150 kDa but no 25 kDa band; and β-mercaptoethanol breaks disulfide bonds, not peptide bonds, so a single 150 kDa chain wouldn't split. Trap: Forgetting that the reduced bands must add up to the total mass of the unreduced protein.

questions.q: A template strand has the sequence 3'-TACGGATTC-5'. What is the sequence of the mRNA transcribed from it?
o: 5'-AUGCCUAAG-3'
Correct: The mRNA is the complement of the template, antiparallel, with U instead of T: 5′-AUGCCUAAG-3′.
5'-UACGGAUUC-3'
Not quite. This copies the template with T changed to U instead of complementing, and the polarity is wrong.
3'-AUGCCUAAG-5'
Not quite. The bases are right but the 5′ and 3′ ends are labeled backwards.
5'-ATGCCTAAG-3'
Not quite. mRNA contains uracil, not thymine.
questions.x: Correct: RNA polymerase reads the template strand and builds an mRNA that is complementary to it, meaning each base pairs with its partner: A pairs with U in RNA (not T), T pairs with A, C pairs with G, and G pairs with C. The two strands run in opposite directions (antiparallel). The template is written 3′-TACGGATTC-5′. Pair each base from left to right: T gives A, A gives U, C gives G, G gives C, G gives C, A gives U, T gives A, T gives A, C gives G. That gives A-U-G-C-C-U-A-A-G, which lines up under the template in the 5′ to 3′ direction, since the template's 3′ end pairs with the mRNA's 5′ end. So the mRNA is 5′-AUGCCUAAG-3′. Why the others are wrong: 5′-UACGGAUUC-3′ just copies the template with T swapped for U, which isn't the complement and has the wrong polarity; 3′-AUGCCUAAG-5′ has the right bases but the ends are labeled backwards; and 5′-ATGCCTAAG-3′ has the right order but uses thymine, and mRNA has uracil. Trap: Writing the template with T changed to U instead of making the complement.

questions.q: Cells lacking telomerase activity are cultured through many divisions. Which outcome is most likely?
o: Telomere lengthening through repeated lagging-strand synthesis at chromosome ends
Not quite. Lagging-strand synthesis causes the end-replication problem. It doesn't lengthen telomeres.
Loss of centromeres in daughter chromosomes, causing missegregation at anaphase
Not quite. Centromeres aren't affected by missing telomerase.
Increase in Okazaki fragment length, which slows replication of the lagging strand
Not quite. Okazaki fragment length is unrelated to telomerase.
Progressive telomere shortening, eventually leading to senescence or apoptosis
Correct: Without telomerase, the 3′ end of the lagging strand isn't fully copied, so telomeres shorten each division and cells senesce or die.
questions.x: Correct: Every time a cell copies its DNA, the lagging strand can't be copied all the way to the tip of the chromosome, because the last RNA primer can't be replaced. This is called the end-replication problem, and it leaves a small piece of the telomere (the repeating DNA cap on each chromosome end) uncopied each round. Telomerase is the enzyme that adds the repeats back. In cells lacking telomerase, nothing fixes the loss, so the telomeres get shorter with each division. When they become critically short, the cell reads it as DNA damage and stops dividing (senescence) or self-destructs (apoptosis). Why the others are wrong: lagging-strand synthesis is the cause of the shortening, not a way of lengthening; centromeres are in the middle of the chromosome and aren't affected; and Okazaki fragment length has nothing to do with telomerase. Trap: Believing that lagging-strand synthesis keeps chromosome ends intact without telomerase.

questions.q: Three linked genes have recombination frequencies of 12% between A and B, 5% between B and C, and 7% between A and C. What is the gene order?
o: A-B-C
Not quite. A-B-C would need A to C to be 12 + 5 = 17, but it's 7.
A-C-B
Correct: The largest distance, A to B (12), equals 7 + 5, so C sits between A and B.
B-A-C
Not quite. B-A-C would need B to C to be 12 + 7 = 19, but it's 5.
C-A-B
Not quite. C-A-B would need C to B to be 7 + 12 = 19, but it's 5.
questions.x: Correct: Recombination frequency tells you how far apart two genes are on a chromosome. The more often two genes get separated, the farther apart they are, and distances add up along a line. List the distances: A to B = 12%, B to C = 5%, A to C = 7%. The biggest distance belongs to the two genes on the outside, and the gene in the middle sits between them. The biggest is A to B at 12%. Check if the other two add up to it: 7 + 5 = 12. They do. So C is in the middle, and the order is A-C-B. Why the others are wrong: A-B-C would put B in the middle, so A to C would have to be 12 + 5 = 17, but it's 7; B-A-C would put A in the middle, so B to C would be 12 + 7 = 19, not 5; and C-A-B would put A in the middle, so C to B would be 7 + 12 = 19, not 5. Trap: Ordering the genes by the letters given instead of from the largest distance.

questions.q: In regions where malaria is endemic, the sickle cell allele remains at a substantial frequency in the population. Which concept best explains this?
o: Homozygotes for the sickle cell allele have the highest fitness
Not quite. Sickle cell homozygotes have severe disease, so their fitness isn't highest.
The allele is selectively neutral and maintained by genetic drift
Not quite. A repeatable geographic pattern with malaria points to selection, not random drift.
Heterozygotes have higher fitness than either homozygote
Correct: Heterozygotes are protected from severe malaria without sickle cell disease, which keeps both alleles in the population.
The allele is maintained by repeated back mutation from the normal allele
Not quite. Mutation rates are too low to maintain the allele at a high frequency.
questions.x: Correct: Sickle cell disease is a serious illness in people with two copies of the sickle allele, so you might expect the allele to disappear. But it stays common where malaria is endemic. The reason is that people with one copy (heterozygotes, or carriers) mostly don't get sickle cell disease and are better protected against severe malaria than people with two normal copies. So carriers survive and have children more often than either type of homozygote (a person with two identical copies). Normal homozygotes lose out to malaria and sickle homozygotes lose out to the disease. This is called heterozygote advantage, a form of balancing selection, because it keeps both alleles in the population. Why the others are wrong: sickle cell homozygotes have severe disease, not the highest fitness; drift is random, and a strong pattern that repeats in malarial regions points to selection; and the mutation rate is far too low to keep the allele at a high frequency by back mutation. Trap: Putting a high allele frequency down to dominance or neutrality instead of selection.

questions.q: Which change would most likely increase the activity of phosphofructokinase-1 in a hepatocyte?
o: Increased fructose-2,6-bisphosphate
Correct: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is the most potent allosteric activator of PFK-1, promoting glycolysis in the fed state.
Increased citrate
Not quite. Citrate signals abundant building blocks and inhibits PFK-1.
Increased ATP
Not quite. High ATP is an allosteric inhibitor of PFK-1.
Decreased AMP
Not quite. AMP activates PFK-1, so a decrease would lower its activity.
questions.x: Correct: Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) is the main control point of glycolysis, the pathway that breaks glucose down for energy. Its activators are signs that the cell needs energy or has plenty of glucose, and its inhibitors are signs that energy is already abundant. The strongest activator is fructose-2,6-bisphosphate. In the fed state, insulin raises fructose-2,6-bisphosphate in the liver, which switches PFK-1 on so glucose gets used. Why the others are wrong: citrate is a sign that the cell has plenty of building blocks and energy from the citric acid cycle, so it inhibits PFK-1; high ATP means energy is plentiful, so ATP binds a regulatory site and inhibits PFK-1; and a decrease in AMP would lower activity, since AMP activates PFK-1 when energy is low, and less of it means less activation. Trap: Mixing up inhibitors and activators when thinking about the cell's energy state.

questions.q: Complete β-oxidation of one molecule of palmitoyl-CoA (16 carbons) produces how many FADH₂?
o: Not quite. 8 is the number of acetyl-CoA, not the number of rounds.
Not quite. 15 isn't related to the number of cycles.
Not quite. 16 is the number of carbons, not the number of FADH₂.
Correct: A 16-carbon chain needs 7 rounds, and each round makes one FADH₂ (and one NADH), giving 7 FADH₂ and 8 acetyl-CoA.
questions.x: Correct: β-oxidation breaks a fatty acid into two-carbon acetyl-CoA pieces. Each round (cycle) of the spiral chops two carbons off the end and makes one FADH₂ and one NADH. For a 16-carbon chain, work out how many rounds are needed. Round 1 takes it from 16 to 14 carbons, round 2 to 12, round 3 to 10, round 4 to 8, round 5 to 6, round 6 to 4. Round 7 takes the last 4 carbons and splits them into two acetyl-CoA. So there are 7 rounds, and 7 rounds make 7 FADH₂ (and 7 NADH). The number of acetyl-CoA is 16 ÷ 2 = 8. Why the others are wrong: 8 is the number of acetyl-CoA, which is one more than the number of rounds because the last round makes two; 15 has no link to a cycle that removes two carbons; and 16 is the number of carbons in the chain. Trap: Equating the number of rounds with the number of acetyl-CoA produced.

questions.q: A mutation in the genes encoding claudins disrupts the tight junctions of an epithelium. Which defect would most likely result?
o: Increased paracellular leakage and loss of apical-basolateral protein segregation
Correct: Tight junctions seal the space between cells and keep apical and basolateral proteins apart. Losing claudins causes leaks and loss of segregation.
Loss of the ability to anchor cells to the basal lamina through integrin-based contacts
Not quite. Hemidesmosomes anchor cells to the basal lamina through integrins.
Loss of cytoplasmic communication between adjacent cells through connexin channels
Not quite. Gap junctions, made of connexins, allow cytoplasmic communication.
Loss of the keratin network inside cells, weakening their resistance to mechanical stress
Not quite. Keratin is a cytoplasmic intermediate filament. It isn't a claudin.
questions.x: Correct: Claudins are the main proteins that build tight junctions, the bands that run around the top of epithelial cells and bind neighboring cells together. A tight junction does two jobs. It seals the gap between cells, so substances can't leak through the space between them (the paracellular route). It also works like a fence in the cell membrane, keeping apical proteins (top surface) and basolateral proteins (sides and bottom) from mixing. If claudins are mutated, the seal leaks and the proteins can drift across, so polarity is lost. Why the others are wrong: anchoring cells to the basal lamina through integrins is done by hemidesmosomes; letting the cytoplasm of neighbors communicate through connexin channels is the job of gap junctions; and keratin is an intermediate filament inside the cell, not a claudin, so a claudin mutation wouldn't remove it. Trap: Confusing the jobs of tight junctions, gap junctions and desmosomes.

questions.q: A drug blocks reverse transcriptase in cells infected with a retrovirus. Which step is directly prevented?
o: Synthesis of DNA from the viral RNA genome
Correct: Reverse transcriptase copies viral RNA into DNA, so blocking it stops synthesis of DNA from the viral genome.
Translation of viral proteins from viral RNA
Not quite. Translation uses host ribosomes and doesn't need reverse transcriptase.
Assembly of virions at the plasma membrane
Not quite. Assembly happens later and doesn't need reverse transcriptase.
Entry of the virus by receptor-mediated endocytosis
Not quite. Entry happens before reverse transcription.
questions.x: Correct: A retrovirus, like HIV, carries its genes as RNA. To get into the host's genome it first has to turn that RNA into DNA. Reverse transcriptase is the enzyme that does this, reading the viral RNA and building DNA from it (the reverse of the usual DNA-to-RNA direction). The new viral DNA then enters the nucleus and is stitched into the host chromosome by integrase. So a drug that blocks reverse transcriptase directly stops the making of DNA from the viral RNA genome. Why the others are wrong: translation of viral proteins uses the host's ribosomes and doesn't need reverse transcriptase; assembly of new virus particles at the plasma membrane happens later, after the proteins are made; and entry into the cell by endocytosis happens before the virus has any reason to make DNA. Trap: Assigning the enzyme to translation or assembly just because those steps also involve viral RNA.

questions.q: Nondisjunction of one homologous pair during meiosis I in a human spermatocyte would result in:
o: four gametes, none of which has the normal chromosome number for that pair
Correct: In meiosis I the homologs fail to separate, so both daughter cells are abnormal. All four gametes are n + 1 or n − 1 for that pair.
two normal gametes and two with an extra chromosome
Not quite. Two normal gametes appear only with a meiosis II error, which also gives one n + 1 and one n − 1.
Two gametes with the normal number of chromosomes and two lacking that chromosome
Not quite. A meiosis I error affects both daughter cells, so two normal gametes can't result.
one abnormal gamete and three normal gametes
Not quite. One abnormal gamete and three normal ones doesn't fit either meiotic division.
questions.x: Correct: In meiosis I, the two homologs of each chromosome pair are supposed to separate into the two daughter cells. Nondisjunction means a pair fails to separate, so one daughter cell gets both homologs and the other gets none. Then in meiosis II, each of those two cells splits again. The cell that got both homologs gives two gametes with an extra chromosome (n + 1). The cell that got none gives two gametes missing that chromosome (n − 1). So all four gametes are abnormal for that chromosome, and none has the right number. Why the others are wrong: two normal gametes and two with an extra chromosome doesn't match any pattern, because an error in meiosis II gives two normal gametes, one n + 1 and one n − 1; two normal gametes and two lacking the chromosome can't be, since a meiosis I error affects both daughter cells; and one abnormal and three normal gametes doesn't fit either meiotic division. Trap: Confusing the results of nondisjunction in meiosis I and meiosis II.

questions.q: A cell with a loss-of-function mutation in TP53 experiences DNA damage. Compared with a normal cell, it is more likely to:
o: arrest in G1 so that the damage can be repaired
Not quite. G1 arrest depends on p53 inducing p21, so it would be less likely.
continue through the cell cycle without repair or apoptosis
Correct: Without p53, the p21 and apoptosis responses fail, so the damaged cell keeps cycling without repair.
undergo apoptosis through activation of caspases
Not quite. p53 promotes apoptosis, so a cell lacking it is less likely to undergo it.
increase expression of the CDK inhibitor p21
Not quite. p21 is a p53 target, so it wouldn't increase without p53.
questions.x: Correct: TP53 makes p53, a tumor suppressor, which means a protein that guards against cancer. When DNA is damaged, p53 turns on genes that protect the cell: p21, which blocks the cell cycle so the damage can be repaired, and genes that trigger apoptosis (cell suicide) if the damage is too bad. A loss-of-function mutation means the protein doesn't work. Without p53, neither response happens. The cell doesn't pause, doesn't repair and doesn't die, so it carries on through the cell cycle and passes the damaged DNA on to its daughter cells. That's how mutations build up and cancer can start. Why the others are wrong: arrest in G1 for repair is caused by p53 turning on p21, and it's missing here; apoptosis through caspases is promoted by p53, so it would be less likely; and increased p21 would need p53 to turn it on, so it wouldn't go up. Trap: Reversing the effect of a loss-of-function mutation in a tumor suppressor.

questions.q: Damage to the dorsal root of a spinal nerve would most likely cause:
o: loss of motor function in the corresponding region, with sensation preserved there
Not quite. Motor deficits come from ventral root damage.
loss of both sensation and motor function in the corresponding region of the body
Not quite. Losing both would need both roots to be damaged.
loss of the autonomic control of the heart and of voluntary movement in the arm
Not quite. Heart control uses cranial and sympathetic pathways, not this root.
loss of sensation from the corresponding region with preserved motor function
Correct: Sensory neurons enter through the dorsal root, so damage removes sensation while the ventral motor root keeps motor function.
questions.x: Correct: Each spinal nerve joins the spinal cord by two roots. The dorsal root (toward the back) carries sensory information into the cord, and its cell bodies sit in the dorsal root ganglion. The ventral root (toward the front) carries motor commands out from the cord to the muscles. A way to remember it: the dorsal root is for sensation going in, the ventral root is for movement going out. If the dorsal root is damaged, signals from that region of the body can no longer reach the cord, so sensation is lost there. The ventral root is intact, so motor function is preserved. Why the others are wrong: loss of motor function with preserved sensation would be damage to the ventral root; losing both sensation and motor function would need both roots to be damaged; and heart control uses cranial and sympathetic pathways, not a single spinal dorsal root. Trap: Reversing the dorsal (sensory) and ventral (motor) roots.

questions.q: During intense exercise, hemoglobin in the muscle capillaries most likely shows:
o: increased oxygen affinity from increased CO₂ and H⁺, so less oxygen is released
Not quite. More CO₂ and H⁺ lower hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen.
decreased oxygen affinity from decreased temperature, so more oxygen is released
Not quite. Exercise raises temperature, and a lower temperature would increase affinity.
increased oxygen affinity from increased 2,3-BPG, so less oxygen is released
Not quite. 2,3-BPG lowers affinity, which helps release oxygen.
decreased oxygen affinity from increased CO₂ and H⁺, releasing more oxygen
Correct: Lower pH, more CO₂ and higher temperature shift the curve right (the Bohr effect), so hemoglobin releases more oxygen.
questions.x: Correct: Hemoglobin holds oxygen at the lungs and lets go of it at working tissues. Working muscle makes CO₂ and acid (H⁺), and gets warm. All three of these push hemoglobin to hold oxygen less tightly, so it releases more oxygen exactly where it is needed. This is the Bohr effect. On the oxygen dissociation curve, the curve shifts to the right (lower affinity). Lower pH, higher CO₂, higher temperature and higher 2,3-BPG all shift it right. Why the others are wrong: increased affinity from more CO₂ and H⁺ gets the direction backwards, since they lower affinity; exercise raises temperature, doesn't lower it, and a lower temperature would raise the affinity; and 2,3-BPG lowers affinity, which helps release oxygen, so increased affinity from more 2,3-BPG is also backwards. Trap: Shifting the curve in the wrong direction for the Bohr effect.

questions.q: Acidic chyme entering the duodenum stimulates the release of secretin, which acts on the pancreas to:
o: increase bicarbonate secretion to neutralize acid
Correct: Secretin makes the pancreas secrete bicarbonate-rich juice, which neutralizes the acid and raises duodenal pH.
increase secretion of pancreatic lipase only
Not quite. Lipase secretion is stimulated mainly by cholecystokinin.
decrease secretion of bicarbonate
Not quite. Secretin increases bicarbonate secretion. It doesn't decrease it.
stimulate release of gastric acid from parietal cells
Not quite. Gastrin, not secretin, stimulates parietal cells to release acid.
questions.x: Correct: When acidic chyme (partly digested food from the stomach) enters the duodenum, S cells in the duodenal wall release secretin into the blood. Secretin travels to the pancreas and tells its duct cells to release a watery fluid rich in bicarbonate. Bicarbonate is a base, so it neutralizes the acid. That protects the intestinal lining and raises the pH to a level where the pancreatic digestive enzymes can work. Why the others are wrong: lipase release from the pancreas is stimulated mainly by cholecystokinin (CCK), which is triggered by fats and proteins; saying secretin decreases bicarbonate gets the direction backwards, because bicarbonate goes up; and it's gastrin, not secretin, that stimulates parietal cells to release gastric acid. Trap: Confusing the roles of secretin (bicarbonate) and cholecystokinin (enzymes and bile).

questions.q: A ball is thrown horizontally at 20 m/s from the edge of a 45 m cliff. Neglecting air resistance and using g = 10 m/s², how far from the base of the cliff does it land?
o: Correct: 45 = ½(10)t² gives t = 3 s, so x = 20 × 3 = 60 m.
Not quite. 30 m uses a 1.5 s fall time, which is only about an 11 m drop, not 45 m.
Not quite. 90 m uses t = h/g = 4.5 s, which is the wrong fall-time formula.
Not quite. 120 m uses t = 6 s, double the correct fall time.
questions.x: Correct: Split the throw into two separate motions. Sideways, nothing speeds it up or slows it down, so the speed stays 20 m/s. Downward, it starts with zero vertical speed and falls like a dropped ball. The fall time sets how long the ball has to travel sideways. Formula for the fall: h = ½gt², so t = √(2h/g). Values: h = 45 m, g = 10 m/s². Plug in: 45 = ½ × 10 × t² = 5t², so t² = 45 ÷ 5 = 9, and t = 3 s. Now the sideways distance: x = vₓt = 20 m/s × 3 s = 60 m. Why the others are wrong: 30 m comes from a 1.5 s fall time, which is too short for a 45 m drop (it would only drop about 11 m); 90 m uses t = h/g = 4.5 s, which isn't the right fall-time formula; 120 m uses a 6 s fall, double the correct time. Trap: Using t = h/g instead of t = √(2h/g).

questions.q: A 40 kg child sits 1.5 m from the pivot of a uniform seesaw. At what distance from the pivot on the other side must a 30 kg child sit to balance the seesaw?
o: Correct: 40 × 1.5 = 30 × d gives d = 2.0 m. The lighter child needs a longer lever arm.
Not quite. 1.1 m comes from inverting the ratio (1.5 × 30 ÷ 40).
Not quite. 1.5 m would balance only if the masses were equal.
Not quite. 3.0 m would need a 2:1 mass ratio, but 40:30 is not 2:1.
questions.x: Correct: A seesaw balances when the twisting effect (torque) on each side matches. Torque = force × distance from the pivot, and each force here is mg. The g is the same on both sides, so it cancels and masses are enough: m₁d₁ = m₂d₂. Values: m₁ = 40 kg, d₁ = 1.5 m, m₂ = 30 kg, d₂ = ?. Plug in: 40 × 1.5 = 30 × d₂. 40 × 1.5 = 60, so 60 = 30d₂. Divide both sides by 30: d₂ = 60 ÷ 30 = 2.0 m. The lighter child has to sit farther from the pivot to make up for the smaller weight. Why the others are wrong: 1.1 m flips the mass ratio (1.5 × 30 ÷ 40 = 1.125); 1.5 m would balance only if both children had equal mass; 3.0 m would need the mass ratio to be 2:1, but 40:30 is only 4:3. Trap: Inverting the mass ratio so the lighter child sits closer.

questions.q: What is the approximate absolute pressure at the bottom of a lake at a depth of 10 m? (Density of water = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 m/s², atmospheric pressure = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa)
o: Not quite. 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa is only atmospheric pressure and ignores the water.
Not quite. 9.8 × 10⁴ Pa is the gauge pressure and leaves out the atmosphere.
Not quite. 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa would be reached at about 20 m depth.
questions.x: Correct: Absolute pressure means the pressure counted from zero, so it includes the air pressing on the lake's surface plus the weight of the water above you. Formula: P = P<sub>atm</sub> + ρgh. Values: P<sub>atm</sub> = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 m/s², h = 10 m. Plug in: P = 1.0 × 10⁵ + (1000)(9.8)(10). 1000 × 9.8 = 9,800, and 9,800 × 10 = 98,000 Pa = 0.98 × 10⁵ Pa. Add: 1.0 × 10⁵ + 0.98 × 10⁵ = 1.98 × 10⁵ Pa, which is about 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa. A handy fact: every 10 m of water adds about one atmosphere. Why the others are wrong: 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa is the atmosphere alone and leaves out the water; 9.8 × 10⁴ Pa is the gauge pressure (just the water's part), which skips the atmosphere; 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa would be reached at about 20 m, not 10 m. Trap: Giving gauge pressure when absolute pressure is asked for.

questions.q: In the circuit, a 12 V battery is connected in series to a 4.0 Ω resistor, which is in series with a parallel combination of a 6.0 Ω resistor and a 3.0 Ω resistor. What is the current through the 6.0 Ω resistor?
o: Not quite. 1.3 A is the current in the 3.0 Ω resistor (4.0 ÷ 3.0).
Not quite. 2.0 A is the total current, which splits between the two parallel branches.
Not quite. 1.0 A would come from an equal split or a wrong voltage.
Correct: The parallel pair has 4.0 V across it, so I = 4.0 ÷ 6.0 = 0.67 A.
questions.x: Correct: Work from the whole circuit down to the one resistor. Parallel resistors: 1/R = 1/6 + 1/3, or the product over sum, (6.0 × 3.0) ÷ (6.0 + 3.0) = 18 ÷ 9 = 2.0 Ω. That pair is in series with the 4.0 Ω resistor, so the total is R = 4.0 + 2.0 = 6.0 Ω. Ohm's law: I = V ÷ R = 12 V ÷ 6.0 Ω = 2.0 A flowing from the battery. That 2.0 A all goes through the 4.0 Ω resistor, then splits between the two parallel branches. The voltage across the parallel pair is V = IR = 2.0 A × 2.0 Ω = 4.0 V, and both branches have the same voltage. So the current in the 6.0 Ω resistor is I = V ÷ R = 4.0 V ÷ 6.0 Ω = 0.67 A. Why the others are wrong: 1.3 A is the current in the 3.0 Ω branch (4.0 ÷ 3.0); 2.0 A is the total current, which splits between the branches; 1.0 A would come from an equal split or a wrong voltage. Trap: Giving the total current instead of one branch's current.

questions.q: A parallel-plate capacitor remains connected to a battery while the plate separation is doubled. What happens to the energy stored in the capacitor?
o: It doubles.
Not quite. Pulling the plates apart lowers capacitance, so energy doesn't go up.
It is reduced to one quarter of its original value.
Not quite. A quarter would need both C and V to halve, but the battery fixes V.
It is reduced to half its original value.
Correct: Doubling d halves C, and with V fixed, U = ½CV² is halved.
It stays the same.
Not quite. U depends on C, and C changed.
questions.x: Correct: A battery that stays connected keeps the voltage V fixed. The stored energy is U = ½CV². For a parallel-plate capacitor, C = ε₀A/d, so capacitance is inversely proportional to the plate separation d. Values: the separation goes from d to 2d, and V and A stay the same. Plug in: new C = ε₀A ÷ (2d) = ½ × (ε₀A/d), so C is cut in half. Then U<sub>new</sub> = ½ × (½C) × V² = ½ × U<sub>old</sub>. So the energy drops to half its original value. (The battery pulls charge back off the plates to keep V constant.) Why the others are wrong: doubling would need C to go up, but pulling plates apart lowers C; one quarter would need both C and V to halve, but the battery holds V fixed; staying the same ignores that U depends on C, which changed. Trap: Assuming the charge is fixed when the battery is still connected, when it's the voltage that is fixed.

questions.q: An object is placed 30 cm from a converging lens with focal length 10 cm. Which describes the image?
o: Virtual, upright, and larger than the object
Not quite. A virtual, upright, larger image needs the object inside the focal length.
Real, inverted, and smaller than the object
Correct: 1/i = 1/10 − 1/30 = 1/15, so i = +15 cm, real, with m = −0.5 (inverted, half size).
Real, inverted, and the same size as the object
Not quite. A same-size real image needs the object at 2f (20 cm).
Virtual, upright, and smaller than the object
Not quite. A converging lens makes virtual images only for objects inside f, and those are enlarged.
questions.x: Correct: Use the lens equation, 1/f = 1/o + 1/i. Values: f = +10 cm (converging lens) and o = 30 cm. We want i. Rearrange: 1/i = 1/f − 1/o = 1/10 − 1/30. Give them the same bottom number: 1/10 = 3/30, so 1/i = 3/30 − 1/30 = 2/30 = 1/15, and i = +15 cm. Positive means a real image, on the opposite side of the lens from the object. Magnification m = −i/o = −15 ÷ 30 = −0.5. The minus sign means inverted, and 0.5 means half the size, so smaller. The object is beyond 2f (20 cm), which always gives a real, inverted, smaller image. Why the others are wrong: virtual, upright and larger happens only when the object is inside the focal length; same size happens only when the object sits exactly at 2f, which is 20 cm; virtual, upright and smaller doesn't happen for a converging lens, whose virtual images are enlarged. Trap: Mixing up the 2f case with an object beyond 2f.

questions.q: A pipe closed at one end and open at the other has length 0.85 m. If the speed of sound is 340 m/s, what is the fundamental frequency?
o: 100 Hz
Correct: Closed pipe, so λ = 4L = 3.4 m and f = 340 ÷ 3.4 = 100 Hz.
200 Hz
Not quite. 200 Hz is the fundamental of a pipe open at both ends (v ÷ 2L).
400 Hz
Not quite. 400 Hz would need a wavelength equal to L, which fits neither pipe type.
50 Hz
Not quite. 50 Hz would fit a pipe twice as long (1.7 m).
questions.x: Correct: In a pipe closed at one end, the closed end is a node (air can't move) and the open end is an antinode (air moves most). The simplest standing wave that fits has just a quarter of a wavelength in the pipe, so λ = 4L. Values: L = 0.85 m, v = 340 m/s. Plug in: λ = 4 × 0.85 = 3.4 m. Then f = v ÷ λ = 340 ÷ 3.4 = 100 Hz. Why the others are wrong: 200 Hz is v ÷ 2L, the fundamental of a pipe open at both ends (340 ÷ 1.7 = 200); 400 Hz would need λ = L (340 ÷ 0.85 = 400), which fits no pipe; 50 Hz would belong to a pipe twice as long (1.7 m closed), or λ = 6.8 m. Trap: Using λ = 2L, which belongs to a pipe open at both ends.

questions.q: Light of wavelength 400 nm strikes a metal with work function 2.0 eV. Use hc = 1240 eV·nm. What is the maximum kinetic energy of ejected electrons?
o: 2.0 eV
Not quite. 2.0 eV is the work function, the energy needed just to free an electron.
3.1 eV
Not quite. 3.1 eV is the total photon energy, before subtracting the work function.
1.1 eV
Correct: E = 1240 ÷ 400 = 3.1 eV, then KEmax = 3.1 − 2.0 = 1.1 eV.
5.1 eV
Not quite. 5.1 eV adds the work function instead of subtracting it.
questions.x: Correct: A photon's energy goes first to pull an electron out of the metal (the work function) and the rest becomes the electron's kinetic energy. Formula: KEmax = hf − φ, and photon energy is E = hc/λ. Values: hc = 1240 eV·nm, λ = 400 nm, φ = 2.0 eV. Photon energy: E = 1240 ÷ 400 = 3.1 eV. Then KEmax = 3.1 − 2.0 = 1.1 eV. The electron pays 2.0 eV to get out and keeps the remaining 1.1 eV. Why the others are wrong: 2.0 eV is the work function, the cost to free the electron, not what is left over; 3.1 eV is the whole photon energy and forgets the cost; 5.1 eV adds the work function instead of subtracting it, which would give the electron more energy than the photon brought. Trap: Adding the work function to the photon energy instead of subtracting it.

questions.q: The Kₛₚ of AgCl is 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰. What is the equilibrium concentration of Ag⁺ in a saturated solution of AgCl that is also 0.10 M in NaCl?
o: Not quite. 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ M is the solubility in pure water, without the common ion.
Not quite. 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ is Kₛₚ itself, not a concentration.
Not quite. 1.8 × 10⁻¹¹ comes from dividing by 10 instead of by 0.10.
questions.x: Correct: Kₛₚ for AgCl is [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰. The NaCl in the solution already supplies chloride, which pushes the AgCl equilibrium back toward solid (the common-ion effect). Values: Kₛₚ = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰, [Cl⁻] = 0.10 M. The tiny amount of Cl⁻ from AgCl is negligible next to 0.10 M. Plug in: [Ag⁺] = Kₛₚ ÷ [Cl⁻] = (1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) ÷ 0.10. Dividing by 0.10 is the same as multiplying by 10, so [Ag⁺] = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 10 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ M (the exponent goes up by 1: −10 + 1 = −9). Compare pure water: √(1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ M, so the solubility is thousands of times lower here. Why the others are wrong: 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ M is the pure water answer and ignores the common ion; 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ is Kₛₚ itself, which has no units of concentration; 1.8 × 10⁻¹¹ divides by 10 instead of by 0.10. Trap: Using the pure-water solubility despite the common ion.

questions.q: Carbon dioxide has polar C=O bonds, yet the CO₂ molecule is nonpolar. Which explains this?
o: The molecule is linear, so the two bond dipoles cancel.
Correct: CO₂ is linear, so its two equal and opposite bond dipoles cancel.
The C=O bonds are actually nonpolar because carbon and oxygen have equal electronegativity.
Not quite. Oxygen is much more electronegative than carbon, so each C=O bond is polar.
The molecule is bent, which gives dipoles that cancel.
Not quite. A bent shape would leave a net dipole, as in water or SO₂.
Carbon dioxide has lone pairs on carbon that cancel the dipoles.
Not quite. The carbon in CO₂ has no lone pairs.
questions.x: Correct: A bond is polar when one atom pulls the shared electrons harder, and oxygen pulls harder than carbon, so each C=O bond has a dipole pointing toward oxygen. But a molecule is polar only if those dipoles add up to something. CO₂ is linear: O=C=O, with the two oxygens on opposite sides of the carbon. VSEPR (which spreads electron groups as far apart as possible) gives two groups around carbon and no lone pairs, so 180°. The two dipoles are equal in size and point in opposite directions, so they cancel and the net dipole is zero. Why the others are wrong: C=O bonds are polar because oxygen is much more electronegative than carbon; CO₂ isn't bent (bent molecules like water and SO₂ keep a net dipole); carbon in CO₂ has no lone pairs. Trap: Assuming polar bonds always make a polar molecule.

questions.q: In SDS-PAGE, a mixture of proteins of 15 kDa, 50 kDa, and 150 kDa is separated. Which statement is correct after the run?
o: The 15 kDa protein migrates farthest toward the anode.
Correct: SDS gives similar charge per mass, so the gel sieves by size and the smallest protein runs farthest toward the anode.
The 150 kDa protein migrates farthest toward the anode.
Not quite. Larger proteins are slowed more by the gel pores, so they migrate less.
All three proteins migrate the same distance because SDS gives them equal charge.
Not quite. Equal charge per mass doesn't mean equal distance. The gel still sieves by size.
The proteins migrate toward the cathode, with the smallest protein moving most.
Not quite. SDS-coated proteins are negative and move toward the anode, the positive electrode.
questions.x: Correct: SDS is a detergent that unfolds proteins and coats them with negative charge in proportion to their size. That leaves all of them with about the same charge per unit mass, so charge no longer separates them. In the gel, the proteins are pulled toward the positive electrode (the anode), and the gel acts like a sieve with tiny holes. Small proteins slip through the holes easily and run far. Big ones get tangled and lag behind. So the 15 kDa protein travels the farthest, the 50 kDa protein is in the middle, and the 150 kDa protein is nearest the well. Why the others are wrong: the 150 kDa protein is slowed most by the pores, not least; saying all three move the same distance mistakes equal charge density for equal speed, since the sieving still separates them; moving toward the cathode is backward, because SDS-coated proteins are negative and go to the anode. Trap: Forgetting that equal charge density means size alone decides how far a protein runs.

questions.q: Alanine is dissolved in a solution of pH 1.0. Which statement describes the predominant form of the amino acid?
o: It is a zwitterion with no net charge.
Not quite. The zwitterion dominates near the isoelectric point (about pH 6), not at pH 1.
The amino group is protonated and the carboxylate is deprotonated, with net charge −1.
Not quite. At pH 1 the carboxyl group is protonated, so the net charge can't be −1.
Both the amino group and the carboxyl group are protonated, and the net charge is +1.
Correct: At pH 1 both groups hold their H⁺, so COOH is neutral and NH₃⁺ is +1, giving net +1.
The amino group is neutral and the carboxylic acid is deprotonated, with net charge −1.
Not quite. At low pH the amine is protonated, and the net charge isn't negative.
questions.x: Correct: An amino acid has two groups that can gain or lose H⁺: the carboxyl group (pKₐ about 2.3) and the amino group (pKₐ about 9.7). Rule: if the pH is below a group's pKₐ, the group holds its H⁺; if above, it loses it. At pH 1.0, which is below both numbers, both groups hold their H⁺. The carboxyl group is COOH, which is neutral. The amino group is NH₃⁺, which is +1. Net charge: 0 + 1 = +1. The zwitterion (NH₃⁺ and COO⁻) only shows up between the two pKₐ values, around pH 6 for alanine. Why the others are wrong: the zwitterion dominates near the isoelectric point, not at pH 1; a deprotonated carboxylate with net −1 isn't possible at pH 1, where the carboxyl group is protonated; a neutral amine with a carboxylate would need a pH well above 9.7. Trap: Assuming the zwitterion dominates at any pH.

questions.q: 1-Propanol is treated with pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) in dichloromethane. What is the major organic product?
o: Propanoic acid
Not quite. Propanoic acid comes from a strong aqueous oxidant such as Jones reagent.
Propanal
Correct: PCC is a mild, water-free oxidant, so a primary alcohol stops at the aldehyde.
Propanone
Not quite. Propanone comes from oxidizing 2-propanol, a secondary alcohol.
Propene
Not quite. PCC isn't a dehydrating agent, so no alkene forms.
questions.x: Correct: Oxidizing a primary alcohol takes it first to an aldehyde, and a strong oxidant in water can push it on to a carboxylic acid. PCC (pyridinium chlorochromate) in dichloromethane is a mild oxidant used without water. With no water, the aldehyde can't form the hydrate that would be oxidized again, so the reaction stops at the aldehyde. 1-Propanol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH, becomes propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO. Why the others are wrong: propanoic acid is what you'd get from a strong aqueous oxidant like Jones reagent (chromic acid); propanone comes from oxidizing 2-propanol, a secondary alcohol, and 1-propanol is primary; propene would need a dehydrating agent, and PCC is an oxidant. Trap: Over-oxidizing a primary alcohol to the carboxylic acid when a mild oxidant is used.

questions.q: Given C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −394 kJ/mol, and CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −283 kJ/mol, what is ΔH for C(s) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g)?
o: −111 kJ/mol
Correct: Reverse the second reaction (+283) and add it to the first (−394): −111 kJ/mol.
−677 kJ/mol
Not quite. −677 adds both values without reversing the second equation.
+111 kJ/mol
Not quite. +111 has the right size but the wrong sign.
−283 kJ/mol
Not quite. −283 is the value for oxidizing CO to CO₂, not for forming CO.
questions.x: Correct: Hess's law says you can add reactions together and add their ΔH values. Our target is C + ½O₂ → CO. Reaction 1 is C + O₂ → CO₂ (ΔH = −394 kJ/mol). Reaction 2 is CO + ½O₂ → CO₂ (ΔH = −283 kJ/mol). We need CO as a product, but reaction 2 has it as a reactant. So reverse reaction 2: CO₂ → CO + ½O₂, and flip the sign of ΔH to +283 kJ/mol. Now add: C + O₂ + CO₂ → CO₂ + CO + ½O₂. Cancel the CO₂ on both sides, and cancel ½O₂ from the O₂, leaving C + ½O₂ → CO. ΔH = −394 + 283 = −111 kJ/mol. Why the others are wrong: −677 adds both values (−394 − 283) without reversing the second equation; +111 has the right size but the wrong sign; −283 is the heat for burning CO to CO₂, not for making CO. Trap: Forgetting to flip the sign of ΔH when you reverse an equation.

questions.q: The Haber process, N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), is exothermic. What is the effect of increasing the temperature on the equilibrium constant K and the equilibrium yield of NH₃?
o: K increases, and the equilibrium yield of NH₃ increases.
Not quite. K and yield rise with temperature only for an endothermic reaction.
K decreases, and the equilibrium yield of NH₃ decreases.
Correct: Heat acts as a product, so more heat shifts toward reactants. K and the NH₃ yield both decrease.
K is unchanged, and the equilibrium yield of NH₃ decreases.
Not quite. K depends on temperature, so it changes when T changes.
K decreases, and the equilibrium yield of NH₃ increases.
Not quite. A smaller K means less product at equilibrium, not more.
questions.x: Correct: Treat heat as a product of an exothermic reaction: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ + heat. Raising the temperature is like adding more product, so by Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts left, toward the reactants. That means less NH₃ at equilibrium, so the yield falls. The equilibrium constant K = [NH₃]² ÷ ([N₂][H₂]³) also gets smaller, because the product concentrations in the top of that fraction shrink. K depends on temperature (and only on temperature), so when T changes, K changes. For an exothermic reaction, K decreases as T rises. This is the tradeoff in the real Haber process: hot gives faster rates but a lower yield. Why the others are wrong: K and yield both rising would happen for an endothermic reaction; K unchanged is wrong because K changes whenever T changes; K falling while yield rises can't both be true, since a smaller K means less product at equilibrium. Trap: Thinking K stays constant when temperature changes.

questions.q: A person rubs her elbow immediately after striking it, and the pain lessens. According to the gate control theory of pain, this occurs because:
o: rubbing destroys the nociceptors in the elbow so pain signals can no longer be generated or transmitted.
Not quite. Rubbing doesn't destroy nociceptors. It changes how their signals are passed on.
rubbing triggers release of cortisol, which blocks transmission along C fibers.
Not quite. Cortisol is a slow hormone and can't explain relief that happens right away.
activation of large-diameter touch fibers excites inhibitory interneurons that reduce pain transmission in the spinal cord.
Correct: Touch fibers excite inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord, which closes the gate on pain signals.
touch fibers travel to the thalamus faster than pain fibers and cancel the pain signals in the cortex.
Not quite. The gate is in the spinal cord, before the thalamus and cortex.
questions.x: Correct: Gate control theory says pain signals have to pass a 'gate' in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord before going up to the brain. Pain travels on small, slow fibers. Touch travels on large-diameter fibers (A-β fibers). When you rub your elbow, the touch fibers fire and excite inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord, which are cells that quiet other cells. Those interneurons turn down the relay of the pain signal, so the gate closes and the pain feels less. Why the others are wrong: rubbing doesn't destroy nociceptors (the pain-sensing nerve endings), it only changes how their signals are passed along; cortisol is a slow hormone, so it can't explain relief that happens right away; the gate sits in the spinal cord, before the thalamus and cortex, so touch signals don't cancel pain in the cortex. Trap: Putting the pain-blocking step in the brain instead of in the spinal cord.

questions.q: In a signal detection experiment, an observer adopts a stricter criterion for reporting that a faint tone was present, while sensitivity does not change. Compared with before, the observer will have:
o: more hits and more false alarms, with no change in sensitivity.
Not quite. More hits and more false alarms comes from a more lenient criterion, not a stricter one.
fewer hits and more false alarms, with no change in sensitivity.
Not quite. A criterion shift moves hits and false alarms in the same direction, not opposite ways.
fewer hits and fewer false alarms, with no change in sensitivity.
Correct: A stricter criterion makes the observer say yes less often, lowering hits and false alarms with sensitivity unchanged.
more hits and fewer false alarms, with no change in sensitivity.
Not quite. More hits with fewer false alarms would need better sensitivity, which didn't change.
questions.x: Correct: In signal detection, an observer decides 'yes, I heard the tone' or 'no' using a criterion, which is how much evidence they need before saying yes. Sensitivity (d') is how well they can tell the tone from the background noise, and here it does not change. A stricter criterion means they demand more evidence before saying yes, so they say yes less often overall. That lowers hits (saying yes when the tone is there) and also lowers false alarms (saying yes when there's no tone). Both go down together. Why the others are wrong: more hits and more false alarms is what a lenient criterion does, the opposite shift; fewer hits and more false alarms moves the two rates in opposite directions, which a criterion shift alone can't do; more hits with fewer false alarms would mean the observer got better at telling tone from noise, which is a rise in sensitivity. Trap: Believing a criterion shift trades hits for false alarms in opposite directions.

questions.q: A patient with bilateral hippocampal damage cannot recall meeting her doctor earlier in the day but improves from day to day on a mirror-tracing task without any memory of having practiced. These findings indicate that:
o: explicit and procedural memory share a single system located in the hippocampus and temporal lobes.
Not quite. If one hippocampal system served both, her skill learning would be lost too.
procedural memory depends on systems other than those needed for new explicit memories.
Correct: Skill learning survived while new explicit memories failed, so procedural memory uses other systems like the basal ganglia and cerebellum.
the patient has retrograde amnesia only, with intact formation of new memories.
Not quite. She can't form new memories, which is anterograde amnesia. Retrograde is loss of old memories.
procedural memories are stored in Wernicke's area and retrieved there.
Not quite. Wernicke's area is for understanding language, not storing skills.
questions.x: Correct: Explicit memory is facts and events you can consciously recall, like meeting the doctor this morning. Procedural memory is skills and habits, like tracing a shape in a mirror. The patient can't make new explicit memories, because her hippocampus (the brain area that files new facts and events) is damaged on both sides. Yet she gets better at mirror tracing each day. That is a dissociation: one kind of memory is lost while another is fine. It tells us skill learning depends on other brain systems, mainly the basal ganglia and cerebellum. Why the others are wrong: if both memory types shared one system in the hippocampus, the skill learning would be wiped out too; she can't form new memories, which is anterograde amnesia, while retrograde amnesia is losing old memories; Wernicke's area handles understanding language, not storing skills. Trap: Assuming every kind of memory depends on the hippocampus.

questions.q: A 6-year-old watches water poured from a short, wide glass into a tall, thin glass and says that the tall glass now holds more water. According to Piaget, this child is most likely in the:
o: preoperational stage.
Correct: Judging by one dimension (height) and failing to conserve volume is typical of the preoperational stage.
sensorimotor stage.
Not quite. The sensorimotor stage is birth to about age 2, when object permanence develops.
concrete operational stage.
Not quite. Concrete operational children understand conservation, so they'd say the amounts are equal.
formal operational stage.
Not quite. The formal operational stage is about abstract, hypothetical reasoning in adolescence.
questions.x: Correct: The key clue is the water. Seeing the same amount of water poured into a taller, thinner glass and saying it now holds more means the child hasn't learned conservation, the idea that an amount stays the same when its looks change. Piaget said this fits the preoperational stage (about ages 2 to 7). Kids at this stage focus on one feature at a time, here height, and ignore the width. A 6-year-old fits that age range too. Why the others are wrong: the sensorimotor stage is birth to about 2, when babies learn through senses and movement and develop object permanence; the concrete operational stage (about 7 to 11) is when children do understand conservation, so this child would say the amounts are equal; the formal operational stage is adolescence, with abstract and hypothetical thinking. Trap: Picking the stage by age alone without using the conservation clue.

questions.q: A man feels his heart pounding and his hands trembling after a near-collision, and he concludes that he must be afraid. This sequence is most consistent with:
o: the Cannon-Bard theory of emotion.
Not quite. Cannon-Bard says arousal and feeling happen at the same time and independently, which isn't the order here.
the Yerkes-Dodson law.
Not quite. Yerkes-Dodson links arousal to performance, not to how emotions start.
the James-Lange theory of emotion.
Correct: James-Lange says noticing bodily arousal produces the emotion. Here the pounding heart comes first, then the label 'afraid'.
the opponent-process theory of emotion.
Not quite. Opponent-process is about aftereffects of emotions, not how they begin.
questions.x: Correct: Look at the order in the story. First his heart pounds and his hands tremble (body arousal). Then he thinks, 'I must be afraid.' That is the James-Lange theory: the emotion comes from noticing your own body's reactions. You don't tremble because you're scared. You're scared because you notice you're trembling. Why the others are wrong: the Cannon-Bard theory says the body response and the feeling happen at the same time and separately, but here the feeling is figured out after noticing the body; the Yerkes-Dodson law is about how arousal affects performance (best at a medium level), not where an emotion comes from; opponent-process theory is about how an emotion is followed by an opposite aftereffect, like relief after fear, not how an emotion starts. Trap: Choosing a better-known multi-part theory when the story is just body arousal first, then the feeling.

questions.q: In a twin study of a personality trait, the twin correlation is r = 0.50 for monozygotic pairs and r = 0.20 for dizygotic pairs. Using Falconer's formula, heritability = 2 × (r<sub>MZ</sub> - r<sub>DZ</sub>), the estimated heritability is:
o: Not quite. 0.30 is the difference without multiplying by 2.
Not quite. 0.70 adds 0.50 and 0.20, but the formula subtracts them before doubling.
Not quite. 1.00 would mean the trait is entirely genetic, and these data don't show that.
questions.x: Correct: Falconer's formula is heritability = 2 × (r<sub>MZ</sub> − r<sub>DZ</sub>). Here r<sub>MZ</sub> = 0.50 is the trait correlation in monozygotic (identical) twins, and r<sub>DZ</sub> = 0.20 is the correlation in dizygotic (fraternal) twins. Plug in: 2 × (0.50 − 0.20). Parentheses first: 0.50 − 0.20 = 0.30. Then 2 × 0.30 = 0.60. So the estimated heritability is 0.60, meaning about 60% of the differences between people in this trait are linked to genetic differences. Identical twins share about 100% of their genes and fraternal twins about 50%, which is why the difference gets doubled. Why the others are wrong: 0.30 is the difference without the factor of 2; 0.70 adds the two correlations (0.50 + 0.20), but the formula subtracts them; 1.00 would mean all differences come from genes, and these twin correlations don't show that. Trap: Leaving out the factor of 2.

questions.q: A gambler keeps pulling a slot machine lever even though wins are unpredictable and sporadic. Which reinforcement schedule is operating, and why does it produce this pattern?
o: Fixed ratio, which yields a pause after each reinforcement and then a rapid burst of responding.
Not quite. Fixed ratio pays after a set number of responses, but slot wins come after an unpredictable number.
Variable interval, which yields a slow and steady rate of responding with moderate extinction resistance.
Not quite. Variable interval depends on elapsed time, not on the number of pulls.
Variable ratio, which yields a high and steady rate of responding that is resistant to extinction.
Correct: Wins after an unpredictable number of pulls make a variable ratio schedule, which gives high steady responding that resists extinction.
Fixed interval, which yields a scalloped pattern of responding that accelerates before reinforcement.
Not quite. Fixed interval depends on elapsed time, and slot wins don't.
questions.x: Correct: Reinforcement schedules are rules for when a behavior gets rewarded. Ratio schedules count responses (pulls), and interval schedules count time. On a slot machine, you get a win after an unpredictable number of pulls, so it is a variable ratio schedule. Because you can never tell which pull will pay, you keep pulling at a high, steady rate with no pause, and the behavior is very resistant to extinction (it takes a long time to stop when the rewards stop). Why the others are wrong: fixed ratio pays off after a set number of responses and creates a pause after each reward, but slot wins aren't on a fixed count; variable interval depends on unpredictable time passing, not number of pulls, and gives a slow steady rate; fixed interval pays the first response after a set time and makes a scalloped pattern where responding speeds up as the time nears. Trap: Matching the schedule by name instead of asking whether payoff depends on responses or on time.

questions.q: A viewer who is not interested in the topic of an advertisement for a car is persuaded because the commercial features an attractive celebrity. According to the elaboration likelihood model, this is an example of:
o: the central route to persuasion, which relies on careful evaluation of the argument.
Not quite. The central route needs careful thought about the arguments, and this viewer isn't interested.
cognitive dissonance reduction, in which attitudes change to match behavior.
Not quite. Dissonance reduction means changing an attitude to match behavior, and nothing like that is described.
the peripheral route to persuasion, which relies on superficial cues.
Correct: With low interest, a superficial cue like an attractive celebrity persuades, which is the peripheral route.
the sleeper effect, in which a message persuades more after the source is forgotten.
Not quite. The sleeper effect is persuasion growing over time as the source is forgotten.
questions.x: Correct: The elaboration likelihood model says there are two routes to persuasion. The central route is for people who care and think hard, so they weigh how good the arguments are. The peripheral route is for people who aren't paying attention or aren't interested, so they are swayed by surface cues like how attractive, famous, or likable the speaker is. This viewer isn't interested in the car, and the thing that persuades the viewer is the attractive celebrity, not facts about the car. That is the peripheral route. Why the others are wrong: the central route needs careful evaluation of the argument, and the viewer isn't doing that; cognitive dissonance reduction is changing an attitude to match your behavior after feeling inconsistent, and nothing like that is described; the sleeper effect is when a message becomes more persuasive over time as people forget a not-so-credible source, which isn't the case here. Trap: Calling a celebrity endorsement the central route because it's memorable.

questions.q: An experienced pianist plays a well-rehearsed piece. Her performance is likely to be best when she plays in front of a large audience, compared with when she is alone. This is an example of:
o: social facilitation, because an audience raises arousal and enhances well-learned tasks.
Correct: An audience raises arousal, which strengthens the dominant response, and for a well-learned piece that improves performance.
social loafing, because individual effort is reduced when people work together in groups.
Not quite. Social loafing is reduced effort when work is pooled in a group, which isn't the situation.
groupthink, because the audience suppresses dissent in favor of consensus.
Not quite. Groupthink is poor group decision-making under pressure for agreement, not performance in front of an audience.
deindividuation, because the audience provides anonymity and reduces self-awareness.
Not quite. Deindividuation needs anonymity, and the pianist is plainly identifiable.
questions.x: Correct: Social facilitation means that other people being around us changes how well we perform. An audience raises our arousal (we feel more energized and alert). Higher arousal strengthens the dominant response, which is whatever we do most easily or best. For a skill the person has practiced a lot, like an experienced pianist playing a well-rehearsed piece, the dominant response is the correct one, so performance gets better. For a new or hard task the dominant response is often wrong, so an audience can make it worse. Why the others are wrong: social loafing is people putting in less effort when their work is pooled in a group, and the pianist is performing alone; groupthink is a group wanting agreement so much that it makes poor decisions, and an audience isn't making a decision; deindividuation is losing self-awareness in a crowd when you feel anonymous, but a pianist on stage is clearly identifiable. Trap: Predicting that an audience always hurts performance, forgetting that it depends on how well the task is learned.

questions.q: A teenager changes her goals and the way she dresses after noticing that her peers regard her as shy and unreliable. This is the best illustration of:
o: the self-serving bias.
Not quite. Self-serving bias is crediting yourself for success and blaming outside causes for failure.
Cooley's looking-glass self.
Correct: Her self-concept changed based on how she imagines peers see and judge her, which is the looking-glass self.
the actual self matching the ideal self.
Not quite. The story doesn't describe her actual self matching her ideal self.
the spotlight effect.
Not quite. The spotlight effect is overestimating how much others notice us, not building a self-concept.
questions.x: Correct: The looking-glass self, from Charles Cooley, says we build our sense of who we are by imagining how other people see us and judge us, then reacting to that. The teenager noticed that her peers think she is shy and unreliable, and she changed her goals and the way she dresses in response. Her self-concept moved because of what she thinks others think of her. Why the others are wrong: the self-serving bias is crediting yourself for successes and blaming outside causes for failures, which isn't what she's doing; the actual self matching the ideal self would mean who you are lines up with who you want to be, and the story doesn't say this; the spotlight effect is overestimating how much other people notice us, which is about attention and not about how the self-concept is formed. Trap: Picking the self-concept term that sounds closest without checking where the change came from.

questions.q: A driver who is cut off in traffic concludes that the other driver is selfish and reckless. When the same person later cuts off another car, he explains that he was late for an important meeting. This pattern illustrates:
o: the self-serving bias exclusively, in which people credit successes to themselves and failures to others.
Not quite. Self-serving bias concerns success and failure, not the different explanations we give for our own and others' behavior.
the actor-observer bias, including the fundamental attribution error when judging others.
Correct: He blames others' behavior on character but his own on the situation, which is the actor-observer difference.
the just-world hypothesis, in which people believe outcomes are deserved.
Not quite. The just-world hypothesis is believing people get what they deserve, which isn't shown here.
the halo effect, in which one positive trait colors judgments of other traits.
Not quite. The halo effect is when one positive trait colors judgments of other traits.
questions.x: Correct: When the driver is cut off, he explains the other driver's act by their character: selfish and reckless. When he does the same thing himself, he explains it by the situation: he was late for a meeting. That's the actor-observer bias. As the observer we blame the person's disposition, and as the actor we blame the situation. Blaming others' behavior too much on their character is the fundamental attribution error. Why the others are wrong: the self-serving bias is about taking credit for successes and blaming others or circumstances for failures, and this story is about two different people's explanations, not success and failure; the just-world hypothesis is the belief that people get what they deserve, which isn't shown here; the halo effect is one positive trait coloring how we see other traits, such as assuming an attractive person is also smart. Trap: Picking the self-serving bias because the person excuses his own behavior.

questions.q: A researcher recruits adults who volunteer for a new therapy program and compares them with adults who did not volunteer, finding that the volunteers have better outcomes at 6 months. The most serious threat to the validity of concluding that the therapy caused the improvement is:
o: a ceiling effect on all outcome measures, which compresses variability in the scores.
Not quite. Nothing in the description suggests scores bunched at the top of the scale.
observer drift in blinded raters, which gradually changes how outcomes are scored.
Not quite. Observer drift is a measurement issue that the description doesn't mention.
selection bias, because volunteers may differ in motivation from non-volunteers.
Correct: Without random assignment, volunteers may differ in motivation, which confounds the effect of therapy.
the Hawthorne effect in the non-volunteer group, who changed behavior because they were observed.
Not quite. Non-volunteers weren't enrolled, so they wouldn't be reacting to being observed.
questions.x: Correct: The researcher compared people who chose to join the program with people who didn't. Nobody was randomly assigned. People who volunteer for therapy may be more motivated, more hopeful, or have more support, and those traits could improve their outcomes by themselves. That is selection bias, where the groups were different from the start. So we can't tell whether therapy or the type of person caused the better results. Random assignment would solve it. Why the others are wrong: a ceiling effect is when scores bunch up at the top of a scale, and nothing in the description suggests that; observer drift is when raters slowly change how they score, a measurement issue that isn't mentioned; the Hawthorne effect is when people change behavior because they know they're being watched, but non-volunteers weren't enrolled so they wouldn't have that reaction. Trap: Overlooking that people choosing their own group prevents a cause-and-effect conclusion.

questions.q: In a country with a high birth rate that has begun to improve sanitation and medical care, death rates fall while birth rates remain high. According to the demographic transition model, the population will most likely:
o: grow rapidly.
Correct: Falling death rates with persistently high birth rates (stage 2) gives a large natural increase and rapid growth.
shrink rapidly.
Not quite. Shrinking needs deaths to exceed births, and here births are high while deaths fall.
remain stable.
Not quite. Stability comes when both rates are low and nearly equal (stage 4), which hasn't happened yet.
age rapidly with few children.
Not quite. Rapid aging comes from low birth rates, but this country's birth rates are still high.
questions.x: Correct: The demographic transition model describes how birth and death rates change as a country develops. Stage 1 has high birth and high death rates, so population is steady. In stage 2, which this country is in, sanitation and medical care improve, so death rates fall quickly. But birth rates stay high because habits and family size take longer to change. When births are far higher than deaths, there is a big natural increase, so the population grows rapidly. Why the others are wrong: shrinking would need deaths to exceed births, which isn't happening while births stay high and deaths fall; staying stable happens when both rates are low and nearly equal (stage 4), which this country hasn't reached; rapid aging with few children comes from low birth rates, but birth rates here are still high. Trap: Mixing up the early stage of the transition with the late stage.

questions.q: A study shows that Black women in the United States experience worse maternal outcomes than would be expected by considering race alone or gender alone. Which concept best describes the framework used to explain this?
o: Anomie, in which social norms fail to regulate behavior during rapid social change.
Not quite. Anomie means normlessness during social change, not overlapping identities.
Meritocracy, in which rewards are distributed according to individual effort.
Not quite. Meritocracy is about rewards by effort and doesn't explain outcomes tied to identity.
Assimilation, in which a minority group adopts the dominant culture.
Not quite. Assimilation is a minority group adopting the dominant culture, not a theory of combined disadvantage.
Intersectionality, the overlap of social identities that yields distinct disadvantage.
Correct: Intersectionality says overlapping identities like race and gender combine to create distinct disadvantage.
questions.x: Correct: The finding is that Black women have worse maternal outcomes than you'd predict by looking at race alone or gender alone. That means being both Black and a woman combines into a distinct kind of disadvantage, not just two separate ones added up. This idea is called intersectionality: overlapping social identities, like race and gender, create unique experiences of advantage or disadvantage. Why the others are wrong: anomie is a state of normlessness when social norms stop guiding behavior, often during rapid change, and it isn't about overlapping identities; meritocracy is the idea that rewards go to people based on talent and effort, which can't explain outcomes tied to identity; assimilation is when a minority group takes on the dominant culture, which describes culture adoption and not combined disadvantage. Trap: Treating the effects of race and gender as simply added together.

questions.q: A sociologist studies how a group of hospital nurses and patients come to define a 'good patient' through their daily conversations, gestures, and labels. Which perspective is she using?
o: Functionalism, which views society as interdependent parts
Not quite. Functionalism studies how large social structures keep society stable, not daily interactions.
Conflict theory, which views society as competition over scarce resources
Not quite. Conflict theory is about power and competition among groups, which isn't the focus here.
Symbolic interactionism
Correct: Symbolic interactionism studies how shared meanings are made through face-to-face interaction and symbols.
Rational choice theory, which views behavior as cost-benefit calculation
Not quite. Rational choice theory looks at cost-benefit calculations, not how meanings are created.
questions.x: Correct: The sociologist is looking at how nurses and patients create the meaning of a 'good patient' through everyday conversations, gestures, and labels. Studying how people build shared meanings face to face, using symbols such as words and gestures, is symbolic interactionism. It is a micro-level approach, looking at small-scale interactions between people. Why the others are wrong: functionalism looks at how the parts of society (like institutions) work together to keep society stable, which is a big-picture view; conflict theory looks at power struggles and competition between groups over scarce resources, and nothing in the story is about power or competition; rational choice theory says people weigh costs and benefits to get the most for themselves, but the question is about how meanings are created, not how choices are weighed. Trap: Using a big-picture theory for a small-scale study of how people interact.
